name: A Coruña
fact: A Coruña's Tower of Hercules is the oldest Roman lighthouse still in use, guiding ships on Spain's Atlantic coast.

name: Abalone
fact: Abalone shells are lined with iridescent mother-of-pearl and have a row of holes through which the animal breathes.

name: Abidjan
fact: Abidjan, Ivory Coast's economic capital, became a major Atlantic port in the early 1950s when the Vridi Canal was cut through to its lagoon.

name: Abrolhos Bank
fact: The Abrolhos Bank off Brazil holds the largest coral reefs in the South Atlantic, built into mushroom-shaped pillars found nowhere else.

name: Abyssal grenadier
fact: The abyssal grenadier roams abyssal plains worldwide between about 2,000 and 5,000 metres, following its nose to carcasses that sink from above.

name: Abyssobrotula
fact: Abyssobrotula galatheae is a pale cusk-eel with tiny eyes, recorded from 8,370 metres in the Puerto Rico Trench in 1970, a depth record that stood for decades.

name: Acanthephyra shrimp
fact: Deep-sea Acanthephyra shrimp are blood-red, which looks black in the depths, and spit a cloud of glowing blue liquid into a predator's face.

name: Achilles tang
fact: The Achilles tang is a black surgeonfish with a teardrop of bright orange around its tail blade, living in the surge zone of Pacific reefs.

name: Acropora
fact: Acropora is the largest genus of reef-building corals, including the staghorn and table corals, and is among the first to bleach when the water warms.

name: Adélie penguin
fact: Adélie penguins eat mostly krill, and the pink stains of their guano show up from space, letting scientists count colonies by satellite.

name: Admiral Graf Spee
fact: The German pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spee was scuttled by its own crew off Montevideo in December 1939 after the Battle of the River Plate.

name: Adriatic Sea
fact: The Adriatic Sea separates Italy from the Balkans and is the arm of the Mediterranean on which Venice was built.

name: Adriatic trout
fact: The Adriatic, or softmouth, trout of the Balkans has a soft fleshy snout unlike any other trout and lives in a few rivers draining to the Adriatic.

name: Aegean Sea
fact: The Aegean Sea between Greece and Turkey is scattered with hundreds of islands, and its ancient trade routes made it the cradle of Greek civilisation.

name: African lungfish
fact: When its pool dries up the African lungfish burrows into mud, wraps itself in a mucus cocoon and breathes air for months, even years, until rain returns.

name: African penguin
fact: The African penguin of South Africa and Namibia was declared critically endangered in 2024 as its sardine and anchovy prey dwindled.

name: African sharptooth catfish
fact: The African sharptooth catfish can breathe air and crawl between pools, and is farmed widely across Africa and Asia as a cheap protein.

name: African tigerfish
fact: The African tigerfish has been filmed leaping from the water to snatch swallows out of the air, the first freshwater fish confirmed to catch birds in flight.

name: Aggregating anemone
fact: Aggregating anemones clone themselves by splitting in two, forming dense carpets where rival clone armies fight along their borders.

name: Agulhas Current
fact: The Agulhas Current races south along the east coast of South Africa and, meeting opposing winds, produces some of the world's most dangerous rogue waves.

name: Akademik Mstislav Keldysh
fact: The Russian research ship Akademik Mstislav Keldysh carries the Mir submersibles and appears as itself in the opening scenes of the film Titanic.

name: Akagi
fact: The Japanese carrier Akagi, flagship of the Pearl Harbor attack, was sunk at Midway in 1942 and found in 2019 more than 5,000 metres down.

name: Akiami paste shrimp
fact: The thumbnail-sized Akiami paste shrimp is caught in bigger tonnages than any other shrimp species, mostly for shrimp paste and dried shrimp in Asia.

name: Alaska Current
fact: The Alaska Current carries relatively warm water anticlockwise around the Gulf of Alaska, keeping the coast of the Alaska panhandle milder and wetter.

name: Alaska pollock
fact: Alaska pollock is the most-caught fish in the United States and the fish inside most fish fingers, fast-food fish sandwiches and surimi crab sticks.

name: Albacore
fact: Albacore, the 'white tuna' of canned tuna, has the longest pectoral fins of any tuna and is served as shiro maguro in sushi bars.

name: Albatross
fact: Albatrosses lock their wings open with a special shoulder tendon and can glide for hours over the ocean without a single flap.

name: Alboran Sea
fact: The Alboran Sea is the westernmost part of the Mediterranean, just inside the Strait of Gibraltar, where Atlantic water first flows in.

name: Aldabra Atoll
fact: Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles is one of the largest raised coral atolls in the world and home to about 100,000 giant tortoises.

name: Aleutian Islands
fact: The Aleutian Islands are a chain of volcanic islands stretching about 1,900 kilometres west from Alaska towards Russia.

name: Aleutian Trench
fact: The Aleutian Trench curves for about 3,400 kilometres south of Alaska's Aleutian Islands and reaches more than 7,600 metres deep.

name: Alewife
fact: The alewife is a small herring that migrates from the sea into rivers to spawn, and landlocked populations invaded the Great Lakes through canals.

name: Algae octopus
fact: The algae octopus disguises itself as a shell overgrown with weed and can walk away on two arms while holding the other six in a ball.

name: Aliwal Shoal
fact: Aliwal Shoal off South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal coast is famous for baited dives with tiger sharks and the winter gathering of ragged-tooth sharks.

name: Allard's clownfish
fact: Allard's clownfish is a dark anemonefish with two white bars and a yellow tail found only off East Africa, from Kenya to South Africa.

name: Alligator gar
fact: The alligator gar can grow well over 2 metres long and gulps air at the surface through a swim bladder that works like a lung.

name: Alligator pipefish
fact: The alligator pipefish drifts among seagrass and floating weed in the Indo-Pacific and has a prehensile tail with no tail fin at all.

name: Alvin
fact: Alvin is the US deep-diving submersible that explored the wreck of the Titanic in 1986 and found the first hydrothermal vent communities in 1977.

name: Alvinocaris shrimp
fact: Alvinocaris shrimp were among the first animals described from the Galápagos Rift vents after their discovery in 1977, scavenging among tube worms and clams.

name: Amazon Reef
fact: The Amazon Reef was only fully described in 2016, a reef system hidden under the muddy plume of the Amazon River where few thought reefs could grow.

name: Amazon river dolphin
fact: The Amazon river dolphin turns pink with age and has an unfused neck that lets it turn its head to hunt among flooded trees.

name: American bullfrog
fact: The American bullfrog, farmed for frogs' legs, has invaded ponds across Europe, Asia and the western USA, eating anything that fits in its mouth.

name: American crocodile
fact: American crocodiles live in coastal mangroves and lagoons from Florida to Peru and have salt glands that let them tolerate the sea.

name: American eel
fact: The American eel grows up in rivers from Greenland to Brazil and returns to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, like its European cousin.

name: American lobster
fact: The American lobster is the heaviest crustacean ever recorded, with a 20-kilogram giant caught off Nova Scotia in 1977.

name: American plaice
fact: The American plaice, called the long rough dab in Europe, is a cold-water flatfish with a large mouth that lives on both sides of the North Atlantic.

name: American shad
fact: American shad live at sea and surge up east-coast rivers each spring to spawn, and the shad is the official state fish of Connecticut.

name: Ammonite
fact: Ammonites were coiled-shelled relatives of squid that filled the seas for over 300 million years and vanished with the dinosaurs.

name: Amphipod
fact: Scavenging amphipods swarm onto any bait lowered to the floor of the Mariana Trench within minutes, even at the very bottom of the Challenger Deep.

name: Amundsen Sea
fact: The Amundsen Sea off West Antarctica is named after the Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen and is where the fast-melting Thwaites Glacier flows into the sea.

name: Anchovy
fact: Anchovies swim with their mouths wide open to sieve plankton with their gill rakers, and the Peruvian anchoveta is the most heavily fished species on Earth.

name: Andrea Doria
fact: The Italian liner Andrea Doria sank in 1956 after colliding with the Stockholm off Nantucket, and its wreck at about 73 metres is called the Mount Everest of wreck diving.

name: Andrews' beaked whale
fact: Andrews' beaked whale is known almost entirely from strandings in Australia and New Zealand and is named after explorer Roy Chapman Andrews.

name: Andros Barrier Reef
fact: The Andros Barrier Reef in the Bahamas runs about 190 kilometres and drops away into the Tongue of the Ocean, a deep ocean trench.

name: Anemone porcelain crab
fact: The spotted porcelain crab lives among the tentacles of large sea anemones, filtering plankton from the water with its feathery mouthparts.

name: Anemone shrimp
fact: The glass anemone shrimp is transparent apart from a few white and orange spots, and lives unharmed among the stinging tentacles of its host anemone.

name: Angel shark
fact: The angel shark is a flattened ambush predator that buries itself in sand for days, then snaps up passing fish in a tenth of a second.

name: Angelfish
fact: Marine angelfish are among the most colourful reef fish, and many change their pattern completely as they grow from juvenile to adult.

name: Anglerfish
fact: The female deep-sea anglerfish dangles a glowing lure of bacteria in front of her mouth, and in some species the tiny male fuses onto her body for life.

name: Angular roughshark
fact: The angular roughshark has tall sail-like dorsal fins and a stocky, triangular body, and lives on muddy slopes down to around 700 metres.

name: Annulated sea snake
fact: The annulated sea snake can take in oxygen through a network of blood vessels on top of its head, which works a little like a snorkel.

name: Anomalocaris
fact: Anomalocaris was the top predator of the Cambrian seas about 500 million years ago, a metre-long hunter with grasping front limbs and a circular mouth.

name: Antarctic Circumpolar Current
fact: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current circles the whole of Antarctica unbroken by land and is the largest ocean current on Earth, carrying more water than any other.

name: Antarctic fur seal
fact: Antarctic fur seals were nearly wiped out by 19th-century sealers but now breed by the millions on South Georgia.

name: Antarctic minke whale
fact: Antarctic minke whales live among the pack ice and were the main target of Japan's so-called scientific whaling in the Southern Ocean.

name: Antarctic petrel
fact: The Antarctic petrel breeds in huge colonies on inland Antarctic mountains, some about 200 kilometres from the open sea.

name: Antarctic prion
fact: The Antarctic prion filters krill through comb-like plates in its bill, like a tiny flying baleen whale, which is why sailors called prions whalebirds.

name: Antarctic silverfish
fact: The Antarctic silverfish is the key fish of the Antarctic food web, eating krill and copepods and in turn feeding penguins, seals and toothfish.

name: Antarctic toothfish
fact: The Antarctic toothfish grows to 2 metres in the Ross Sea, and its blood carries antifreeze proteins that stop ice crystals forming.

name: Anthias
fact: Anthias are the small orange fish that shimmer in clouds above Indo-Pacific reefs, each male guarding a harem of females.

name: Antilles Current
fact: The Antilles Current flows north-west along the outer edge of the Caribbean islands and joins the Florida Current to form the Gulf Stream.

name: Apache trout
fact: The Apache trout is found only in the White Mountains of Arizona and is the official state fish of Arizona.

name: Apo Reef
fact: Apo Reef off Mindoro in the Philippines is the largest atoll-like reef in the country and is often described as the second-largest contiguous coral reef in the world.

name: ARA San Juan
fact: The Argentine submarine ARA San Juan vanished in November 2017 with 44 crew and was found a year later about 900 metres down in the South Atlantic.

name: Arabian Picasso triggerfish
fact: The Arabian Picasso triggerfish, with its painted-on stripes, is found only in the Red Sea and the seas around Arabia.

name: Araguaian river dolphin
fact: The Araguaian river dolphin of Brazil was described in 2014, the first new river dolphin species recognised in almost a century.

name: Arapaima
fact: The arapaima of the Amazon must surface regularly to gulp air and has been verified at just over 3 metres long.

name: Archelon
fact: Archelon was the largest turtle ever, about 4 metres long, and swam the inland sea of Cretaceous North America.

name: Archerfish
fact: Archerfish shoot down insects with a jet of water spat from the mouth, correcting for the bending of light at the surface, and will also leap out to grab prey.

name: Archimède
fact: The French bathyscaphe Archimède dived to about 9,500 metres in the Kuril Trench in 1962 and later explored the Mid-Atlantic Ridge in Project FAMOUS.

name: Arctic char
fact: Arctic char live further north than any other freshwater fish, and sea-run char feed in Arctic coastal waters each summer.

name: Arctic cod
fact: Arctic cod carry antifreeze proteins in their blood and live right under the sea ice, feeding seals, whales and seabirds.

name: Arctic skate
fact: The Arctic skate lives on deep, cold seabeds across the Arctic basin and lays its eggs in tough leathery cases.

name: Arctic tern
fact: The Arctic tern flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back each year, the longest migration of any animal, around 70,000 kilometres or more.

name: Argentine hake
fact: The Argentine hake is the most important fish of Argentina's fisheries, trawled over the Patagonian shelf.

name: Argentine shortfin squid
fact: Hundreds of jigging boats light up the night off Argentina to catch this squid, one of the most heavily fished squid species on Earth.

name: Argonaut
fact: The female argonaut, an octopus, secretes a thin, papery shell that she uses as a floating egg case and buoyancy aid.

name: Arnoux's beaked whale
fact: Arnoux's beaked whale lives in the cold Southern Ocean and has been seen diving beneath Antarctic sea ice.

name: Arowana
fact: Arowanas can breathe air using their swim bladder and are famous for leaping out of the water to snatch insects from overhanging branches.

name: Arrow crab
fact: The arrow crab of Caribbean reefs has spindly legs and a pointed head, and is kept in aquariums to eat bristle worms.

name: Arrow worm
fact: Arrow worms are glassy, torpedo-shaped predators of the plankton that grab copepods with hooked spines and a venom like that of pufferfish.

name: Arrowtooth flounder
fact: The arrowtooth flounder is the most abundant groundfish in the Gulf of Alaska, but an enzyme turns its flesh to mush when cooked, so it was long discarded.

name: Ascension Island
fact: Ascension Island is a volcanic island in the mid-Atlantic to which green turtles swim about 2,000 kilometres from Brazil to nest on its beaches.

name: Asian carp
fact: Asian carp, a group of imported Chinese carp species, have overrun the Mississippi basin, and electric barriers try to keep them out of the Great Lakes.

name: Asian clam
fact: The Asian clam has spread through rivers across North America, South America and Europe and fouls the cooling systems of power stations.

name: Asian shore crab
fact: The Asian shore crab turned up in New Jersey in 1988 and is now the most common crab on many rocky shores from Maine to North Carolina.

name: Asian tiger shrimp
fact: The Asian tiger shrimp, a farmed prawn up to 30 centimetres long, has escaped into the Gulf of Mexico and the south-eastern US coast.

name: Atlantic blue tang
fact: The Atlantic blue tang is a Caribbean surgeonfish that is bright yellow as a juvenile and turns deep blue as it grows.

name: Atlantic bonito
fact: The Atlantic bonito is a fast, striped, tuna-like schooling fish of the Atlantic and Mediterranean, eaten salted or grilled in Turkey as palamut.

name: Atlantic croaker
fact: The Atlantic croaker croaks by rapidly contracting muscles against its swim bladder, loudly enough to be heard when it is hauled into a boat.

name: Atlantic halibut
fact: Atlantic halibut can live for 50 years and females take about 10 years to mature, so the species is easily overfished.

name: Atlantic horse mackerel
fact: The Atlantic horse mackerel is a schooling jack of the North Sea and eastern Atlantic with a line of bony scutes along its side.

name: Atlantic humpback dolphin
fact: The Atlantic humpback dolphin lives in estuaries and shallow coasts of West Africa and is critically endangered, with fewer than 3,000 left.

name: Atlantic mackerel
fact: Atlantic mackerel feed on copepods and krill as they swim constantly to breathe, and are the species the British fleet catches in the largest quantity.

name: Atlantic puffin
fact: Atlantic puffins can carry a dozen or more small fish crosswise in their beaks at once and spend the winter alone far out at sea.

name: Atlantic pygmy octopus
fact: The Atlantic pygmy octopus is small enough to live inside an empty clam shell, which it pulls shut around itself with its suckers.

name: Atlantic salmon
fact: Atlantic salmon return from the sea to the river where they hatched, and unlike Pacific salmon some survive spawning and go back to sea to spawn again.

name: Atlantic sharpnose shark
fact: The Atlantic sharpnose shark is a small, common shark of the US Atlantic and Gulf coasts, often the first shark a beach angler catches.

name: Atlantic silverside
fact: The Atlantic silverside is a small schooling fish of US Atlantic estuaries whose sex is decided by the water temperature its eggs develop in.

name: Atlantic spotted dolphin
fact: Atlantic spotted dolphins are born spotless and gain more spots with age, and the Bahamas population has been studied for over 30 years.

name: Atlantic stingray
fact: The Atlantic stingray tolerates fresh water and has a permanent population in Florida's St Johns River.

name: Atlantic sturgeon
fact: The Atlantic sturgeon lives in coastal seas and swims up rivers to spawn, and in the past grew to more than 4 metres long.

name: Atlantic thread herring
fact: The Atlantic thread herring, named for a long trailing ray on its dorsal fin, schools along the Gulf of Mexico coast and is netted for bait.

name: Atlantic tomcod
fact: The Atlantic tomcod is a small cod of North American estuaries; those in the Hudson River evolved resistance to PCB pollution in just a few decades.

name: Atlantic torpedo
fact: The Atlantic torpedo is the largest electric ray, up to about 1.8 metres and 90 kilograms, and delivers shocks of around 220 volts.

name: Atlantic white-sided dolphin
fact: The Atlantic white-sided dolphin has a bold yellow-ochre streak on its tail stock and lives in cool North Atlantic waters.

name: Atlantis
fact: Atlantis is the Woods Hole research ship that serves as the mothership for the submersible Alvin.

name: Auguste Piccard
fact: Auguste Piccard invented the bathyscaphe, a free-diving deep submersible, after first setting altitude records in a stratospheric balloon.

name: Australian humpback dolphin
fact: The Australian humpback dolphin was described in 2014 and lives in shallow coastal waters and estuaries of northern Australia and New Guinea.

name: Australian lungfish
fact: The Australian lungfish has a single lung and surfaces to gulp air when its river water runs low in oxygen.

name: Australian sea lion
fact: The Australian sea lion is one of the rarest sea lions and has an unusual 17- to 18-month breeding cycle.

name: Australian snubfin dolphin
fact: The Australian snubfin dolphin was only recognised as a species in 2005 and spits water to herd fish in northern Australia's estuaries.

name: Ayu
fact: The ayu, or sweetfish, hatches in Japanese rivers, spends the winter at sea, and returns to the river to graze algae from the rocks.

name: Azores
fact: The Azores are nine volcanic Portuguese islands in the mid-Atlantic, about 1,500 kilometres west of Lisbon, and a famous whale-watching spot.

name: Bab-el-Mandeb
fact: The Bab-el-Mandeb, whose name means Gate of Tears, joins the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden between Yemen and Djibouti.

name: Baffin Bay
fact: Baffin Bay between Greenland and Baffin Island is named after William Baffin, the English navigator who explored it in 1616.

name: Bahamas
fact: The Bahamas are about 700 islands and cays on shallow banks in the Atlantic, where Columbus made his first landfall in 1492.

name: Baiji
fact: The baiji of the Yangtze was declared functionally extinct in 2006 after a survey failed to find a single animal.

name: Baikal seal
fact: The Baikal seal lives only in Lake Baikal in Siberia and is the only seal that spends its whole life in fresh water.

name: Baird's beaked whale
fact: Baird's beaked whale is the largest beaked whale, up to about 13 metres, and is still hunted off Japan in small numbers.

name: Bald eagle
fact: Bald eagles snatch fish from the surface with their talons and gather by the hundred on Alaskan coasts when salmon and herring run.

name: Balearic Sea
fact: The Balearic Sea lies between the east coast of Spain and the Balearic Islands of Majorca, Minorca and Ibiza.

name: Baleen whale
fact: Baleen whales have no teeth; instead they strain krill and small fish from mouthfuls of water through fringed plates of baleen.

name: Ballan wrasse
fact: The ballan wrasse is the largest wrasse in British waters, used in salmon farms to eat sea lice off the salmon.

name: Baltic Sea
fact: The Baltic Sea is a brackish arm of the Atlantic so diluted by rivers that parts of it freeze over every winter.

name: Bamboo coral
fact: Bamboo corals of the deep sea have skeletons of limestone segments joined by dark, flexible nodes, like a bamboo stem.

name: Bamboo shark
fact: Bamboo sharks are small, slender reef sharks that lay eggs, and their egg cases are a staple of public and home aquariums.

name: Banda Sea
fact: The Banda Sea in eastern Indonesia is a deep basin surrounding the Banda Islands, the original source of nutmeg and mace.

name: Banded coral shrimp
fact: The banded coral shrimp waves long white antennae from reef crevices to attract fish, which it then cleans of parasites.

name: Banded pipefish
fact: The banded pipefish has red and white rings and a paddle-shaped tail, and pairs of them work as cleaner fish on Indo-Pacific reefs.

name: Banded sea krait
fact: Banded sea kraits hunt eels on reefs but return to land to digest their meals, shed their skins and lay eggs.

name: Banggai cardinalfish
fact: The male Banggai cardinalfish broods the eggs and then the hatched young in his mouth for weeks, so the species never has a drifting larval stage.

name: Banjo catfish
fact: The banjo catfish is a flat, lumpy South American catfish shaped like a banjo that lies buried in sand and leaf litter by day.

name: Bar-tailed godwit
fact: In 2022 a young bar-tailed godwit flew non-stop from Alaska to Tasmania, 13,560 kilometres in 11 days, the longest non-stop flight ever recorded for a bird.

name: Barbel
fact: The barbel is a bottom-feeding fish of fast European rivers, named for the four whiskers around its mouth.

name: Barents Sea
fact: The Barents Sea north of Norway and Russia is named after the Dutch navigator Willem Barentsz, who died there in 1597 after wintering on Novaya Zemlya.

name: Bargibant's pygmy seahorse
fact: Bargibant's pygmy seahorse grows to about 2 centimetres and lives only on Muricella sea fans, matching their colour and knobbly texture so well it was found by accident in 1969.

name: Barnacle
fact: Barnacles are crustaceans, relatives of crabs, that glue their heads to rocks and build limestone shells around themselves.

name: Barndoor skate
fact: The barndoor skate is one of the largest skates of the north-west Atlantic, reaching 1.5 metres, and was nearly wiped out as bycatch.

name: Barracuda
fact: The great barracuda is a torpedo-shaped reef predator with fang-like teeth that hunts in sudden short bursts of speed.

name: Barramundi
fact: Barramundi hatch in estuaries, grow up in fresh water and return to the sea to spawn, with most starting life as males and later changing into females.

name: Barrel jellyfish
fact: The barrel jellyfish, the largest jellyfish in British waters, can reach the size of a dustbin lid and is harmless enough to be food for leatherback turtles.

name: Barreleye
fact: The barreleye has a transparent dome over its head and tubular green eyes that rotate inside it to look up through its own skull.

name: Basilosaurus
fact: Basilosaurus was an early whale about 18 metres long with tiny hind legs, and its name means 'king lizard' because it was first mistaken for a reptile.

name: Basket star
fact: A basket star is a brittle star whose arms branch again and again into a tangled net that it spreads at night to catch plankton.

name: Basking shark
fact: The basking shark is the second-largest fish and filters plankton through a gaping mouth as it cruises slowly along.

name: Bass Strait
fact: Bass Strait separates Tasmania from mainland Australia and is named after George Bass, the ship's surgeon who proved Tasmania was an island in 1798.

name: Bat ray
fact: Bat rays flap over the sandy bottoms of California bays, digging up clams with their wings, and can span nearly 2 metres.

name: Bat star
fact: The bat star has webbing between its arms like a bat's wing and comes in almost every colour from red to purple to mottled.

name: Batavia
fact: The Dutch East India Company ship Batavia was wrecked on a reef off Western Australia in 1629, and a bloody mutiny followed among the survivors.

name: Bathysphere
fact: The bathysphere was a steel ball on a cable in which William Beebe and Otis Barton descended to about 920 metres off Bermuda in 1934, a record that stood for 15 years.

name: Bay anchovy
fact: The bay anchovy is probably the most abundant fish on the US Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico coasts, yet few people have ever seen one.

name: Bay of All Saints
fact: The Bay of All Saints at Salvador is the largest bay in Brazil and was named by Portuguese explorers who arrived on All Saints' Day in 1501.

name: Bay of Biscay
fact: The Bay of Biscay, between France and Spain, is notorious among sailors for its violent Atlantic storms.

name: Bay of Campeche
fact: The Bay of Campeche is the southern bight of the Gulf of Mexico, site of the huge Cantarell oil field and part of the Chicxulub impact crater.

name: Bay of Fundy
fact: The Bay of Fundy between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick has the highest tides in the world, rising and falling by as much as 16 metres.

name: Bay of Pigs
fact: The Bay of Pigs is an inlet on Cuba's southern Caribbean coast, famous for the failed 1961 invasion by CIA-trained Cuban exiles.

name: Bay of Plenty
fact: The Bay of Plenty on New Zealand's North Island was named by Captain Cook in 1769 for the friendly welcome and abundant supplies he found there.

name: Bay pipefish
fact: The bay pipefish hides upright among eelgrass blades along North America's Pacific coast, from Alaska to Baja California.

name: Beadlet anemone
fact: The beadlet anemone of British rock pools is a red blob at low tide, and fights its neighbours with a ring of blue stinging beads under its tentacles.

name: Beaked sea snake
fact: The beaked sea snake causes most sea snake bites and deaths, especially among fishermen pulling nets in South and Southeast Asia.

name: Beaked whale
fact: Beaked whales are deep-diving, elusive whales with just one or two pairs of teeth, and some species are known only from stranded animals.

name: Bearded seal
fact: Bearded seals have long white whiskers for finding clams and crabs on the Arctic seabed, and males sing long trilling songs under the ice.

name: Beaufort Gyre
fact: The Beaufort Gyre is a wind-driven clockwise circulation in the Arctic Ocean north of Alaska that stores a huge volume of fresh water from melting ice.

name: Beaufort Sea
fact: The Beaufort Sea north of Alaska and Canada is named after Sir Francis Beaufort, the British admiral who devised the Beaufort wind scale.

name: Beaugregory
fact: The beaugregory is a Caribbean damselfish, yellow below and blue above as a juvenile, that fiercely defends a small patch of reef.

name: Belcher's sea snake
fact: Belcher's sea snake is often wrongly called the world's most venomous snake; its venom is potent, but it is docile and rarely bites.

name: Belemnite
fact: Belemnites were squid-like animals with an internal bullet-shaped shell, and their fossils were once thought to be thunderbolts.

name: Belize Barrier Reef
fact: The Belize Barrier Reef runs about 300 kilometres along the coast of Belize and is the largest section of the Mesoamerican Reef.

name: Bellingshausen Sea
fact: The Bellingshausen Sea off Antarctica is named after Fabian Gottlieb von Bellingshausen, the Russian officer whose expedition sighted the continent in 1820.

name: Beluga sturgeon
fact: The beluga sturgeon of the Caspian and Black Seas can live for more than 100 years and is the source of the most expensive caviar.

name: Beluga whale
fact: Belugas are nicknamed sea canaries for their chirps and whistles, and they can turn their heads because their neck bones are not fused.

name: Ben Franklin
fact: In 1969 the submersible Ben Franklin drifted silently for 30 days inside the Gulf Stream with six men aboard, a mission NASA studied as a model for long space flights.

name: Bengal tiger
fact: Bengal tigers of the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest, swim between islands and hunt along the tidal creeks.

name: Benguela Current
fact: The Benguela Current carries cold, nutrient-rich water north along the coast of Namibia and South Africa, supporting vast shoals of sardines and the Namib coast's fogs.

name: Benthesicymus
fact: The prawn Benthesicymus crenatus was filmed in the Kermadec and Japan trenches at about 7,700 metres, the first decapod seen in the hadal zone.

name: Bering Sea
fact: The Bering Sea separates Alaska from Siberia and is named after Vitus Bering, the Danish navigator who sailed through it for Russia in 1728.

name: Bering Strait
fact: The Bering Strait, named after the Danish navigator Vitus Bering, separates Russia from Alaska by about 82 kilometres and links the Pacific to the Arctic.

name: Bermuda
fact: Bermuda is a lone group of islands in the North Atlantic about 1,000 kilometres from the US coast, with the most northerly coral reefs in the world.

name: Bermuda fireworm
fact: Bermuda fireworms rise to the surface a few nights after each summer full moon and spin in glowing green circles to mate, a display Columbus may have seen in 1492.

name: Betta
fact: Bettas have a labyrinth organ above the gills that lets them gulp air at the surface, which is why they survive in still, oxygen-poor water.

name: Bichir
fact: Bichirs have paired lungs and can breathe air, and young bichirs even have external gills like a salamander larva.

name: Bicolor damselfish
fact: The bicolor damselfish of the Caribbean is dark in front and pale behind, and tends algae gardens that it guards from other grazers.

name: Big-belly seahorse
fact: The big-belly seahorse of Australia and New Zealand is one of the largest seahorses, reaching about 35 centimetres, and the male's pouch swells hugely with eggs.

name: Big red jellyfish
fact: Big red is a metre-wide deep-sea jellyfish discovered in 2003 that has no tentacles at all, feeding instead with four to seven thick fleshy arms.

name: Bigeye thresher shark
fact: The bigeye thresher has huge upward-facing eyes for hunting in dim water hundreds of metres down, where it spends its days.

name: Bigeye tuna
fact: The bigeye tuna, with large eyes for hunting in dim deep water, is a major catch for longline fleets and is sold as sashimi-grade ahi in Hawaii.

name: Bigfin reef squid
fact: Bigfin reef squid have one of the fastest growth rates of any large invertebrate, reaching well over half a kilogram within about four months.

name: Bigfin squid
fact: Bigfin squid dangle ten thin, elbowed arms that stretch to a total length of about 8 metres, and one was filmed 6,212 metres down in the Philippine Trench.

name: Bighead carp
fact: The bighead carp is farmed in huge quantities in China, where its large head is prized for soups.

name: Bight of Benin
fact: The Bight of Benin is a bay in the Gulf of Guinea whose shore was once known as the Slave Coast.

name: Bight of Biafra
fact: The Bight of Biafra, now officially the Bight of Bonny, is the easternmost corner of the Gulf of Guinea, off Nigeria and Cameroon.

name: Bikini Atoll
fact: Bikini Atoll's reef was blasted by 23 nuclear tests between 1946 and 1958, yet its corals have since grown back vigorously.

name: Bilbao
fact: Bilbao's port on the Bay of Biscay is one of Spain's busiest, and the city was reinvented by the Guggenheim museum in 1997.

name: Bioko
fact: Bioko is a volcanic island in the Gulf of Guinea that holds Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea, far from the country's mainland.

name: Bird wrasse
fact: The bird wrasse has a long, curved beak-like snout that it uses to pluck small animals from crevices on Indo-Pacific reefs.

name: Birdbeak dogfish
fact: The birdbeak dogfish has an extremely long, flattened snout and lives on continental slopes down to around 1,500 metres.

name: Bismarck
fact: The battleship Bismarck was sunk in May 1941 after a three-day chase, and Robert Ballard found the wreck in 1989 standing upright about 4,700 metres down.

name: Bismarck Sea
fact: The Bismarck Sea lies north-east of New Guinea and is named, like the Bismarck Archipelago, after the German chancellor Otto von Bismarck.

name: Black-banded sea krait
fact: The black-banded sea krait, or erabu, is caught and smoked in Okinawa to make a traditional soup called irabu-jiru.

name: Black-blotched stingray
fact: The blotched fantail ray can grow nearly 2 metres across and is often seen at cleaning stations on Indo-Pacific reefs.

name: Black coral
fact: Black coral has a dark, flexible skeleton that has been carved into jewellery, and some colonies are more than 4,000 years old.

name: Black crappie
fact: Crappie are schooling sunfish of North American lakes, and anglers catch them in numbers around sunken brush in spring.

name: Black dogfish
fact: The black dogfish is a small glowing shark of the deep North Atlantic that gathers in large schools on the continental slope.

name: Black drum
fact: Black drum make such loud, low booming calls while spawning that Florida residents have complained of a mysterious hum coming through their walls.

name: Black ghost knifefish
fact: The black ghost knifefish swims backwards as easily as forwards by rippling one long fin and senses its world with a weak electric field.

name: Black grouper
fact: The black grouper is a large grouper of the western Atlantic, growing to about 1.5 metres, with rectangular dark blotches on its sides.

name: Black marlin
fact: The black marlin of the Indo-Pacific is often claimed to be the fastest fish of all, and its rigid pectoral fins cannot be folded flat against the body.

name: Black molly
fact: The black molly is a jet-black aquarium strain of a Central American livebearer that gives birth to free-swimming fry.

name: Black scabbardfish
fact: The black scabbardfish is a jet-black, eel-like deep-sea fish with fangs, hauled up from about 1,000 metres on long lines off Madeira, where it is served with banana.

name: Black Sea
fact: The Black Sea connects to the Mediterranean only through the Bosporus and Dardanelles, and below about 150 metres its water contains no oxygen at all.

name: Black sea bass
fact: The black sea bass of the US east coast starts life as a female and later changes into a male with a bright blue hump on its nape.

name: Black sea nettle
fact: The black sea nettle has a bell up to a metre across and oral arms about 8 metres long, yet it was not formally described until 1997.

name: Black skimmer
fact: The black skimmer flies low with its longer lower beak slicing the water, snapping shut the instant it touches a fish.

name: Black swallower
fact: The black swallower can gulp down fish more than twice its own length, stretching its stomach so far that it sometimes bursts.

name: Black turban snail
fact: The black turban snail is a common grazer of Pacific tide pools whose empty shells are favourite homes for hermit crabs.

name: Blackfin tuna
fact: The blackfin tuna is the smallest of the true tunas, rarely over a metre long, and is found only in the western Atlantic.

name: Blacknose shark
fact: The small blacknose shark has a dark smudge on its snout tip and is common in the warm shallows of the western Atlantic.

name: Blacksmith
fact: The blacksmith is a blue-grey damselfish of California's kelp forests that shelters in rock crevices at night and feeds on plankton by day.

name: Blackspot tuskfish
fact: The blackspot tuskfish was filmed on the Great Barrier Reef smashing clams against a rock anvil, one of the first documented cases of tool use in a fish.

name: Blackspotted puffer
fact: The blackspotted puffer, nicknamed the dog-faced puffer, has a grey body with black spots and a muzzle like a puppy's.

name: Blacktip reef shark
fact: Blacktip reef sharks patrol reef flats so shallow that their black-tipped dorsal fins often poke above the surface.

name: Blacktip shark
fact: Blacktip sharks leap and spin out of the water when chasing fish and migrate along the Florida coast in large numbers each year.

name: Bladderwrack
fact: Bladderwrack is the brown seaweed with paired air bladders along its fronds, common on rocky shores and the original source of iodine.

name: Blainville's beaked whale
fact: Blainville's beaked whale has the densest bone known in any animal, in its beak, and is named after French zoologist Henri de Blainville.

name: Blanket octopus
fact: A female blanket octopus can be 2 metres long while the male is barely 2 centimetres, and they rip stinging tentacles from Portuguese man o' war to use as weapons.

name: Blenny
fact: Blennies are small scaleless fish that wedge themselves into cracks in rock pools, and some can hop between pools over wet rock.

name: Blind shark
fact: The blind shark is not blind at all; it got its name because it closes its eyelids when lifted out of the water.

name: Blobfish
fact: The blobfish looks normal at its home depth of 600 to 1,200 metres; its famous droopy face is what happens when its jelly-like flesh is hauled to the surface.

name: Blood star
fact: The blood star is a small, slender sea star of rocky northern shores, usually a vivid orange-red, with arms much longer than its body is wide.

name: Bloodybelly comb jelly
fact: The bloodybelly comb jelly is deep red so that the glowing prey in its stomach cannot be seen by predators in the dark depths.

name: Blue antimora
fact: The blue antimora is a deep-sea cod relative with a violet sheen, common on continental slopes from about 800 to 3,000 metres.

name: Blue blubber jellyfish
fact: The blue blubber of Australian estuaries has no trailing tentacles, feeding with eight stubby arms, and is fished and dried for export to Asia.

name: Blue button
fact: The blue button is a coin-sized floating colony of hydroids with a hard golden disc and a fringe of blue tentacles, often washed up with by-the-wind sailors.

name: Blue catfish
fact: The blue catfish is the largest catfish in North America, reaching over 60 kilograms, and has become an invasive species in Chesapeake Bay.

name: Blue chromis
fact: The blue chromis is a brilliant blue Caribbean damselfish that feeds on plankton in open water above the reef.

name: Blue cod
fact: The blue cod is not a cod but a sandperch found only around New Zealand, where it is the favourite catch of shore anglers.

name: Blue coral
fact: Blue coral is the only living coral with a blue skeleton, coloured by iron salts, and is the sole survivor of an ancient group.

name: Blue Corner
fact: Blue Corner in Palau is a current-swept reef wall where divers hook onto the rock to watch sharks and schooling fish stream past.

name: Blue crab
fact: The blue crab's scientific name means 'beautiful savoury swimmer', and freshly moulted ones are eaten whole as soft-shell crabs.

name: Blue devil damselfish
fact: The blue devil damselfish, a brilliant electric-blue fish of the western Pacific, is a hardy aquarium favourite with a devilish temper for its size.

name: Blue dragon
fact: The blue dragon sea slug floats upside down at the surface, eats Portuguese man o' war and stores their stinging cells in its finger-like tips to fire at attackers.

name: Blue-footed booby
fact: Blue-footed boobies fold their wings and plunge-dive into shoals of sardines, and the males show off their bright blue feet in a high-stepping dance.

name: Blue-green chromis
fact: The blue-green chromis is a shimmering damselfish that hovers in large shoals above branching corals, darting in when danger threatens.

name: Blue-lipped sea krait
fact: The blue-lipped sea krait comes ashore on Pacific and Indian Ocean islands to rest and lay its eggs in caves and crevices.

name: Blue mackerel
fact: The blue mackerel, or slimy mackerel, is a spotted mackerel of Australian and New Zealand waters, mostly used as bait and for canning.

name: Blue marlin
fact: The Atlantic blue marlin can top 4 metres and is one of the fastest, hardest-fighting fish in the sea; females grow far larger than males.

name: Blue mussel
fact: Blue mussels carpet rocky shores and sandbanks of the North and Baltic seas, anchored by tough threads they spin themselves.

name: Blue parrotfish
fact: The blue parrotfish is a uniform powder-blue Caribbean parrotfish that spends most of its day grinding sand and rock for algae.

name: Blue-ringed octopus
fact: A golf-ball-sized blue-ringed octopus carries enough tetrodotoxin to kill several adults, and its blue rings flash as a warning when it is alarmed.

name: Blue rockfish
fact: Blue rockfish school in the water column of California kelp forests and are among the fish divers see most often there.

name: Blue shark
fact: Blue sharks cross whole oceans, with tagged individuals travelling from New England to Spain and back.

name: Blue-spotted ribbontail ray
fact: The bluespotted ribbontail ray's bright blue spots warn predators that its tail carries two venomous spines.

name: Blue starfish
fact: The blue starfish of Indo-Pacific reefs is a vivid blue and can regrow lost arms; its close relative Linckia multifora can even grow a whole new star from a single severed arm.

name: Blue stingray
fact: The blue stingray of southern African waters has blue markings on its back and is a favourite of shore anglers.

name: Blue tang
fact: The blue tang, the fish behind Dory, has a razor-sharp spine on each side of its tail that it flicks out in defence.

name: Blue whale
fact: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, reaching about 30 metres and well over 150 tonnes.

name: Blue whiting
fact: Blue whiting is a small cod relative of the North Atlantic caught by the million tonnes for fishmeal and surimi.

name: Blueback herring
fact: The blueback herring runs up rivers from Florida to Nova Scotia each spring to spawn and is hard to tell from the alewife.

name: Bluefin tuna
fact: The Atlantic bluefin tuna can weigh more than 600 kilograms and is warm-blooded, keeping its muscles warmer than the sea so it can sprint after prey.

name: Bluefish
fact: Bluefish hunt in savage packs along the US Atlantic coast and will keep biting even after they are full.

name: Bluegill
fact: Male bluegill dig saucer-shaped nests in colonies and guard the eggs, while small 'sneaker' males dart in to fertilise some on the sly.

name: Bluehead wrasse
fact: The bluehead wrasse of the Caribbean can change from female to male in days, and the big blue-headed males defend spawning sites.

name: Bluespotted maskray
fact: The bluespotted maskray has a dark mask across its eyes and is often confused with the bluespotted ribbontail ray.

name: Bluespotted ribbontail ray
fact: The bluespotted ribbontail ray has electric-blue spots and two venomous tail spines, and hides under table corals on Red Sea reefs.

name: Bluestripe snapper
fact: The bluestripe snapper, yellow with four blue stripes, schools in hundreds on Indian Ocean and Red Sea reefs.

name: Bluntnose stingray
fact: The bluntnose stingray of the western Atlantic has a rounded snout and glides over sandy flats from Massachusetts to Brazil.

name: Boaty McBoatface
fact: Boaty McBoatface is a yellow robot submarine that won its name in a public vote and has since made long journeys under Antarctic sea ice and deep in the Southern Ocean.

name: Bobbit worm
fact: The bobbit worm lurks buried in sand with only its jaws showing and ambushes fish at night, growing up to about 3 metres long.

name: Bobtail snipe eel
fact: The bobtail snipe eel is a stubby, dart-shaped deep-sea eel with long thin jaws, found in the dark waters below 1,000 metres.

name: Bobtail squid
fact: Bobtail squid are small, round cephalopods that bury themselves in sand by day and hunt shrimp at night, and many carry glowing bacteria.

name: Bohai Sea
fact: The Bohai Sea is the innermost gulf of the Yellow Sea, almost enclosed by China's coast, and the sea approach to the port of Tianjin.

name: Bolivian river dolphin
fact: The Bolivian river dolphin lives in the upper Madeira basin, cut off from the Amazon by rapids, and was declared part of Bolivia's natural heritage in 2012.

name: Bombay duck
fact: Bombay duck is not a duck but a lizardfish caught in huge numbers off western India, where it is dried in the open air and fried.

name: Bonaire National Marine Park
fact: Bonaire's entire coastline has been a marine park since 1979, and divers simply walk in from shore to reach its reefs.

name: Bonefish
fact: The bonefish is the 'grey ghost' of tropical flats, a shy, fast-sprinting fish that can strip line from a fly reel in seconds.

name: Bonito
fact: Bonitos are striped, tuna-like fish of the mackerel family; in Japan 'bonito' usually means the skipjack, seared as katsuo tataki or dried into bonito flakes.

name: Bonnethead
fact: The bonnethead is the only shark known to eat and digest seagrass, which can make up over half of its diet.

name: Bony-eared assfish
fact: The bony-eared assfish is a cusk-eel from 1,000 to 4,400 metres with the smallest brain for its body size of any known vertebrate, and an unfortunate name.

name: Booby
fact: Boobies are tropical plunge-divers named from the Spanish 'bobo', meaning foolish, because they were so easy for sailors to catch.

name: Bootlace worm
fact: The bootlace worm is a ribbon worm of North Sea shores; one found in Scotland in 1864 measured about 55 metres, the longest animal ever recorded.

name: Bora Bora
fact: Bora Bora is a volcanic island in French Polynesia surrounded by a turquoise lagoon and a ring of reef islets.

name: Bosporus
fact: The Bosporus runs through the middle of Istanbul, linking the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and dividing Europe from Asia.

name: Boston
fact: Boston's harbour on the Atlantic was the scene of the Boston Tea Party in 1773, when colonists dumped tea into the water in protest at British taxes.

name: Botany Bay
fact: Botany Bay south of Sydney is where Captain Cook first landed in Australia in 1770, named for the plants collected there by Joseph Banks.

name: Bottlenose dolphin
fact: Bottlenose dolphins call each other by name using signature whistles that each dolphin invents as a calf.

name: Bougainville Trench
fact: The Bougainville Trench curves through the northern Solomon Sea west of Bougainville Island, continuing the New Britain Trench, whose Planet Deep exceeds 9,000 metres.

name: Bouvet Island
fact: Bouvet Island is the most remote island on Earth, an ice-covered volcanic island in the South Atlantic about 1,700 kilometres from Antarctica with no permanent inhabitants.

name: Bowfin
fact: The bowfin can breathe air using its swim bladder and is the only living member of a lineage dating back to the age of dinosaurs.

name: Bowhead whale
fact: Bowhead whales can live more than 200 years and use their huge heads to break through sea ice.

name: Bowie Seamount
fact: Bowie Seamount off British Columbia rises from about 3,000 metres to within roughly 25 metres of the surface and is a Canadian marine protected area.

name: Bowmouth guitarfish
fact: The bowmouth guitarfish, or shark ray, has ridges of spiky thorns over its eyes and back and looks like a cross between a shark and a ray.

name: Box jellyfish
fact: The Australian box jellyfish has 24 eyes and a sting that can stop a human heart within minutes, and it is almost invisible in the water.

name: Boxfish
fact: Boxfish are encased in a rigid bony box and, when stressed, release a poisonous mucus that can kill every other fish in an aquarium.

name: Brain coral
fact: Brain coral grows into a dome furrowed with grooves like a human brain, and single colonies can live for centuries.

name: Bramble shark
fact: The bramble shark is covered in large thorn-like denticles and is so rarely encountered that little is known about its life.

name: Bransfield Strait
fact: Bransfield Strait between the South Shetland Islands and the Antarctic Peninsula is named after Edward Bransfield, who charted the area in 1820.

name: Brant goose
fact: The brant is a small sea goose that depends on eelgrass; when disease wiped out eelgrass on both sides of the Atlantic in the 1930s, brant numbers crashed.

name: Brazil Current
fact: The Brazil Current carries warm tropical water south along the coast of Brazil until it meets the cold Falkland Current off Argentina.

name: Brest
fact: Brest, on the far western tip of Brittany, is one of France's two main naval bases, with a huge natural harbour opening onto the Atlantic.

name: Brill
fact: Brill are close relatives of turbot with a more oval body and a frilled front edge to the dorsal fin.

name: Bristle worm
fact: Bristle worms are segmented worms with paddle-like feet fringed with bristles, and they have been collected from trench floors more than 10,000 metres down.

name: Bristlemouth
fact: Bristlemouths are tiny, glowing deep-sea fish that may number in the hundreds of trillions, making them the most abundant vertebrates on Earth.

name: Bristlenose pleco
fact: The bristlenose pleco is a small armoured catfish whose males grow a bush of fleshy tentacles on the snout; it is a popular aquarium algae eater.

name: Britannic
fact: The Britannic, Titanic's larger sister, struck a mine while serving as a hospital ship in 1916 and lies on its side at about 120 metres off the Greek island of Kea.

name: Brittle star
fact: Brittle stars snap off arms to escape predators and grow them back, and they have been seen in large numbers on the floor of the South Sandwich Trench below 6,000 metres.

name: Broadclub cuttlefish
fact: The broadclub cuttlefish hypnotises crabs by flashing moving bands of dark colour down its arms before striking.

name: Broadnose sevengill shark
fact: Broadnose sevengill sharks have seven gill slits rather than five and have been seen hunting seals in groups off South Africa.

name: Brook trout
fact: The brook trout is actually a char, with light spots on a dark background, and is the official state fish of several US states.

name: Brown pelican
fact: The brown pelican dives head-first into the sea from 10 to 20 metres up, unlike most pelicans, which fish from the surface.

name: Brown shrimp
fact: The brown shrimp of the North Sea is caught by horseback shrimpers in Belgium and potted in butter around Morecambe Bay.

name: Brown trout
fact: Brown trout that migrate to sea come back silver and much larger, and are then known as sea trout.

name: Brownbanded bamboo shark
fact: The brownbanded bamboo shark is born with dark bands that fade with age and can survive for hours out of water on exposed reef flats.

name: Bryde's whale
fact: Bryde's whale is named after Johan Bryde, a Norwegian who set up South Africa's first whaling stations, and it stays in warm waters all year.

name: Bryozoan
fact: Bryozoans, or moss animals, are colonies of tiny filter feeders that form crusts and fronds, each individual catching food with a ring of tentacles.

name: Bubble coral
fact: Bubble coral inflates grape-like bladders by day to catch sunlight for its algae and withdraws them at night to feed with its tentacles.

name: Bubblegum coral
fact: Bubblegum coral is a deep-sea soft coral that grows into pink, tree-like colonies up to several metres tall, with branch tips like blobs of chewed gum.

name: Buenos Aires
fact: Buenos Aires sits on the Río de la Plata estuary, which opens into the Atlantic, and its name means 'fair winds'.

name: Bull kelp
fact: Bull kelp grows a single long stem topped by a gas-filled float the size of a grapefruit, and can reach more than 30 metres in a single season.

name: Bull shark
fact: Bull sharks can live in fresh water and have been found far up the Mississippi and Amazon rivers.

name: Bull trout
fact: The bull trout is a char of cold, clean rivers in north-west North America and is so sensitive to warm water that it is listed as threatened.

name: Bullet tuna
fact: The bullet tuna is one of the smallest members of the tuna family, found worldwide in warm seas and rarely more than 50 centimetres long.

name: Bullethead parrotfish
fact: The bullethead parrotfish is one of the most common Pacific parrotfish, with a blunt bullet-shaped head and a green male phase.

name: Bullhead catfish
fact: Bullheads are small, dark catfish of North American ponds and slow rivers that can survive in warm, low-oxygen water that kills other fish.

name: Bumblebee goby
fact: The bumblebee goby is a banded black-and-yellow goby of Southeast Asian estuaries that grows to under 4 centimetres.

name: Bumphead parrotfish
fact: The bumphead parrotfish is the largest parrotfish, reaching about 1.3 metres, and rams its forehead into coral to break it up for feeding.

name: Bunaken National Park
fact: Bunaken, off Sulawesi in Indonesia, is known for coral walls that drop almost vertically into deep water right beside the shore.

name: Buoy barnacle
fact: The buoy barnacle makes its own float, a foam of cement bubbles, and drifts across the open ocean hanging beneath it.

name: Burbot
fact: The burbot is the only member of the cod family that lives in fresh water, a bottom-dwelling, eel-like fish that spawns under the ice in midwinter.

name: Burmeister's porpoise
fact: Burmeister's porpoise of South America is named after German zoologist Hermann Burmeister and has a strange backward-leaning dorsal fin.

name: Butterfly kingfish
fact: The butterfly kingfish is the oddest member of the tuna family, a cold-water Southern Ocean fish with big scales and a heater organ that warms its brain and eyes.

name: Butterfly ray
fact: Butterfly rays are much wider than they are long, with a very short tail, and bury themselves in sand in warm shallows.

name: Butterflyfish
fact: Butterflyfish are thin, bright reef fish that often pair for life and use their pointed snouts to pick at coral polyps.

name: By-the-wind sailor
fact: The by-the-wind sailor floats on the surface under a stiff diagonal sail, so whole fleets of them are blown ashore in the same storm.

name: Cabezon
fact: The cabezon is a big-headed, scaleless sculpin of Pacific kelp beds whose eggs are poisonous to eat; the male guards them until they hatch.

name: Cabo Pulmo National Park
fact: Cabo Pulmo in Baja California saw its fish biomass rise more than fourfold within a decade after fishing was banned, a celebrated conservation success.

name: Cabot Strait
fact: Cabot Strait between Newfoundland and Cape Breton Island is named after the explorer John Cabot and is the main entrance to the Gulf of St Lawrence.

name: Cádiz
fact: Cádiz, on a narrow spit into the Atlantic, was founded by the Phoenicians and is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in western Europe.

name: Calanus
fact: Calanus finmarchicus is a rice-grain-sized copepod so rich in oil that it is the main food of herring, mackerel and the North Atlantic right whale.

name: California Current
fact: The California Current flows south along the US west coast, bringing cold water and the fog for which San Francisco is famous.

name: California halibut
fact: The California halibut is a left-eyed flounder, yet nearly half of all individuals turn out right-eyed, a quirk almost unique among flatfish.

name: California sea lion
fact: California sea lions are the trained 'seals' of circuses and aquarium shows and haul out in noisy crowds on San Francisco's Pier 39.

name: California sheephead
fact: The California sheephead is a big-toothed wrasse of kelp forests that crushes sea urchins; all start life as females and the largest turn into black-and-red males.

name: California two-spot octopus
fact: The California two-spot octopus has a false blue eye-spot under each real eye and was the first octopus to have its full genome sequenced.

name: Calypso
fact: Calypso was a former minesweeper that Jacques Cousteau turned into the floating base for his films and expeditions from 1950 until it sank in Singapore harbour in 1996.

name: Canary Current
fact: The Canary Current flows south past north-west Africa and the Canary Islands and helped carry Columbus's ships towards the Caribbean.

name: Canary Islands
fact: The Canary Islands are Spanish volcanic islands off north-west Africa, named not after birds but probably after dogs, from the Latin canaria.

name: Candiru
fact: The candiru is a tiny, slender Amazon catfish that slips under the gill covers of larger fish to drink their blood, and is feared far out of proportion to its size.

name: Cannonball jellyfish
fact: The cannonball jellyfish is fished off Georgia and Florida, dried and exported to Asia as a crunchy salad ingredient.

name: Canoe
fact: Polynesian voyagers crossed thousands of kilometres of open Pacific in double-hulled sailing canoes, settling islands as far apart as Hawaii and New Zealand.

name: Cape fur seal
fact: Cape fur seals breed in huge colonies on the coasts of South Africa and Namibia, where great whites ambush them at Seal Island.

name: Cape hake
fact: The Cape hake is the backbone of the South African and Namibian fishing industries, caught by trawlers over the continental shelf.

name: Cape Town
fact: Cape Town's harbour on Table Bay faces the Atlantic, where the cold Benguela Current keeps the sea far chillier than on the Indian Ocean side of the Cape.

name: Cape Verde
fact: Cape Verde is a group of ten volcanic islands off the coast of Senegal, and many Atlantic hurricanes begin as storms passing nearby.

name: Capelin
fact: Capelin are small silvery fish that spawn on Arctic and sub-Arctic beaches in their millions and feed cod, whales and puffins.

name: Caravel
fact: The caravel was the small, nimble Portuguese ship of the 1400s used by explorers along the African coast; Columbus's Niña and Pinta were caravels.

name: Cardigan Bay
fact: Cardigan Bay is the largest bay in Wales and home to a resident population of bottlenose dolphins.

name: Cardinal tetra
fact: The cardinal tetra, with red running the full length of its body, is still mostly caught wild in the Rio Negro for the aquarium trade.

name: Cardinalfish
fact: Cardinalfish are small nocturnal reef fish, and in most species the male broods the eggs in his mouth without eating until they hatch.

name: Caribbean monk seal
fact: The Caribbean monk seal was hunted for its oil and was declared extinct in 2008, the last confirmed sighting having been in 1952.

name: Caribbean reef octopus
fact: The Caribbean reef octopus spreads its webbed arms like a parachute over coral heads to trap crabs and shrimp underneath.

name: Caribbean reef shark
fact: The Caribbean reef shark is the shark most often seen on feeding dives in the Bahamas and is rarely found outside the western Atlantic.

name: Caribbean reef squid
fact: Caribbean reef squid talk with rapidly shifting skin patterns and can show one display to a mate and another to a rival at the same time.

name: Caribbean Sea
fact: The Caribbean Sea is a marginal sea of the Atlantic enclosed by the Antilles and Central America, and its Cayman Trough is more than 7,000 metres deep.

name: Caribbean spiny lobster
fact: The Caribbean spiny lobster can navigate home using the Earth's magnetic field, the first invertebrate shown to have a magnetic map sense.

name: Carnation coral
fact: Carnation corals are soft corals that puff up into brilliant pink, red and purple bushes at night and collapse into limp blobs by day.

name: Carp
fact: Common carp has been farmed for food for more than 2,000 years and is still the traditional Christmas Eve dish in Poland and the Czech Republic.

name: Carpathia
fact: Carpathia, the ship that rescued Titanic's survivors, was itself torpedoed and sunk in the Atlantic in 1918.

name: Carrack
fact: The carrack was the big, round-hulled ocean ship of the 1400s and 1500s; Columbus's Santa María and Magellan's Victoria were carracks.

name: Casablanca
fact: Casablanca is Morocco's biggest city and its main Atlantic port, famous around the world thanks to the 1942 film.

name: Casper octopus
fact: A ghost-white octopus nicknamed Casper was discovered off Hawaii in 2016 at about 4,000 metres, laying its eggs on dead sponge stalks attached to metal nodules.

name: Caspian seal
fact: The Caspian seal lives only in the landlocked Caspian Sea, where it breeds on winter ice in the north.

name: Catamaran
fact: A catamaran has two parallel hulls joined by a frame, a design borrowed from the fishing craft of southern India; the name comes from the Tamil for 'tied wood'.

name: Catfish
fact: Catfish are whiskered bottom-dwellers; the channel catfish is the most farmed fish in the United States, and Vietnamese basa fills supermarket freezers worldwide.

name: Caulerpa taxifolia
fact: Caulerpa taxifolia, the 'killer alga', escaped from an aquarium into the Mediterranean in the 1980s and smothered thousands of hectares of seabed.

name: Cauliflower coral
fact: Cauliflower coral grows in knobbly clumps and is one of the first corals to settle on new reef, but also one of the first to bleach.

name: Cayman Trough
fact: The Cayman Trough is the deepest part of the Caribbean Sea, at about 7,500 metres, and holds the deepest known hydrothermal vents, the Beebe vent field.

name: Celebes Sea
fact: The Celebes Sea between Indonesia and the Philippines is a deep basin of more than 6,000 metres, famous for the rich reefs around Sipadan.

name: Celestial pearl danio
fact: The celestial pearl danio, a 2-centimetre fish spangled with pearly spots, was found in Myanmar in 2006 and caused such a craze that it was nearly collected to extinction.

name: Celtic Sea
fact: The Celtic Sea lies south of Ireland and west of Cornwall and was only given its name in 1921.

name: Cenderawasih Bay
fact: Cenderawasih Bay in Indonesian New Guinea is famous for whale sharks that gather beneath fishing platforms to feed on baitfish.

name: Cero
fact: The cero is a Spanish mackerel of the Caribbean with a row of yellow-orange streaks and spots along its sides.

name: Chagos Marine Protected Area
fact: The Chagos Archipelago in the Indian Ocean was declared a no-take marine reserve in 2010 around some of the cleanest coral reefs in the world.

name: Chain moray
fact: The chain moray of the Caribbean, patterned with yellow chain links, can leave the water to hunt crabs on rocks at low tide.

name: Chalk bass
fact: The chalk bass is a tiny Caribbean sea bass, barely 8 centimetres long, that is both male and female at once and takes turns laying eggs with its partner.

name: Challenger Deep
fact: Challenger Deep, the floor of the Mariana Trench, was first reached by Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh in the bathyscaphe Trieste in 1960.

name: Chambered nautilus
fact: The chambered nautilus adds new chambers to its spiral shell as it grows and adjusts the gas inside them to rise and sink.

name: Channel catfish
fact: The channel catfish is the most farmed fish in the United States and the official state fish of several southern and midwestern states.

name: Channel Islands
fact: The Channel Islands of Jersey, Guernsey, Alderney and Sark lie off Normandy and were the only British soil occupied by Germany in the Second World War.

name: Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary
fact: The Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary off southern California protects kelp forests where cold northern and warm southern currents meet.

name: Channelled wrack
fact: Channelled wrack lives at the very top of the shore, where it can dry out for days between tides and still revive.

name: Charles Wyville Thomson
fact: Charles Wyville Thomson was the chief scientist of the Challenger expedition of 1872 to 1876, which laid the foundations of oceanography.

name: Charleston
fact: Charleston's harbour, where the Ashley and Cooper rivers meet the Atlantic, saw the first shots of the American Civil War at Fort Sumter in 1861.

name: Chatham Islands
fact: The Chatham Islands east of New Zealand are among the first inhabited places on Earth to see each new day.

name: Chatham Rise
fact: The Chatham Rise is a broad submarine plateau east of New Zealand that supports one of the country's most important fishing grounds, including hoki.

name: Chemosynthetic bacteria
fact: Chemosynthetic bacteria make food from the hydrogen sulphide in vent water instead of from sunlight, feeding every animal at a hydrothermal vent.

name: Cherry barb
fact: The cherry barb, a small red fish from Sri Lankan streams, is far more common in aquariums than in the wild.

name: Chesapeake Bay
fact: Chesapeake Bay is the largest estuary in the United States and is famous for its blue crabs and oysters.

name: Chikyu
fact: Chikyu is a Japanese drilling ship with a derrick about 120 metres above the water, built to drill deeper into the sea floor than any ship before it.

name: Chilean dolphin
fact: The Chilean dolphin is a small, shy dolphin of Chile's fjords, channels and estuaries and is found nowhere else.

name: Chilean jack mackerel
fact: The Chilean jack mackerel supported one of the largest fisheries in the world in the 1990s, with catches of about 5 million tonnes, before the stock crashed.

name: Chili rasbora
fact: The chili rasbora of Borneo's blackwater streams is a brilliant red fish barely 2 centimetres long, one of the smallest aquarium fish.

name: Chimaera
fact: Chimaeras, or ghost sharks, are cartilaginous deep-water relatives of sharks with electric-sensing pores on their rabbit-like heads.

name: Chinese mitten crab
fact: The Chinese mitten crab has furry claws, lives in rivers but breeds in the sea, and has invaded the Thames, the Elbe and San Francisco Bay.

name: Chinese sturgeon
fact: The Chinese sturgeon, which migrates between the sea and the Yangtze, is critically endangered since dams blocked its spawning grounds.

name: Chinook salmon
fact: The chinook, or king salmon, is the largest Pacific salmon and some swim about 3,000 kilometres up the Yukon River to spawn.

name: Chinstrap penguin
fact: Chinstrap penguins feed almost entirely on krill, and their numbers have crashed as warming has thinned the krill swarms near the Antarctic Peninsula.

name: Chiton
fact: Chitons wear a shell of eight overlapping plates and can roll into a ball like a woodlouse when prised from a rock.

name: Chocolate chip sea star
fact: The chocolate chip sea star gets its name from the dark, knobbly spines dotted across its back like chocolate chips.

name: Chokka squid
fact: Chokka squid gather in huge spawning swarms off South Africa's southern coast, where they are hand-jigged for export as calamari.

name: Christmas Island red crab
fact: Tens of millions of Christmas Island red crabs march from the forest to the sea each year to breed, closing roads across the island.

name: Christmas tree worm
fact: The Christmas tree worm lives in a tube bored into coral and unfurls two spiral crowns of tentacles that snap back inside in a blink.

name: Christopher Columbus
fact: Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492 on a voyage that opened lasting contact between Europe and the Americas.

name: Chub
fact: The chub is a big-mouthed European river fish that will eat almost anything, from cherries to small fish.

name: Chub mackerel
fact: The chub mackerel is one of the world's biggest fish catches, taken in huge numbers off Japan, Chile and Peru, and is the saba of Japanese sushi bars.

name: Chum salmon
fact: Chum salmon have the widest range of any Pacific salmon, from California to Korea, and spawning males develop tiger-like purple stripes.

name: Cichlid
fact: Many cichlids, from African lakes to the Amazon, brood their eggs and fry in their mouths or guard them fiercely as a pair.

name: Cinnamon clownfish
fact: The cinnamon clownfish, or fire clownfish, is a dark red-brown anemonefish with one white head bar and a bluish tint, from the western Pacific.

name: Cisco
fact: The cisco, or lake herring, schools in cold North American lakes and is a whitefish rather than a true herring.

name: Cladoselache
fact: Cladoselache is one of the earliest well-known sharks, preserved in Devonian shales around Cleveland, Ohio, about 370 million years old.

name: Clam
fact: Clams pull themselves through sand with a muscular foot and draw in water through a siphon to filter out food.

name: Clarion angelfish
fact: The clarion angelfish lives only around Mexico's Revillagigedo Islands and Clipperton, where it cleans parasites from giant manta rays.

name: Clark's anemonefish
fact: Clark's anemonefish is the least fussy clownfish, able to live in all ten species of host anemone, and ranges from the Persian Gulf to Japan.

name: Clawed armhook squid
fact: The clawed armhook squid was the first squid seen brooding its eggs, carrying a sac of thousands of eggs in its arms for months in the deep.

name: Cleaner shrimp
fact: Cleaner shrimp wave their white antennae to advertise a cleaning service, and reef fish queue up and open their mouths to have parasites picked off.

name: Cleaner wrasse
fact: The bluestreak cleaner wrasse runs a cleaning station where bigger fish queue to have parasites picked from their skin, gills and even mouths.

name: Climbing perch
fact: The climbing perch breathes air and can travel over land between ponds, pulling itself along with its gill covers and fins.

name: Clingfish
fact: The northern clingfish grips wet, slimy rock with a suction disc on its belly strong enough to hold many times its own weight.

name: Clipper ship
fact: Clipper ships were the fast sailing ships of the mid-1800s, built for speed on the tea and wool runs; Cutty Sark is the most famous survivor.

name: Clipperton Island
fact: Clipperton Island is a tiny uninhabited French atoll in the eastern Pacific, more than 1,000 kilometres from Mexico, ringed by a lagoon and overrun by land crabs.

name: Clown killifish
fact: The clown killifish is a 3-centimetre West African fish with a banded body and a rocket-flame tail that spends its life just under the surface.

name: Clown loach
fact: The clown loach, orange with black bands, clicks audibly, sleeps on its side and can grow to 30 centimetres.

name: Clown triggerfish
fact: The clown triggerfish has large white spots on its black belly and a yellow mouth, making it one of the most recognisable reef fish.

name: Clownfish
fact: Clownfish are immune to the stings of their host anemone, and if the female of a group dies the largest male changes sex to take her place.

name: Clymene dolphin
fact: The Clymene dolphin of the Atlantic is the only confirmed case of a marine mammal species that arose as a hybrid, from spinner and striped dolphins.

name: Cobb Seamount
fact: Cobb Seamount, about 500 kilometres off Washington State, is a flat-topped underwater volcano whose summit lies just a few dozen metres below the surface.

name: Cobia
fact: Cobia is a fast-growing open-water fish now farmed in sea cages in Vietnam, Taiwan and Panama for its firm white flesh.

name: Coccolithophore
fact: Coccolithophores are single-celled algae armoured with chalk discs, and their blooms can turn whole seas milky white in satellite images.

name: Cockle
fact: Cockles live buried just under the sand of tidal flats and can leap away from predators by flexing their foot.

name: Coconut crab
fact: The coconut crab is the largest land-living arthropod, climbs trees and cracks coconuts with claws whose pinch, estimated at up to about 3,300 newtons, is stronger than most animals' bites.

name: Coconut octopus
fact: The coconut octopus carries coconut shells across the seabed to use as a portable shelter, one of the clearest examples of tool use in an invertebrate.

name: Cocos Island
fact: Cocos Island, about 550 kilometres off Costa Rica, is a World Heritage site where divers come for huge schools of scalloped hammerheads.

name: Cod
fact: Atlantic cod built the economies of Newfoundland and New England and is the classic fish of British fish and chips; its stocks collapsed off Canada in 1992.

name: Coelacanth
fact: The coelacanth was thought extinct for 66 million years until a fisherman landed one off South Africa in 1938; it lives in caves around 200 metres down.

name: Cog
fact: The cog was the sturdy single-masted cargo ship of the medieval Hanseatic League, trading across the North Sea and the Baltic.

name: Coho salmon
fact: Coho, or silver salmon, spend about a year in fresh water and roughly 18 months at sea before returning to spawn with hooked jaws and red flanks.

name: Cold-seep tubeworm
fact: Tubeworms at cold seeps in the Gulf of Mexico grow so slowly that some are estimated to be more than 200 years old, among the longest-lived of all animals.

name: Coleman shrimp
fact: Coleman shrimps live in pairs on the venomous fire urchin, clearing a patch of spines to sit among its brilliant colours.

name: Colossal squid
fact: The colossal squid of the Southern Ocean is the heaviest invertebrate on Earth, reaching about 500 kilograms, with swivelling hooks on its tentacles.

name: Columbus crab
fact: The Columbus crab lives on floating sargassum and on the backs of loggerhead turtles, hitching rides across the open Atlantic.

name: Comb jelly
fact: Comb jellies are not true jellyfish: they swim with eight rows of beating cilia that scatter light into rainbows, and most species also glow blue in the dark.

name: Commerson's dolphin
fact: Commerson's dolphin, with its black-and-white panda colouring, lives off Patagonia and, oddly, in the far-off Kerguelen Islands.

name: Common cuttlefish
fact: The common cuttlefish has W-shaped pupils and can send rippling waves of colour across its skin even though it is thought to be colour-blind.

name: Common dolphin
fact: Common dolphins have a bold hourglass pattern on their sides and gather in superpods of thousands.

name: Common guillemot
fact: Common guillemots, called murres in North America, swim down after fish to depths of over 100 metres and lay a single pointed egg on a bare cliff ledge.

name: Common loon
fact: The common loon, or great northern diver, breeds on lakes but winters on the sea, chasing fish underwater with powerful kicks of its feet.

name: Common octopus
fact: The common octopus can squeeze through any gap larger than its beak and is a famous escape artist in aquariums and research labs.

name: Common prawn
fact: The common prawn of European rock pools is almost transparent with faint stripes, and is netted along British and Irish coasts for the table.

name: Common skate
fact: The common skate, once abundant in European seas, can grow over 2 metres long and is now critically endangered.

name: Common starfish
fact: The common starfish of the North Atlantic pries open mussels and pushes its stomach out through its mouth to digest them inside the shell.

name: Common stingray
fact: The common stingray of the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean was described by ancient Greek and Roman writers, who feared its venomous spine.

name: Common sunstar
fact: The common sunstar has between about 8 and 14 arms ringed in red and white and preys on other starfish.

name: Common thresher shark
fact: The common thresher's scythe-like upper tail lobe can make up half of its total length.

name: Compass jellyfish
fact: The compass jellyfish has brown V-shaped markings radiating across its bell like the points of a compass, and it starts life male and becomes female.

name: Conch
fact: The queen conch builds a heavy pink-lipped shell and hops along the seabed by pole-vaulting on a claw-like foot.

name: Cone snail
fact: Cone snails fire a venomous harpoon from their beautiful shells, and a few species can kill a person.

name: Conger eel
fact: Conger eel, anago, is a saltwater eel simmered until soft and served with a sweet sauce in sushi; it is leaner than freshwater unagi.

name: Conodont
fact: Conodonts were eel-like early vertebrates known mainly from tiny tooth-like fossils, which geologists use to date rocks.

name: Container ship
fact: The biggest container ships are about 400 metres long and can carry more than 20,000 standard shipping containers.

name: Convict cichlid
fact: The convict cichlid, striped like a prison uniform, breeds so readily that it is used to study parental care in fish.

name: Convict tang
fact: The convict tang is a pale surgeonfish with black bars like a prisoner's uniform that grazes in huge schools that overwhelm territorial damselfish.

name: Cook Islands
fact: The Cook Islands are 15 islands in the South Pacific named after Captain James Cook and self-governing in free association with New Zealand.

name: Cook Strait
fact: Cook Strait separates New Zealand's North and South Islands and is named after Captain James Cook, who sailed through it in 1770.

name: Cookiecutter shark
fact: The small cookiecutter shark bites neat round plugs of flesh out of whales, tuna and even the rubber domes of submarines.

name: Copepod
fact: Copepods are the most numerous animals in the sea by a wide margin, and have been found in the mud at the bottom of the Challenger Deep.

name: Copperband butterflyfish
fact: The copperband butterflyfish has a long snout for picking food from crevices and a false eyespot on its dorsal fin; aquarists use it to eat pest anemones.

name: Coracle
fact: A coracle is a small, round boat of woven wood covered in hide or canvas, still used by a few fishermen in Wales and India.

name: Coral
fact: Coral is built by tiny animals called polyps, each a ring of stinging tentacles around a mouth, which together lay down reefs visible from space.

name: Coral beauty
fact: The coral beauty is a hardy dwarf angelfish, purple-blue with an orange belly, that is one of the most commonly kept marine angelfish.

name: Coral catshark
fact: The coral catshark hides in reef crevices by day and is small enough that it is often kept in home aquariums.

name: Coral goby
fact: Coral gobies are tiny fish that live their whole lives among the branches of a single Acropora coral colony, which they defend from seaweed.

name: Coral hind
fact: The coral hind is a vivid orange-red grouper covered in bright blue spots, common on Indo-Pacific and Red Sea reefs.

name: Coral Sea
