fact: The Coral Sea off north-east Australia contains the Great Barrier Reef, and a 1942 battle fought there was the first in which opposing ships never sighted each other.

name: Coral trout
fact: The coral trout is a red, blue-spotted grouper of the Great Barrier Reef, not a trout at all, and one of the most valuable fish in Queensland's reef fishery.

name: Coralline algae
fact: Coralline algae are red seaweeds that lay down hard limestone skeletons, cementing coral reefs together like pink mortar.

name: Cork
fact: Cork harbour is one of the largest natural harbours in the world, and Cobh at its mouth was the Titanic's last port of call.

name: Corkwing wrasse
fact: The corkwing wrasse of European coasts builds a nest of seaweed in a rock crevice, which the male guards until the eggs hatch.

name: Cormorant
fact: Cormorants have feathers that soak up water, which helps them dive after fish, so they stand with wings spread to dry afterwards.

name: Cornetfish
fact: The cornetfish is an extremely slender reef fish up to 1.5 metres long, with a tubular snout and a whip-like filament trailing from its tail.

name: Corvina
fact: Corvinas are drum fish of the eastern Pacific and elsewhere that croak with swim-bladder muscles, and some gather in deafening spawning choruses.

name: Corydoras
fact: Corydoras catfish dart to the surface to gulp air and absorb the oxygen through the lining of the gut.

name: Costa Concordia
fact: The cruise ship Costa Concordia struck rocks and capsized off the Italian island of Giglio in January 2012; it was refloated two years later and scrapped.

name: Cownose ray
fact: Cownose rays migrate in schools of thousands along the US east coast and feed by digging clams out of the sand.

name: Cowrie
fact: Cowrie shells stay smooth and glossy because the living animal wraps its mantle over the outside, and they once served as money across Africa and Asia.

name: Cowtail stingray
fact: The cowtail stingray has a flap of skin under its tail like a feather, and its rough skin has been used to make shagreen leather.

name: Cozumel Reefs National Park
fact: Cozumel's reefs off Mexico's Yucatán are known for drift diving, where the current carries divers along walls such as Palancar and Santa Rosa.

name: Crab
fact: Crabs must shed their hard shells to grow, hiding away while the soft new shell underneath hardens.

name: Crab boat
fact: Crab boats work the Bering Sea in winter, hauling heavy steel pots in freezing seas, a job made famous by the television series Deadliest Catch.

name: Crab-eating macaque
fact: Crab-eating macaques forage in South-East Asian mangroves at low tide, cracking crabs and shellfish, and some use stone tools to do it.

name: Crab larva
fact: Crab larvae, called zoea, drift in the plankton wearing a spiky helmet and look nothing like the adults they will become.

name: Crabeater seal
fact: Crabeater seals do not eat crabs at all; they strain krill through their intricately lobed teeth and are probably the most numerous seal on Earth.

name: Crayfish
fact: Crayfish are freshwater relatives of lobsters, and Louisiana alone boils up tens of thousands of tonnes of them every year.

name: Creole wrasse
fact: The creole wrasse is a purple Caribbean wrasse that, unlike most wrasses, feeds in schools on plankton high above the reef.

name: Cretoxyrhina
fact: Cretoxyrhina, the 'ginsu shark', was a 7-metre Cretaceous shark whose bite marks are found on mosasaur and plesiosaur bones.

name: Crinoid shrimp
fact: Crinoid shrimps live hidden among the arms of feather stars and match their host's colours exactly, from yellow to black.

name: Crinoid squat lobster
fact: The crinoid squat lobster lives among the arms of feather stars, striped to match its host.

name: Crocodile icefish
fact: Icefish of the Southern Ocean are the only vertebrates with no red blood cells or haemoglobin, so their blood runs clear and their hearts are oversized.

name: Crocodile shark
fact: The crocodile shark, the smallest of the mackerel sharks, has huge eyes for hunting in dim water and snaps hard when hauled aboard.

name: Crocodilefish
fact: The crocodilefish lies flat on the sand with a crocodile-like head and lacy eyelids that break up the outline of its eyes.

name: Cromwell Current
fact: The Cromwell Current is a hidden river of water flowing east beneath the surface of the equatorial Pacific, discovered only in 1952.

name: Crown jellyfish
fact: The deep-sea crown jellyfish Atolla sets off a spinning blue 'burglar alarm' of light when attacked, calling in bigger predators to eat its attacker.

name: Crown-of-thorns starfish
fact: The crown-of-thorns starfish is covered in venomous spines and eats living coral, and outbreaks of it have stripped large areas of the Great Barrier Reef.

name: Cruise ship
fact: The largest cruise ships today carry more than 5,000 passengers and are longer than three football pitches laid end to end.

name: Crusty nautilus
fact: The crusty nautilus of Papua New Guinea has a shell coated in a hairy, slimy layer and was not seen alive for about 30 years until 2015.

name: Crystal goby
fact: The crystal goby is an almost invisible, glass-bodied fish that lives in open water off European coasts rather than on the seabed like most gobies.

name: Crystal jelly
fact: The transparent crystal jelly is the source of green fluorescent protein, which won a Nobel Prize and now lights up cells in labs worldwide.

name: Cuba
fact: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean, sitting where the Atlantic, the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea meet.

name: Cubera snapper
fact: The cubera snapper is the largest snapper in the Atlantic, reaching over 1.5 metres, with thick canine teeth like a dog's.

name: Cuckoo ray
fact: The cuckoo ray has a big dark-and-yellow eye spot on each wing and lives on sandy bottoms of the north-east Atlantic.

name: Cuckoo wrasse
fact: The cuckoo wrasse male is one of Britain's most colourful fish, vivid blue and orange, while the female is pink; all start life as females.

name: Cunner
fact: The cunner is a small wrasse of the northwest Atlantic that becomes torpid in winter, hiding in crevices and barely moving in the cold.

name: Curled octopus
fact: The curled octopus, common around Britain, holds its arms curled upward at the tips and has just a single row of suckers on each arm.

name: Currach
fact: The currach is an Irish boat of tarred canvas or hide stretched over a wooden frame, used for fishing in the Atlantic off the west coast.

name: Cushion sea star
fact: The cushion sea star is the big orange starfish of Caribbean seagrass beds, often stacked up by snorkellers for photos.

name: Cusk
fact: The cusk, or tusk, is a single-dorsal-finned cod relative of deep North Atlantic waters, eaten in Norway and New England.

name: Cusk-eel
fact: Cusk-eels back tail-first into burrows in sand, and one species was trawled from 8,370 metres in the Puerto Rico Trench, long the record for the deepest fish.

name: Cutthroat eel
fact: Cutthroat eels are deep-sea eels named for the slit-like gill openings low on the throat, found on the seabed down to several thousand metres.

name: Cutthroat trout
fact: Cutthroat trout are named for the red slash under the jaw, and coastal populations migrate down to the sea and back.

name: Cuttlefish
fact: Cuttlefish control their buoyancy with a porous internal shell, the cuttlebone, and can change colour and skin texture in a fraction of a second.

name: Cuvier's beaked whale
fact: Cuvier's beaked whale holds the mammal diving records, with dives to nearly 3,000 metres and lasting over three hours.

name: Cyanobacteria
fact: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic bacteria whose ancestors first filled the atmosphere with oxygen more than 2 billion years ago.

name: Dab
fact: The dab is a small, common flatfish of north European sandy seabeds, with rough skin and a lateral line that curves over the pectoral fin.

name: Dahab Blue Hole
fact: The Blue Hole at Dahab in Egypt is a 100-metre-deep sinkhole in the Red Sea reef whose deep arch has claimed many divers' lives.

name: Dakar
fact: Dakar, on the Cap-Vert peninsula, is the westernmost city on the African mainland and a major Atlantic port.

name: Dall's porpoise
fact: Dall's porpoise is one of the fastest small cetaceans, throwing up a rooster tail of spray, and Japan's hunt of it was for decades the largest direct hunt of any cetacean.

name: Dampier Strait
fact: Dampier Strait in Papua New Guinea is named after William Dampier, the English buccaneer and naturalist who sailed through it in 1700.

name: Damselfish
fact: Damselfish are small, feisty reef fish; some farm patches of algae on the reef and chase off intruders many times their size.

name: Dana octopus squid
fact: The Dana octopus squid carries the largest light organs in the animal kingdom, lemon-sized photophores on two of its arms that it flashes to stun prey.

name: Dandelion siphonophore
fact: The dandelion siphonophore tethers itself to rocks at Pacific vents with fine threads, looking like a dandelion seed head, and eats scraps from the vent community.

name: Danionella cerebrum
fact: Danionella cerebrum, a transparent 12-millimetre fish from Myanmar, makes drumming sounds as loud as a pneumatic drill and has the smallest known vertebrate brain.

name: Dardanelles
fact: The Dardanelles, known in ancient times as the Hellespont, link the Sea of Marmara to the Aegean and were the scene of the Gallipoli campaign in 1915.

name: Darwin's Arch
fact: Darwin's Arch in the northern Galápagos was a natural rock arch above a legendary hammerhead dive site until it collapsed into the sea in 2021.

name: Davidson Seamount
fact: Davidson Seamount off central California is a huge extinct volcano whose deep flanks hold forests of ancient corals and an 'octopus garden' of brooding mothers.

name: Davis Strait
fact: Davis Strait between Baffin Island and Greenland is named after the English explorer John Davis, who sailed through it in the 1580s seeking the Northwest Passage.

name: Day octopus
fact: The day octopus hunts on tropical reefs in daylight, changing colour and texture many times a minute as it crosses different backgrounds.

name: Dead man's fingers
fact: Dead man's fingers is a dark green, spongy, finger-shaped seaweed that is really a single giant cell with many nuclei.

name: Dean's Blue Hole
fact: Dean's Blue Hole in the Bahamas plunges to about 200 metres from a shallow beach and is a favourite venue for world-record freediving.

name: Decorator crab
fact: Decorator crabs snip bits of sponge, seaweed and anemone and hook them onto bristles on their shell as living camouflage.

name: Deep-sea lizardfish
fact: The deep-sea lizardfish is a toothy ambush predator of abyssal plains between about 1,000 and 3,500 metres, and is both male and female at once.

name: Deepsea Challenger
fact: Deepsea Challenger carried the film director James Cameron alone to the bottom of the Challenger Deep in 2012.

name: Deepstaria
fact: Deepstaria is a deep-sea jellyfish like a loose, bag-shaped sheet that closes around prey the way a drawstring sack does.

name: Delaware Bay
fact: Delaware Bay hosts the world's largest spawning gathering of horseshoe crabs each spring, feeding millions of migrating shorebirds.

name: Denise's pygmy seahorse
fact: Denise's pygmy seahorse is a 2-centimetre orange seahorse found on sea fans across the Coral Triangle, named after the photographer Denise Tackett.

name: Denmark Strait
fact: The Denmark Strait between Greenland and Iceland is where the Bismarck sank HMS Hood in 1941, and it carries the world's biggest underwater waterfall.

name: Dentex
fact: The common dentex is a big-toothed Mediterranean bream prized by spearfishers and famous on Croatian and Greek menus.

name: Devil ray
fact: Devil rays leap metres into the air and belly-flop back down in spectacular group displays off Mexico.

name: Dhow
fact: Dhows are the traditional lateen-rigged sailing vessels of the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean, used for centuries in trade between Arabia, East Africa and India.

name: Diamond squid
fact: The diamond squid swims in lifelong pairs and gets its name from the rhombus shape of fins that run the full length of its body.

name: Diamond stingray
fact: The diamond stingray of the eastern Pacific has a diamond-shaped disc and a tail longer than its body armed with a venomous spine.

name: Diatom
fact: Diatoms are single-celled algae encased in glass-like shells of silica, and they carry out roughly a fifth of all photosynthesis on Earth.

name: Dinghy
fact: A dinghy is a small open boat, often carried aboard or towed behind a larger vessel as a tender to reach the shore.

name: Dinoflagellate
fact: Dinoflagellates are single-celled plankton with two whip-like tails; some cause red tides and others light up the sea at night.

name: Discus
fact: Discus parents feed their fry with a nutritious mucus secreted from their own skin, and the young graze on both parents for weeks.

name: Dog whelk
fact: The dog whelk drills through the shells of mussels and barnacles with its tongue-like radula and was once used to make purple dye.

name: Dogger Bank
fact: Dogger Bank is a large sandbank in the middle of the North Sea that was dry land, part of Doggerland, when sea levels were lower after the last ice age.

name: Dogtooth tuna
fact: The dogtooth tuna is a reef-hunting member of the tuna family with large, conical teeth; it is a bonito rather than a true tuna.

name: Doliolid
fact: Doliolids are transparent, barrel-shaped plankton with muscle bands like hoops, and a single founder can bud a chain of hundreds of clones.

name: Dolly Varden
fact: The Dolly Varden is a char named after a brightly dressed character in a Charles Dickens novel, and many populations migrate to sea and back.

name: Dolphin
fact: Dolphins are toothed whales with cone-shaped teeth and a beak, and they hunt using echolocation clicks.

name: Domino damselfish
fact: Young domino damselfish shelter among the tentacles of sea anemones, like clownfish, before moving onto coral heads as adults.

name: Don Walsh
fact: Don Walsh, a US Navy lieutenant, piloted the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom of the Challenger Deep with Jacques Piccard in 1960.

name: Doña Paz
fact: The Philippine ferry Doña Paz collided with a tanker and sank in December 1987, the deadliest peacetime shipwreck ever, with more than 4,000 dead.

name: Dorudon
fact: Dorudon was a 5-metre early whale whose skeletons lie by the hundred in Egypt's Wadi Al-Hitan, the Valley of the Whales.

name: Dory
fact: The dory is a flat-bottomed, high-sided rowing boat once launched from fishing schooners on the Grand Banks to set cod lines.

name: Dottyback
fact: Dottybacks are small, often vividly coloured reef fish that lurk in crevices, and the orchid dottyback is bred in captivity for aquariums.

name: Dover sole
fact: Dover sole hide in sand by day and hunt worms and small crustaceans at night across the north-east Atlantic.

name: Dragon Hole
fact: The Dragon Hole in the South China Sea plunges roughly 300 metres into the reef and was the deepest known blue hole until the Taam Ja' Blue Hole off Mexico was measured deeper in 2024.

name: Dragon moray
fact: The dragon moray has curved fangs and horn-like nostril tubes, making it one of the most striking eels of Indo-Pacific reefs.

name: Dragon wrasse
fact: The dragon wrasse, or rockmover, flips over rocks with its mouth to find prey; as a juvenile it mimics a drifting piece of seaweed.

name: Dragonet
fact: Dragonets are small, scaleless fish that bury themselves in sand with only their eyes showing; the male common dragonet has a huge sail-like fin.

name: Dragonfish
fact: Deep-sea dragonfish have transparent teeth, a glowing chin barbel, and jaws that can open past 100 degrees.

name: Drake Passage
fact: The Drake Passage between Cape Horn and Antarctica, named after Sir Francis Drake, has some of the roughest seas on Earth.

name: Drum
fact: Drums are named for the drumming sound they make by vibrating special muscles against their swim bladder, mostly to call mates.

name: Dubois' sea snake
fact: Dubois' sea snake of northern Australia has one of the most toxic venoms of any snake, yet it bites only when provoked and hunts fish and moray eels on the seabed.

name: Dugong
fact: Dugongs graze on seagrass meadows and have a fluked tail like a whale's, unlike the manatee's rounded paddle.

name: Dulse
fact: Dulse is a red seaweed eaten for centuries in Ireland, Scotland and Iceland, often dried and sold as a salty snack.

name: Dumbo octopus
fact: Dumbo octopuses flap ear-like fins to swim and have been filmed nearly 7,000 metres down in the Java Trench, deeper than any other octopus.

name: Dungeness crab
fact: The Dungeness crab, named after a small town in Washington State, is one of the most valuable fisheries on the US West Coast.

name: Dunkleosteus
fact: Dunkleosteus was an armoured fish of the Devonian seas that sliced prey with bony blades instead of teeth.

name: Dusky dolphin
fact: Dusky dolphins of New Zealand, South Africa and South America are famous for high, acrobatic leaps and somersaults.

name: Dusky farmerfish
fact: The dusky farmerfish is a damselfish that cultivates a single species of red alga in its territory, weeding out everything else, in one of the only known cases of farming by a fish.

name: Dusky grouper
fact: The dusky grouper is the big grouper of Mediterranean rocky reefs, a favourite of divers in marine reserves after decades of spearfishing made it scarce.

name: Dusky shark
fact: Dusky sharks grow slowly and do not breed until about 20 years old, which makes them very vulnerable to overfishing.

name: Dwarf cuttlefish
fact: The dwarf cuttlefish grows to only about 7 centimetres and is a favourite in research labs and home aquariums for its rapid colour changes.

name: Dwarf gourami
fact: The dwarf gourami breathes air with a labyrinth organ, and the male builds a floating nest of bubbles for the eggs.

name: Dwarf lanternshark
fact: The dwarf lanternshark is probably the smallest shark in the world, fully grown at around 20 centimetres long.

name: Dwarf minke whale
fact: Dwarf minke whales gather on the northern Great Barrier Reef every winter, the only place in the world with licensed tours to swim with them.

name: Dwarf pencilfish
fact: The dwarf pencilfish is a slender 3.5-centimetre fish of Amazon blackwater streams with bold horizontal stripes.

name: Dwarf pygmy goby
fact: The dwarf pygmy goby of Philippine mangrove streams is about 1 centimetre long as an adult and was long considered the smallest fish in the world.

name: Dwarf rasbora
fact: The dwarf rasbora, Boraras maculatus, is a 2-centimetre spotted fish of Malaysian peat swamps.

name: Dwarf seahorse
fact: The dwarf seahorse of Florida's seagrass beds is about 2.5 centimetres long and was once listed as the slowest-moving fish in the world.

name: Dwarf sperm whale
fact: The dwarf sperm whale is the smallest animal commonly called a whale, at about 2.7 metres long, and releases a cloud of dark fluid when alarmed.

name: Eagle ray
fact: Eagle rays flap their pointed wings to fly through the water and sometimes leap clear of the surface.

name: East Australian Current
fact: The East Australian Current sweeps warm water south along Australia's east coast and was the EAC ridden by the turtles in Finding Nemo.

name: East China Sea
fact: The East China Sea lies between China and Japan's Ryukyu Islands and receives the muddy outflow of the Yangtze River.

name: East Greenland Current
fact: The East Greenland Current carries cold water and sea ice south from the Arctic along Greenland's east coast and through the Denmark Strait.

name: East Pacific red octopus
fact: The East Pacific red octopus is the most common shallow-water octopus from Alaska to Baja California, though its body is only about 10 centimetres long.

name: East Pacific Rise
fact: The East Pacific Rise is a fast-spreading mid-ocean ridge where the first black-smoker hydrothermal vents were discovered in 1979.

name: Easter Island
fact: Easter Island is one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth, more than 3,500 kilometres from Chile, and is famous for its giant stone moai.

name: Eastern emerald elysia
fact: The eastern emerald elysia steals chloroplasts from the alga it eats and can then live for months on photosynthesis alone, like a leaf that crawls.

name: Eastern oyster
fact: The eastern oyster builds reefs along the Gulf of Mexico, and the Gulf produces most of the oysters eaten in the United States.

name: Eastern Pacific bonito
fact: The eastern Pacific bonito ranges from Chile to Alaska and is a common catch for anglers off California.

name: Edible crab
fact: The edible or brown crab, with its pie-crust shell edge, is the most heavily fished crab in Western Europe.

name: Edible sea urchin
fact: The edible sea urchin is a large pinkish urchin of the north-east Atlantic that grazes kelp and is harvested for its roe.

name: Eel
fact: Freshwater eels hatch in the open ocean, spend years growing in rivers and lakes, and then return to the sea to spawn and die.

name: Eelgrass
fact: Eelgrass is a seagrass of cool northern coasts whose meadows are nurseries for young cod, herring and crabs.

name: Eelpout
fact: Eelpouts are blunt-headed, eel-shaped fish of cold seas; some live at hydrothermal vents and others on abyssal plains below 4,000 metres.

name: El Faro
fact: The cargo ship El Faro sank in Hurricane Joaquin in October 2015 with all 33 crew, and was found about 4,600 metres down near the Bahamas.

name: Elasmosaurus
fact: Elasmosaurus had a neck of more than 70 vertebrae, and its first describer famously mounted the skull on the wrong end.

name: Electric catfish
fact: The electric catfish of African rivers can deliver shocks of about 350 volts and was pictured in ancient Egyptian tomb art.

name: Electric eel
fact: The electric eel takes about 80 per cent of its oxygen from the air and must surface to breathe every few minutes.

name: Electric ray
fact: Electric rays can deliver shocks of up to about 220 volts from kidney-shaped organs on either side of their head.

name: Elegant sea snake
fact: The elegant sea snake is one of the longest sea snakes, reaching about 2 metres, and lives in the turbid waters off northern Australia.

name: Elephant fish
fact: The elephant fish of Australia and New Zealand is a chimaera that probes the seabed with its trunk-like snout, sensing the electric fields of buried shellfish.

name: Elephant seal
fact: Elephant seals are named for the huge inflatable nose of the males, which amplifies their roars during breeding fights.

name: Elephant shark
fact: The elephant shark of Australia and New Zealand has the slowest-evolving genome of any vertebrate yet studied.

name: Elephantnose fish
fact: Peters's elephantnose fish of African rivers has a finger-like chin extension packed with electric sensors, used to probe the mud for food.

name: Elkhorn coral
fact: Elkhorn coral's thick branches once built the shallow crests of Caribbean reefs, and it was among the first corals listed as threatened in the United States.

name: Elpidia
fact: Elpidia are small, stubby sea cucumbers that plough the mud of trench floors in herds, among the most numerous large animals at hadal depths.

name: Elysia sea slug
fact: The sea slug Elysia marginata can shed its own head, which then regrows an entire new body, heart included, within weeks.

name: Ember tetra
fact: The ember tetra is a fiery orange fish from Brazil's Araguaia river basin that grows to only about 2 centimetres.

name: Emiliania huxleyi
fact: Emiliania huxleyi is the most widespread coccolithophore, a chalk-plated alga whose blooms stretch for hundreds of kilometres and turn the sea turquoise.

name: Emperor angelfish
fact: The emperor angelfish of Indo-Pacific reefs is striped blue and yellow as an adult, but its juvenile is dark blue with white rings, so different it was once thought a separate species.

name: Emperor penguin
fact: Emperor penguins dive deeper than 500 metres for fish, squid and krill, and the males fast for about four months while incubating an egg on their feet.

name: Emperor shrimp
fact: The emperor shrimp rides on sea cucumbers and Spanish dancer nudibranchs, picking food from the sand as its host crawls along.

name: Endler's livebearer
fact: Endler's livebearer is a tiny, brilliantly coloured relative of the guppy from Venezuela, with males under 3 centimetres long.

name: Endurance
fact: Shackleton's ship Endurance, crushed by ice in 1915, was found in March 2022 at 3,008 metres in the Weddell Sea, with its name still legible on the stern.

name: Enewetak Atoll
fact: Enewetak Atoll in the Marshall Islands was the site of 43 nuclear tests, and deep drilling into its reef in 1952 proved Darwin's theory of how atolls form.

name: English Channel
fact: The English Channel separates England from France and joins the Atlantic to the North Sea; it is about 34 kilometres across at the Strait of Dover.

name: Epaulette shark
fact: The epaulette shark can walk across exposed reef flats on its fins and survive for hours with almost no oxygen.

name: Equatorial Counter Current
fact: The Equatorial Counter Current flows eastward against the trade winds in a narrow band near the equator, between the westward-flowing equatorial currents.

name: Escolar
fact: Escolar lives deep in the open ocean, and its flesh is so rich in indigestible wax that eating it can cause oily stomach upsets.

name: Ethereal snailfish
fact: The ethereal snailfish was filmed at 8,145 metres in the Mariana Trench in 2014, a wispy, nearly transparent fish known only from video, as none has yet been caught.

name: Eugenie Clark
fact: Eugenie Clark, the Shark Lady, studied shark behaviour for decades and discovered a Red Sea fish whose secretions repel sharks.

name: Eulachon
fact: The eulachon is a small smelt so oily that a dried fish can be lit like a candle, and it runs from the sea up Pacific north-west rivers each spring.

name: European conger
fact: The European conger is one of the largest eels, reaching about 3 metres and more than 100 kilograms, and lurks in wrecks and rocky holes.

name: European eel
fact: The European eel can spend 20 years or more in rivers before swimming about 5,000 kilometres to spawn in the Sargasso Sea.

name: European flat oyster
fact: The European flat oyster was once so common that it was poor people's food in Victorian London; reefs of it are now being restored around Britain.

name: European flounder
fact: The European flounder moves far up rivers into fresh water and returns to the sea to spawn.

name: European flying squid
fact: The European flying squid ranges from the Arctic to West Africa, and in some years swarms into Norwegian fjords in vast numbers.

name: European hake
fact: The European hake is a slim, sharp-toothed cod relative fished from Norway to West Africa; Spain eats more of it than any other country.

name: European lobster
fact: The European lobster is dark blue when alive and only turns red when it is cooked, as heat breaks down the pigment that masks the red.

name: European perch
fact: The European perch lives in lakes and rivers and in the brackish Baltic Sea, and has become invasive in Australia as the redfin.

name: European spiny lobster
fact: The European spiny lobster, or langouste, has no claws but long spiny antennae, and is the prized lobster of Mediterranean kitchens.

name: European squid
fact: The European squid, the classic calamari of Mediterranean menus, has a body about 30 to 40 centimetres long and hunts fish in coastal waters.

name: Eurythenes plasticus
fact: This amphipod from nearly 7,000 metres down in the Mariana Trench was named 'plasticus' in 2020 because microplastic fibres were found in its gut.

name: Nautilus (research vessel)
fact: The exploration vessel Nautilus, run by Titanic discoverer Robert Ballard's Ocean Exploration Trust, streams its deep-sea dives live to the public.

name: Fabien Cousteau
fact: Fabien Cousteau, grandson of Jacques, spent 31 days living in the undersea laboratory Aquarius in 2014, beating his grandfather's record.

name: Fairy wrasse
fact: Fairy wrasses are small, dazzling wrasses of Indo-Pacific reefs; males flash their colours in courtship displays, and new species are still being named.

name: Falkland Current
fact: The Falkland Current carries cold Antarctic water north along the coast of Argentina, bringing Magellanic penguins as far north as Brazil.

name: Falkland Islands
fact: The Falkland Islands lie in the South Atlantic about 500 kilometres east of Argentina and have far more sheep and penguins than people.

name: Falkor
fact: Falkor and its successor Falkor (too) are research ships run by the Schmidt Ocean Institute that offer free ship time to scientists and have mapped vast areas of sea floor.

name: False catshark
fact: The false catshark is a flabby deep-water shark with a long, low dorsal fin and has been found down to about 1,500 metres.

name: False killer whale
fact: False killer whales are large dark dolphins known for sharing prey with each other and for hunting alongside bottlenose dolphins.

name: Fangtooth
fact: The fangtooth has the largest teeth of any fish relative to its body size, so big that it has sockets in its skull for them to fit into.

name: Fangtooth moray
fact: The fangtooth moray, with glassy, needle-like teeth and a bright yellow head, lives in the warmer rocky waters of the eastern Atlantic, including the Canaries and Madeira.

name: Farallon Islands
fact: The Farallon Islands off San Francisco are a wildlife refuge where great white sharks gather each autumn to hunt seals.

name: Faroe Islands
fact: The Faroe Islands are 18 rugged islands between Norway and Iceland, where sheep outnumber people and the cliffs host huge seabird colonies.

name: Feather duster worm
fact: Feather duster worms spread a fan of feathery tentacles from a parchment tube to trap plankton, and many have eyes on the tentacles to spot shadows.

name: Feather star
fact: Feather stars are crinoids that cling to reefs with tiny claw-like legs and can swim short distances by waving their feathery arms.

name: Felucca
fact: The felucca is a traditional wooden sailing boat with one or two lateen sails, used on the Nile and along the Red Sea and Mediterranean coasts.

name: Fendouzhe
fact: Fendouzhe, meaning Striver, is the Chinese submersible that carried three people to the bottom of the Challenger Deep in 2020.

name: Ferdinand Magellan
fact: Ferdinand Magellan led the first expedition to cross the Pacific, which he named for its calm waters, though he was killed in the Philippines before it completed the first circumnavigation.

name: Fernando de Noronha
fact: Fernando de Noronha is a volcanic archipelago off north-east Brazil famous for its spinner dolphins and strictly limited number of visitors.

name: Ferry
fact: Ferries carry passengers and vehicles on regular routes across the water, and some of the busiest in the world cross the English Channel and the Baltic.

name: Fiddler crab
fact: A male fiddler crab has one claw far bigger than the other and waves it to attract females and warn off rivals.

name: Fiji
fact: Fiji is a nation of more than 300 islands in the South Pacific, and its Great Sea Reef is one of the longest barrier reefs in the world.

name: Filefish
fact: Filefish have skin so rough that it was once used as sandpaper, and a single stout spine on the head that they can lock upright.

name: Fin whale
fact: The fin whale is the second-largest animal and has odd asymmetric colouring, with a white lower right jaw and a dark left one.

name: Finger coral
fact: Finger coral grows in stubby, finger-like branches and is a sturdy, common coral in the shallows of Caribbean and Pacific reefs.

name: Finless porpoise
fact: Finless porpoises have no dorsal fin and live in shallow coastal waters, estuaries and rivers of Asia, including the Yangtze.

name: Fire coral
fact: Fire coral is not a true coral but a relative of jellyfish, and brushing its yellow-brown branches leaves a burning sting.

name: Firefly squid
fact: Every spring millions of firefly squid rise to the surface of Toyama Bay in Japan, lighting the water blue with thousands of tiny photophores.

name: Fish larva
fact: Most sea fish start life as transparent larvae a few millimetres long, drifting in the plankton for weeks before they can swim properly.

name: Fishing cat
fact: The fishing cat of South Asia's wetlands and Sundarbans mangroves dives into the water to catch fish and is a strong swimmer.

name: Fishing smack
fact: A fishing smack was a sailing boat, often with a wet well to keep the catch alive, used around the British coast into the 20th century.

name: Flabby whalefish
fact: Flabby whalefish live below about 1,500 metres and look so different from their own larvae and males that the three were once classed as separate families.

name: Flamboyant cuttlefish
fact: The flamboyant cuttlefish walks along the seabed on its arms and is the only cuttlefish known to have poisonous flesh.

name: Flame angelfish
fact: The flame angelfish is a small, fiery red-orange dwarf angelfish with black bars from the Pacific islands, a prized aquarium fish.

name: Flamingo tongue
fact: The flamingo tongue is a small Caribbean snail whose leopard-spotted colours are on a living mantle wrapped over a plain white shell, and it eats sea fans.

name: Flapjack octopus
fact: The flapjack octopus, a deep-sea dumbo relative that inspired Pearl in Finding Nemo, can flatten its webbed body into a pancake shape.

name: Flapper skate
fact: The flapper skate is the largest skate in the world, reaching about 2.5 metres long, and lays egg cases up to about 25 centimetres long.

name: Flashlight fish
fact: Flashlight fish have bean-shaped pouches of glowing bacteria under each eye, which they blink by rolling or shuttering the organ.

name: Flatback turtle
fact: The flatback turtle nests only on Australian beaches and never leaves the continental shelf, so it is the only sea turtle without an ocean-crossing stage.

name: Flatfish
fact: Flatfish lie on one side on the seabed, and the side facing down loses its colour while the upper side matches the sand.

name: Flathead
fact: Flatheads are flattened Australian fish with a wide, bony head that lie half-buried in sand waiting for prey.

name: Flathead catfish
fact: The flathead catfish is a big, mottled yellow-brown predator that eats only live prey, and is caught by 'noodling' with bare hands in the southern United States.

name: Flemish Cap
fact: The Flemish Cap is an underwater plateau east of the Grand Banks, a fishing ground immortalised in the film The Perfect Storm.

name: Flightless cormorant
fact: The flightless cormorant of the Galápagos has stubby wings about a third the size needed for flight and dives for fish and octopus close to shore.

name: Florida Current
fact: The Florida Current squeezes between Florida and the Bahamas as the start of the Gulf Stream and carries far more water than all the world's rivers combined.

name: Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary
aliases: John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park
fact: The Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary protects the only living coral barrier reef in the continental United States.

name: Florida pompano
fact: The Florida pompano is caught in the Gulf of Mexico surf with sand fleas and is one of the most expensive fish on American menus.

name: Florida Reef
fact: The Florida Reef is the only living coral barrier reef in the continental United States, running from near Miami to the Dry Tortugas.

name: Flounder
fact: Flounders start life with an eye on each side, then one eye migrates across the head as the fish settles flat on the seabed.

name: Flower Garden Banks
aliases: Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary
fact: The Flower Garden Banks are coral reefs growing on top of salt domes in the Gulf of Mexico, about 160 kilometres off the Texas coast.

name: Flower hat jelly
fact: The flower hat jelly of Japan has fluorescent pink-tipped tentacles coiled around its rim and spends the day resting on the seabed.

name: Flower urchin
fact: The flower urchin is the most dangerous sea urchin: its flower-like pincers inject a venom that can cause paralysis and has been blamed for diver deaths.

name: Flying fish
fact: Flying fish sprint to about 60 kilometres per hour to burst from the water, then glide up to 200 metres on wing-like fins; their roe is tobiko in sushi.

name: Football octopus
fact: The football octopus is the only cephalopod with a true swim bladder, and its tiny males ride inside empty salp barrels in the open ocean.

name: Footballfish
fact: Footballfish are round-bodied deep-sea anglers; several have washed up on California beaches, a rare sight of a fish from about 1,000 metres down.

name: Foraminifera
fact: Foraminifera are single-celled, shell-building organisms, and soft-walled species live in the mud at the very bottom of the Challenger Deep.

name: Four-eyed fish
fact: The four-eyed fish of Central and South American estuaries has eyes divided in two, letting it see above and below the surface at the same time.

name: Foureye butterflyfish
fact: The foureye butterflyfish of the Caribbean has a large false eye near the tail, so predators strike at the wrong end.

name: Foxe Basin
fact: Foxe Basin north of Hudson Bay is named after Luke Foxe, the English explorer who searched it for the Northwest Passage in 1631.

name: Fram
fact: Fram was built for Fridtjof Nansen to be frozen into the Arctic ice and drift across the polar sea, and later carried Roald Amundsen to Antarctica.

name: Francis Drake
fact: Sir Francis Drake was the first captain to complete a circumnavigation of the globe, from 1577 to 1580, and the stormy passage below Cape Horn is named after him.

name: Franciscana
fact: The franciscana, or La Plata dolphin, lives in the Río de la Plata estuary and nearby coasts and has the longest beak for its size of any dolphin.

name: Fraser's dolphin
fact: Fraser's dolphin was described in 1956 from a skeleton found in Sarawak and was not seen alive by scientists until the 1970s.

name: Freetown
fact: Freetown, Sierra Leone, was founded in 1792 as a home for freed slaves and has one of the largest natural harbours in the world.

name: French angelfish
fact: The French angelfish is black with golden scale edges, mates for life and often approaches divers; its juveniles clean parasites from other fish.

name: French grunt
fact: French grunts shelter in dense schools on Caribbean reefs by day and spread out over the sand at night to feed.

name: Freshwater angelfish
fact: The freshwater angelfish is an Amazon cichlid with tall triangular fins that pairs for life and guards its eggs on a leaf.

name: Freshwater drum
fact: The freshwater drum of North American rivers grunts with swim-bladder muscles, and its ear bones, 'lucky stones', have been found in ancient sites.

name: Freshwater eel
fact: Freshwater eels spend most of their lives in rivers and lakes, then make a single journey to the sea to spawn and die.

name: Fridtjof Nansen
fact: Fridtjof Nansen let his ship Fram freeze into the Arctic ice to drift across the polar sea and later invented the Nansen bottle for sampling seawater at depth.

name: Fried egg jellyfish
fact: The fried egg jellyfish of the Mediterranean looks exactly like its name, with a yellow dome on a white bell, and small fish shelter among its arms.

name: Frigate tuna
fact: The frigate tuna is a small, torpedo-shaped tuna found worldwide in warm seas, important both as food and as bait.

name: Frigatebird
fact: Frigatebirds avoid landing on water because their feathers are not waterproof, so they snatch flying fish and squid from the surface in flight or steal from other birds.

name: Frilled shark
fact: The eel-like frilled shark has around 300 needle-like teeth and may carry its young for over three years before giving birth.

name: Frobisher Bay
fact: Frobisher Bay on Baffin Island is named after Martin Frobisher, who sailed into it in 1576 searching for the Northwest Passage and brought home worthless ore he took for gold.

name: Frogfish
fact: Frogfish are lumpy, camouflaged anglerfish of the reef that lure prey with a fleshy rod on their head and walk on their fins.

name: Frogspawn coral
fact: Frogspawn coral is named for its bubbly tentacle tips, which look like a mass of frog's eggs.

name: Fur seal
fact: Fur seals have a dense double layer of fur that once made them a target for hunters, and they are more closely related to sea lions than to true seals.

name: Gafftopsail catfish
fact: The gafftopsail catfish is a sea catfish of the western Atlantic with long, sail-like fin filaments and venomous spines.

name: Gag grouper
fact: The gag grouper is the most commonly caught grouper off Florida's Gulf coast, a grey fish with wavy markings that forms spawning groups offshore.

name: Gakkel Ridge
fact: The Gakkel Ridge beneath the Arctic ice is the slowest-spreading mid-ocean ridge known, yet it still hosts active hydrothermal vents.

name: Galápagos bullhead shark
fact: The Galápagos bullhead shark is a small spotted shark that rests on the rocks by day and crunches crabs and molluscs at night.

name: Galápagos fur seal
fact: The Galápagos fur seal is the smallest fur seal and lives further north than any other, right on the equator.

name: Galápagos garden eel
fact: Galápagos garden eels live in colonies of burrows on sandy slopes, swaying in the current like grass and vanishing when divers approach.

name: Galápagos grouper
fact: The Galápagos grouper, known locally as bacalao, is found almost only around the islands and is the most valued fish of the local fishery.

name: Galápagos Islands
fact: The Galápagos Islands straddle the equator about 1,000 kilometres off Ecuador, and their finches and tortoises helped inspire Darwin's theory of evolution.

name: Galápagos Marine Reserve
fact: The Galápagos Marine Reserve covers well over 130,000 square kilometres around the islands and is famous for schooling hammerheads and marine iguanas.

name: Galápagos penguin
fact: The Galápagos penguin is the only penguin living on the equator and is endangered, with fewer than about 2,000 birds.

name: Galápagos sea lion
fact: Galápagos sea lions are so unafraid of people that they sleep on park benches and fish-market floors in the islands' towns.

name: Galápagos shark
fact: Despite its name, the Galápagos shark is found around oceanic islands worldwide, including Bermuda and Ascension in the Atlantic.

name: Galathea
fact: The Danish ship Galathea dredged living animals from more than 10,000 metres in the Philippine Trench in 1951, proving that life exists at the ocean's greatest depths.

name: Gall crab
fact: Gall crabs settle on living coral as larvae and let the coral grow around them, sealing the female inside a chamber for life.

name: Galleon
fact: Galleons were the big, multi-decked sailing ships that carried Spain's silver across the Atlantic in the 16th and 17th centuries.

name: Galley
fact: Galleys were oar-driven warships that dominated the Mediterranean from ancient times until the Battle of Lepanto in 1571.

name: Ganges river dolphin
fact: The Ganges river dolphin is effectively blind, with eyes that lack a lens, and finds its way through muddy rivers by echolocation.

name: Gar
fact: Gars can gulp air into a lung-like swim bladder, letting them survive in warm, stagnant water with little oxygen.

name: Garden eel
fact: Garden eels live in colonies of hundreds, each in its own sand burrow, swaying like grass to catch plankton and sinking out of sight when approached.

name: Garfish
fact: The garfish of the North Sea and Baltic has a needle-like beak and bones that are naturally green.

name: Garibaldi
fact: The garibaldi is a bright orange damselfish of California's kelp forests, the state's official marine fish, and the males fiercely guard nests of red algae.

name: General Belgrano
fact: The Argentine cruiser General Belgrano was torpedoed by a British submarine and sank during the Falklands War in 1982.

name: Gentoo penguin
fact: The gentoo is the fastest-swimming penguin, reaching about 36 kilometres per hour, and feeds on krill and fish close to shore.

name: Geoduck
fact: The geoduck's siphon is so long that it cannot fit inside its shell, and the clam can live for over 150 years buried in the seabed.

name: Geography cone
fact: The geography cone is the deadliest cone snail, nicknamed the cigarette snail because a stung person was said to have time for one cigarette before dying.

name: Georges Bank
fact: Georges Bank is a shallow, fish-rich bank between Cape Cod and Nova Scotia that was once above sea level and later disputed between the USA and Canada.

name: Gerlache Strait
fact: The Gerlache Strait along the Antarctic Peninsula is named after Adrien de Gerlache, the Belgian whose expedition was the first to winter in the Antarctic, in 1898.

name: Gervais' beaked whale
fact: Gervais' beaked whale lives in the deep Atlantic and was first described from a carcass found floating in the English Channel in 1840.

name: Ghost crab
fact: Ghost crabs are pale beach crabs that dig deep burrows and are among the fastest crustaceans on land, sprinting at more than 2 metres per second.

name: Giant Antarctic octopus
fact: The giant Antarctic octopus, the largest octopus in the Southern Ocean, has venom that keeps working at freezing temperatures.

name: Giant barrel sponge
fact: The giant barrel sponge of Caribbean reefs, the 'redwood of the reef', can live for more than 2,000 years.

name: Giant clam
fact: Giant clams can grow over a metre across and get much of their food from algae living in their colourful mantle tissue.

name: Giant cuttlefish
fact: Australian giant cuttlefish gather in their tens of thousands each winter to breed at Whyalla, where small males disguise themselves as females to sneak past rivals.

name: Giant devil ray
fact: The giant devil ray of the Mediterranean can span over 5 metres and gives birth to a single pup after a pregnancy of about two years.

name: Giant freshwater stingray
fact: A giant freshwater stingray caught in the Mekong in 2022 weighed about 300 kilograms, the largest freshwater fish ever recorded.

name: Giant gourami
fact: The giant gourami can grow to about 70 centimetres and uses a labyrinth organ to breathe air.

name: Giant green anemone
fact: The giant green anemone of the Pacific coast gets its colour partly from algae living in its tissues and can grow to about 30 centimetres across.

name: Giant grenadier
fact: The giant grenadier is a deep-water rattail of the North Pacific that grows to over 2 metres long and lives for decades.

name: Giant grouper
fact: The giant grouper, or Queensland grouper, is the largest bony fish on coral reefs, reaching about 2.7 metres and 400 kilograms.

name: Giant isopod
fact: The giant isopod is a deep-sea relative of the woodlouse that grows to about 40 centimetres and can go for years without a meal.

name: Giant kelp
fact: Giant kelp is the largest seaweed, growing up to about 45 metres long and as much as half a metre in a single day.

name: Giant kelpfish
fact: The giant kelpfish mimics a kelp blade, changing colour from green to brown or red to match the seaweed it hides among.

name: Giant larvacean
fact: The giant larvacean builds a mucus house up to a metre across that filters the deep water and, when abandoned, sinks carbon and microplastics to the seafloor.

name: Giant moray
fact: The giant moray can reach 3 metres and is the heaviest moray; it has been filmed hunting cooperatively with groupers on Red Sea reefs.

name: Giant mottled eel
fact: The giant mottled eel is the largest freshwater eel, reaching about 2 metres, and ranges from East Africa to Polynesia.

name: Giant Pacific octopus
fact: The giant Pacific octopus is the largest octopus, with an arm span that can exceed 4 metres, and a female guards her eggs without eating until she dies.

name: Giant petrel
fact: Giant petrels are the vultures of the Southern Ocean, tearing into seal and penguin carcasses, but they also catch fish, squid and krill at sea.

name: Giant river prawn
fact: The giant river prawn, with its long blue claws, is farmed in freshwater ponds across Asia and sold as scampi in India.

name: Giant sea bass
fact: The giant sea bass of California can reach over 2 metres and 250 kilograms, and nearly vanished before fishing for it was banned in 1982.

name: Giant sea spider
fact: Giant sea spiders of the deep and Antarctic seas can span about 70 centimetres, and pump blood with their guts rather than a strong heart.

name: Giant siphonophore
fact: The giant siphonophore Praya dubia can reach 40 to 50 metres long, among the longest animals on Earth, and its stinging tentacles glow when touched.

name: Giant snakehead
fact: The giant snakehead breathes air and can grow to more than a metre long, and the parents aggressively guard their bright red young.

name: Giant squid
fact: The giant squid has the largest eyes of any animal, about the size of a dinner plate, and was not filmed alive in the deep until 2012.

name: Giant trevally
fact: The giant trevally of Indian Ocean reefs has been filmed leaping to snatch terns out of the air, and anglers prize its brutal strength.

name: Giant tube worm
fact: The giant tube worm has no mouth or gut: bacteria inside it turn vent sulphide into food, letting it grow to 2 metres, nearly a metre of it in a single year.

name: Giant warty squid
fact: The giant warty squid of Antarctic waters can reach more than 2 metres in total length and is a food of sperm whales and other Southern Ocean predators.

name: Gila trout
fact: The Gila trout survives in a handful of mountain streams in New Mexico and Arizona and was among the first fish listed as endangered in the United States.

name: Gizzard shad
fact: The gizzard shad, kohada, is the fish by which Tokyo sushi chefs are judged; it is salted and pickled in vinegar before serving.

name: Glass catfish
fact: The glass catfish of Southeast Asia is so transparent you can see its bones and organs, and it turns milky white when it dies.

name: Glass eel
fact: Young eels arriving at European and American coasts after drifting from the Sargasso Sea are called glass eels because their bodies are completely transparent.

name: Glass octopus
fact: The glass octopus is almost completely transparent; only its eyes, optic nerves and digestive tract show as it drifts through the open ocean.

name: Glass sponge
fact: Glass sponges build skeletons of silica glass fibres, and some deep-sea individuals are thought to be more than 10,000 years old.

name: Glass squid
fact: Glass squid are almost completely transparent and keep their one opaque organ, the digestive gland, pointed vertically so it casts the smallest shadow.

name: Glassy sweeper
fact: Glassy sweepers pack Caribbean caves in coppery schools by day and stream out at night to feed on plankton.

name: Globe skimmer dragonfly
fact: The globe skimmer dragonfly crosses the Indian Ocean between India and East Africa on the monsoon winds, a multi-generation round trip of about 14,000 to 18,000 kilometres.

name: Glomar Challenger
fact: The drilling ship Glomar Challenger took cores from the Atlantic floor in 1968 that confirmed sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics.

name: Gloomy octopus
fact: Gloomy octopuses off eastern Australia gather at sites nicknamed Octopolis and Octlantis, where they have been filmed throwing shells and silt at each other.

name: Glover's Reef
fact: Glover's Reef is an atoll off Belize named after the pirate John Glover and is a marine reserve known for its sheer outer walls.

name: Glowing sucker octopus
fact: The glowing sucker octopus has suckers that no longer grip but glow blue-green, probably to lure the tiny copepods it eats.

name: Glowlight tetra
fact: The glowlight tetra is a 3-to-4-centimetre fish from Guyana with a glowing orange-red stripe down its side.

name: Goatfish
fact: Goatfish dig through sand with a pair of chin barbels used like fingers, and some change from yellow to red in seconds when resting or being cleaned.

name: Goblin shark
fact: The goblin shark shoots its jaws forward to snatch prey, and its pink skin comes from blood vessels showing through.

name: Goby
fact: Gobies are tiny bottom-living fish whose pelvic fins are fused into a sucker that holds them onto rocks in surging water.

name: Golden dorado
fact: The golden dorado of South American rivers is a brilliant gold predator that fly anglers travel to Argentina and Bolivia to catch.

name: Golden Gate
fact: The Golden Gate is the strait connecting San Francisco Bay to the Pacific, and its famous bridge was for decades the longest suspension bridge in the world.

name: Golden trout
fact: The golden trout, with its brilliant gold and red colours, lives in the high Sierra Nevada and is the state freshwater fish of California.

name: Goldfish
fact: Goldfish were bred from dull carp in China about a thousand years ago, and released pets now grow huge and invasive in lakes around the world.

name: Goldsinny
fact: The goldsinny is a small orange-brown wrasse of European rocky shores, now farmed as a cleaner fish to eat lice off farmed salmon.

name: Goliath grouper
fact: The Atlantic goliath grouper can reach 2.5 metres and over 300 kilograms, and makes a booming sound to warn off divers.

name: Goliath tigerfish
fact: The goliath tigerfish of the Congo River has 32 dagger-like teeth and has been known to attack crocodiles.

name: Goonch
fact: The goonch, or giant devil catfish, is a huge, mottled catfish of South Asian rivers, blamed in reports from the Kali River for attacks on bathers.

name: Goose barnacle
fact: Goose barnacles, percebes in Spain, are gathered from wave-battered rocks and are among the most expensive seafood in Europe; medieval writers thought geese hatched from them.

name: Gorgonian
fact: Gorgonians are soft corals with a flexible, horn-like skeleton, growing as sea fans, whips and bushes.

name: Gourami
fact: Gouramis have a labyrinth organ that lets them breathe air from the surface, so they thrive in warm, stagnant water.

name: Grand Banks
fact: The Grand Banks off Newfoundland are shallow underwater plateaus whose cod fishery fed Europe for centuries before collapsing in 1992.

name: Grass carp
fact: The grass carp is the most farmed fish on Earth by weight, raised in Chinese ponds on grass and water plants.

name: Gray angelfish
fact: The gray angelfish is a large, drab Caribbean angelfish that often follows divers; its juveniles are black with yellow bars.

name: Grayling
fact: The grayling, 'lady of the stream', carries a tall sail-like dorsal fin and lives only in clean, cold rivers.

name: Gray's beaked whale
fact: Gray's beaked whale, named after British zoologist John Edward Gray, is the beaked whale most often stranded in New Zealand and is seen in cold Southern Ocean waters.

name: Great auk
fact: The great auk, a flightless North Atlantic seabird, was the original 'penguin', and the last known pair was killed on an Icelandic island in 1844.

name: Great Bahama Bank
fact: The Great Bahama Bank is a vast limestone platform so shallow that its turquoise waters are plainly visible from space, with the Tongue of the Ocean cut into it.

name: Great Barrier Reef
fact: The Great Barrier Reef stretches more than 2,300 kilometres along Australia's north-east coast and is the largest structure ever built by living things.

name: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park
fact: The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park protects about 344,000 square kilometres of reef off Queensland, the largest coral reef system on Earth.

name: Great Blue Hole
fact: The Great Blue Hole off Belize is a near-circular sinkhole about 300 metres across and 120 metres deep that was a dry cave before the sea rose.

name: Great Britain
fact: Great Britain is the largest island in Europe and was joined to the continent by dry land until rising seas flooded Doggerland about 8,000 years ago.

name: Great Chagos Bank
fact: The Great Chagos Bank in the Indian Ocean is the largest atoll structure in the world and is almost entirely submerged.

name: Great hammerhead
fact: The great hammerhead, the largest hammerhead at up to about 6 metres, uses its head to pin stingrays to the seabed.

name: Great Sea Reef
fact: Fiji's Great Sea Reef, known locally as Cakaulevu, is the third-longest continuous barrier reef in the world.

name: Great skua
fact: The great skua, nicknamed the bonxie in Shetland, catches fish itself but is better known for robbing gannets and puffins of theirs.

name: Great white shark
fact: Great white sharks can sense the faint electrical fields given off by the muscles and heartbeat of hidden prey.

name: Greater amberjack
fact: The greater amberjack, kanpachi in Japan, is a fast, powerful hunter of the open water, farmed in sea pens and served as firm, mild sashimi.

name: Greater blue-ringed octopus
fact: Despite its name the greater blue-ringed octopus is only about 10 centimetres across; it is the size of its rings that is greater than its relatives'.

name: Greater forkbeard
fact: The greater forkbeard is a deep-water cod relative of the eastern Atlantic with long, forked pelvic fins used to feel for food.

name: Greater pipefish
fact: The greater pipefish of European coasts grows to about 45 centimetres, and the male broods the eggs in a pouch under his tail.

name: Green-lipped mussel
fact: The green-lipped mussel is found only in New Zealand, where it is farmed on ropes and exported worldwide, including as a joint supplement.

name: Green moray
fact: The green moray of the Caribbean is actually brown; a coat of yellow mucus over its skin makes it look green.

name: Green neon tetra
fact: The green neon tetra is a 2.5-centimetre relative of the neon tetra from the upper Orinoco and Rio Negro with a blue-green stripe.

name: Green sawfish
fact: The green sawfish is one of the largest sawfish, reported at over 7 metres long, and is now critically endangered.

name: Green sea urchin
fact: The green sea urchin lives in cold northern waters of both the Atlantic and the Pacific and is harvested for its roe.

name: Green spotted puffer
fact: The green spotted puffer lives in brackish South-East Asian estuaries and is a common, if demanding, aquarium fish.

name: Green turtle
fact: Adult green sea turtles graze on seagrass and algae, which stains their fat green and gives them their name; they may live for 70 years or more.

name: Greenland
fact: Greenland is the largest island in the world, lying between the Atlantic and Arctic oceans, and about 80 per cent of it is buried under an ice sheet.

name: Greenland cod
fact: The Greenland cod is a dark, slow-growing cod of Arctic coastal waters, caught by Inuit through holes in the ice.

name: Greenland halibut
fact: The Greenland halibut's migrating eye stops at the top edge of its head, so it can swim upright as well as lie flat.

name: Greenland shark
fact: Greenland sharks grow about a centimetre a year and may live for several centuries, longer than any other known vertebrate.

name: Grenadier
fact: Grenadiers, or rattails, are the commonest fish on the deep seabed, with big heads and whip-like tails, and have been seen about 7,000 metres down.

name: Grey mullet
fact: The grey mullet grazes algae and mud in estuaries and harbours around the world, and its roe is pressed into bottarga.

name: Grey reef shark
fact: Grey reef sharks warn off intruders with a hunched, exaggerated swimming display before they attack.

name: Grey seal
fact: Grey seal pups are born with white fur and are weaned in under three weeks, after which the mother leaves them to fend for themselves.

name: Grey snapper
fact: The mangrove snapper, or gray snapper, grows up among mangrove roots and is one of the most commonly caught snappers in Florida.

name: Grey triggerfish
fact: The grey triggerfish is found on both sides of the Atlantic, from the Gulf of Mexico to the Mediterranean, and is increasingly seen off Britain.

name: Grey whale
fact: Grey whales feed unlike any other whale, rolling on their sides to suck up mouthfuls of mud and straining out tiny amphipods through their baleen.

name: Grouper
fact: Groupers are big-mouthed reef predators that suck in prey whole, and some species have been seen hunting together with moray eels.

name: Grunion
fact: Grunion ride the highest tides onto Californian beaches at night to spawn in the sand, and crowds come to catch them by hand.

name: Grunt
fact: Grunts are named for the sound they make by grinding their throat teeth together, amplified by the swim bladder, especially when caught.

name: Grunt sculpin
fact: The grunt sculpin of the Pacific Northwest hops along the bottom on its fins and hides inside empty giant barnacle shells.

name: Guam
fact: Guam is the largest of the Mariana Islands and lies close to the Mariana Trench, the deepest part of the ocean.

name: Guanabara Bay
fact: Guanabara Bay is the great bay on which Rio de Janeiro stands, named River of January by Portuguese sailors who reached it in January 1502 and, by tradition, took it for a river mouth.

name: Guanay cormorant
fact: The guanay cormorant of Peru eats anchovies from the Humboldt Current, and its droppings built the guano deposits that made 19th-century fortunes.

name: Guiana dolphin
fact: The Guiana dolphin lives in estuaries and bays along the Atlantic coast of South and Central America and can sense electric fields with its snout.

name: Guinea Current
fact: The Guinea Current flows eastward along the coast of West Africa into the Gulf of Guinea.

name: Guineafowl puffer
fact: The guineafowl puffer is black with tiny white spots like the bird, and some individuals are entirely golden-yellow instead.

name: Guitarfish
fact: Guitarfish are rays shaped like a guitar, with a flattened shark-like body, and they give birth to live young.

name: Gulf corvina
fact: Gulf corvinas gather by the million in the Colorado River delta to spawn, and their chorus is loud enough to damage the hearing of nearby dolphins.

name: Gulf menhaden
fact: The Gulf menhaden is the biggest fishery by weight in the Gulf of Mexico and the main food of its pelicans, dolphins and redfish.

name: Gulf of Alaska
fact: The Gulf of Alaska is a wide arm of the Pacific along Alaska's southern coast where glaciers meet the sea and ferocious winter storms are born.

name: Gulf of Antalya
fact: The Gulf of Antalya on Turkey's southern coast is a wide bay of the Levantine Sea backed by the Taurus Mountains.

name: Gulf of Bothnia
fact: The Gulf of Bothnia, the northern arm of the Baltic, is so fresh and cold that it is largely frozen for months each winter.

name: Gulf of Cádiz
fact: The Gulf of Cádiz lies off south-west Spain and Portugal just outside the Strait of Gibraltar, where salty Mediterranean water pours out into the Atlantic.

name: Gulf of California
fact: The Gulf of California, also called the Sea of Cortez after the conquistador Hernán Cortés, separates Baja California from mainland Mexico and is home to the vaquita.

name: Gulf of Carpentaria
fact: The Gulf of Carpentaria in northern Australia is named after Pieter de Carpentier, a governor-general of the Dutch East Indies, and hosts the Morning Glory cloud.

name: Gulf of Corinth
fact: The Gulf of Corinth nearly cuts the Peloponnese off from mainland Greece, and the Corinth Canal, finished in 1893, links it to the Saronic Gulf.

name: Gulf of Finland
fact: The Gulf of Finland is the easternmost arm of the Baltic Sea, with St Petersburg at its head and Helsinki and Tallinn on its shores.

name: Gulf of Gabès
fact: The Gulf of Gabès off Tunisia has the largest tides in the Mediterranean, up to about 2 metres, in a sea where tides are usually tiny.

name: Gulf of Genoa
fact: The Gulf of Genoa is the northernmost part of the Ligurian Sea, with the port of Genoa, birthplace of Christopher Columbus, at its head.

name: Gulf of Guinea
fact: The Gulf of Guinea is the great bend of the African coast where the equator and the prime meridian cross in open water.

name: Gulf of Hammamet
fact: The Gulf of Hammamet is a bay on Tunisia's east coast lined with beach resorts.

name: Gulf of Honduras
fact: The Gulf of Honduras is a Caribbean inlet bordered by Belize, Guatemala and Honduras at the southern end of the Mesoamerican Reef.

name: Gulf of İskenderun
fact: The Gulf of İskenderun in the far north-east corner of the Mediterranean is where the Turkish coast turns south towards Syria, near the ancient battlefield of Issus.

name: Gulf of Lion
fact: The Gulf of Lion on the south coast of France is swept by the mistral wind and receives the waters of the Rhône.

name: Gulf of Maine
fact: The Gulf of Maine is one of the fastest-warming bodies of water in the world and borders the famous Georges Bank fishing grounds.

name: Gulf of Mexico
fact: The Gulf of Mexico is an ocean basin of the Atlantic almost encircled by Mexico, Cuba and the United States, and the Mississippi River drains into it.

name: Gulf of Naples
fact: The Gulf of Naples is overlooked by Mount Vesuvius, whose eruption in AD 79 buried Pompeii, and holds the islands of Capri and Ischia.

name: Gulf of Panama
fact: The Gulf of Panama is the Pacific entrance to the Panama Canal and has some of the largest tides in the tropics, unlike the tiny tides on the Caribbean side.

name: Gulf of Paria
fact: The Gulf of Paria is a shallow inlet between Trinidad and Venezuela, fed by the muddy waters of the Orinoco delta.

name: Gulf of Riga
fact: The Gulf of Riga is a bay of the Baltic Sea enclosed by Latvia and Estonia and nearly cut off from the open sea by the island of Saaremaa.

name: Gulf of Salerno
fact: The Gulf of Salerno, south of the Amalfi Coast, was where Allied troops landed in Italy in September 1943.

name: Gulf of San Jorge
fact: The Gulf of San Jorge is a wide bay on the Patagonian coast of Argentina, open to the South Atlantic.

name: Gulf of Sidra
fact: The Gulf of Sidra on the coast of Libya was claimed by Gaddafi as Libyan waters behind a Line of Death, leading to clashes with the US Navy in the 1980s.

name: Gulf of St Lawrence
fact: The Gulf of St Lawrence, where the St Lawrence River meets the Atlantic, is one of the largest estuarine systems in the world, and ice covers the whole gulf in January and February.

name: Gulf of Taranto
fact: The Gulf of Taranto is the large bay in the instep of Italy's boot, opening onto the Ionian Sea.

name: Gulf of Tehuantepec
fact: The Gulf of Tehuantepec off southern Mexico is famous for violent gap winds that blast through the mountains and far out to sea.

name: Gulf of Thailand
fact: The Gulf of Thailand is a shallow inlet of the South China Sea, bordered by Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia.

name: Gulf of Tonkin
fact: The Gulf of Tonkin, between northern Vietnam and China, holds Halong Bay and gave its name to the 1964 incident that drew the United States deeper into the Vietnam War.

name: Gulf of Trieste
fact: The Gulf of Trieste is the northernmost point of the Adriatic and of the whole Mediterranean, shared by Italy, Slovenia and Croatia.

name: Gulf of Tunis
fact: The Gulf of Tunis is a bay of the Mediterranean on which the ruins of ancient Carthage stand, near the modern city of Tunis.

name: Gulf of Venezuela
fact: The Gulf of Venezuela opens off the Caribbean and connects through a narrow channel to Lake Maracaibo, one of the world's oldest oil regions.

name: Gulf of Venice
fact: The Gulf of Venice is the northern end of the Adriatic Sea, so shallow that Venice floods whenever strong winds push water into it.

name: Gulf Stream
fact: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico up the US east coast and across the Atlantic, keeping north-west Europe far milder than its latitude suggests.

name: Gulf sturgeon
fact: The Gulf sturgeon spends summers in rivers such as the Suwannee and winters in the Gulf of Mexico, and leaping fish have injured boaters.

name: Gull
fact: Gulls are the ocean's opportunists, snatching fish from the surface, raiding fishing boats and stealing catches from other seabirds.

name: Gulper eel
fact: The gulper eel's mouth is bigger than the rest of its body, and it can balloon out like a pelican's pouch to swallow prey larger than itself.

name: Gulper shark
fact: Gulper sharks live on deep slopes and have only one or two pups every couple of years, so their populations collapse quickly under fishing.

name: Gumboot chiton
fact: The gumboot chiton is the largest chiton in the world, a reddish-brown lump up to about 36 centimetres long nicknamed the wandering meatloaf.

name: Guppy
fact: The guppy, the classic beginner's aquarium fish, now lives wild on every continent except Antarctica after releases to control mosquitoes.

name: Gurnard
fact: Gurnards grunt and growl by vibrating their swim bladder, which gave the fish its name from an old French word for grunting.

name: Gutweed
fact: Gutweed is a bright green, tube-shaped seaweed of upper shores and estuaries, named for its hollow, gut-like fronds.

name: Haddock
fact: Haddock, with a black 'thumbprint' behind the gill, is the favourite fish-and-chips fish in Scotland and northern England and is smoked as finnan haddie.

name: Hagfish
fact: A hagfish can turn a bucket of water into slime in seconds, ties itself in a knot to wipe it off, and feeds on carcasses thousands of metres down.

name: Hairy vent snail
fact: Alviniconcha vent snails have bristly shells and gills packed with bacteria that feed them, so they barely need to eat.

name: Hake
fact: Hake is a slim relative of cod and the favourite fish of Spain, which eats more of it than any other country.

name: Halfbeak
fact: Halfbeaks are slender surface fish with a long lower jaw; many species feed on seagrass and floating algae.

name: Halibut
fact: Halibut are the largest flatfish, and Atlantic halibut can grow to over 2 metres long and more than 300 kilograms.

name: Halifax
fact: Halifax, Nova Scotia, has one of the largest natural harbours in the world, and many of the Titanic's victims are buried in the city's cemeteries.

name: Halimeda
fact: Halimeda is a green seaweed built from chalky segments; its dead flakes make up much of the white sand on tropical beaches.

name: Hallucigenia
fact: Hallucigenia, a spiny Cambrian worm from the Burgess Shale, was so strange that scientists first reconstructed it upside down.

name: Halong Bay
fact: Halong Bay in northern Vietnam is studded with about 1,600 limestone islands and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Halosaur
fact: Halosaurs are long-tailed, eel-like fish of the deep seabed, swimming slowly over abyssal mud below 1,000 metres with a snout that overhangs the mouth.

name: Hammer coral
fact: Hammer coral's tentacles end in hammer or anchor-shaped tips, and it sends out long sweeper tentacles to sting neighbouring corals.

name: Hammerhead shark
fact: A hammerhead's wide head spreads its eyes and electrical sensors across a broad span, helping it sweep the seabed for buried rays.

name: Hanauma Bay
fact: Hanauma Bay on Oahu is a flooded volcanic crater that became Hawaii's first marine life conservation district in 1967.

name: Hangzhou Bay
fact: Hangzhou Bay in eastern China produces the world's largest tidal bore, a wall of water that surges up the Qiantang River.

name: Hans Hass
fact: Hans Hass was an Austrian diving pioneer who made some of the first underwater films of sharks and manta rays in the 1940s and 1950s.

name: Harbour porpoise
fact: The harbour porpoise is the smallest cetacean in European waters and must feed almost constantly to stay warm.

name: Harbour seal
fact: Harbour seals are the most widespread pinniped, hauling out on coasts all around the Northern Hemisphere.

name: Hardhead catfish
fact: The hardhead catfish is a sea catfish of the Gulf of Mexico whose males carry the marble-sized eggs in their mouths for about two months.

name: Harlequin filefish
fact: The harlequin filefish eats only Acropora coral polyps and ends up smelling like the coral it eats, which hides it from predators that hunt by scent.

name: Harlequin rasbora
fact: The harlequin rasbora, with a black triangle on its side, lays its eggs on the underside of leaves in Malaysian and Thai streams.

name: Harlequin shrimp
fact: Harlequin shrimp hunt in pairs and eat only starfish, flipping their prey over and feeding on it alive for days.

name: Harlequin tuskfish
fact: The harlequin tuskfish has bright blue tusk-like teeth and orange bands, and uses the teeth to crush shellfish on Indo-Pacific reefs.

name: Harp seal
fact: Harp seal pups are born on the sea ice with fluffy white coats, and the species was the focus of the famous Canadian seal hunt protests.

name: Harp sponge
fact: The harp sponge, found 3,300 metres down off California in 2012, is a carnivore: it snags tiny crustaceans on Velcro-like hooks along its harp-shaped branches.

name: Hatchetfish
fact: Hatchetfish are silver, blade-thin fish with photophores on their bellies that match the faint light from above, making them invisible from below.

name: Havana
fact: Havana's sheltered harbour on the Straits of Florida was the gathering point for Spain's treasure fleets before they crossed the Atlantic.

name: Hawaii
fact: The Hawaiian Islands are the tops of volcanoes built over a hotspot, and Mauna Kea is the tallest mountain on Earth measured from its base on the sea floor.

name: Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain
fact: The Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain is a line of drowned volcanoes stretching about 6,000 kilometres across the Pacific, built as the plate moved over a hotspot.

name: Hawaiian monk seal
fact: The Hawaiian monk seal is one of the rarest seals, with only around 1,500 left, and its Hawaiian name means 'dog that runs in rough water'.

name: Hawkfish
fact: Hawkfish perch on coral heads using their thick pectoral fins, watching for prey like a hawk before darting out to grab it.

name: Hawksbill turtle
fact: Hawksbill turtles eat sea sponges that are toxic to most animals, and their patterned shells were the source of 'tortoiseshell'.

name: Headless chicken monster
fact: The headless chicken monster is a translucent pink sea cucumber that swims with a webbed collar and sheds a sticky glowing skin onto anything that touches it.

name: Heart urchin
fact: The heart urchin, or sea potato, is a burrowing urchin with a heart-shaped shell that lives hidden in sand below the low-tide mark.

name: Heaviside's dolphin
fact: Heaviside's dolphin, found only off Namibia and South Africa, is named after the wrong man: its specimen came from a Captain Haviside, but was credited to a surgeon called Heaviside.

name: Hebrides
fact: The Hebrides off Scotland's west coast include Skye, Mull, Lewis and Harris, and the tiny island of Staffa with its basalt Fingal's Cave.

name: Hector's beaked whale
fact: Hector's beaked whale is a small, rarely seen Southern Hemisphere beaked whale named after James Hector, a New Zealand scientist.

name: Hector's dolphin
fact: Hector's dolphin of New Zealand is one of the smallest dolphins, about 1.4 metres long, with a rounded dorsal fin like a Mickey Mouse ear.

name: Hedgehog seahorse
fact: The hedgehog seahorse is a spiny Indo-Pacific species that lives on sandy and muddy bottoms, often beside sponges, and is caught in trawls.

name: Helicoprion
fact: Helicoprion was a shark relative with a spiral 'buzzsaw' of teeth in its lower jaw that puzzled scientists for more than a century.

name: Hellenic Trench
fact: The Hellenic Trench, curving south of Greece and Crete, contains the Calypso Deep, the deepest point in the Mediterranean at about 5,100 metres.

name: Helmet jellyfish
fact: The helmet jellyfish lives in deep water and in dark Norwegian fjords, where it has multiplied so much that it has displaced the fish.

name: Herbert Nitsch
fact: Herbert Nitsch, the deepest man on Earth, free-dived to 214 metres on a single breath in 2007.

name: Hermit crab
fact: Hermit crabs have soft abdomens and move into empty snail shells, swapping for larger ones as they grow.

name: Heron
fact: Herons stalk the shallows of estuaries and mangrove channels, striking fish with a lightning jab of their dagger-like bill.

name: Herring
fact: Herring feed on copepods and krill in schools of millions, and communicate at night with bursts of bubbles from their vents.

name: Hijiki
fact: Hijiki is a brown seaweed eaten in Japan, usually dried and black; it is known for holding unusually high levels of arsenic.

name: Hikurangi Trench
fact: The Hikurangi Trench off the east coast of New Zealand's North Island is where the Pacific Plate dives beneath the Australian Plate.

name: Hilsa
fact: The hilsa is a shad that lives in the Bay of Bengal and swims up the Ganges and other rivers to spawn, and it is the national fish of Bangladesh.

name: Hirondellea gigas
fact: Hirondellea gigas amphipods swarm at the bottom of the Challenger Deep and make enzymes that digest sunken wood and plant debris.

name: Hjort Trench
fact: The Hjort Trench south of New Zealand and Macquarie Island is one of the southernmost trenches in the world, reaching about 6,700 metres.

name: H. L. Hunley
fact: The Confederate submarine H. L. Hunley sank in 1864 shortly after becoming the first submarine to sink an enemy warship.

name: HMAS Sydney
fact: HMAS Sydney was lost with all 645 crew after a battle with the German raider Kormoran in 1941, and was found in 2008 about 2,500 metres down off Western Australia.

name: HMS Beagle
fact: HMS Beagle carried the young Charles Darwin on a five-year surveying voyage around the world from 1831 to 1836 that led to his theory of evolution.

name: Bounty
fact: After the famous mutiny, the Bounty was burned and sunk by the mutineers at Pitcairn Island in 1790.

name: HMS Challenger
fact: HMS Challenger sailed around the world from 1872 to 1876 on the first great oceanographic expedition, sounding the deep that now bears its name.

name: HMS Erebus
fact: HMS Erebus, one of the ships of Franklin's lost Arctic expedition, sank in the Canadian Arctic and was found in shallow water in 2014.

name: HMS Hood
fact: HMS Hood blew up and sank in three minutes after a hit from the Bismarck in 1941, with only 3 of 1,418 men surviving; the wreck lies about 2,800 metres down.

name: HMS Terror
fact: HMS Terror, Franklin's second ship, was found almost intact in 2016 in Terror Bay, off King William Island in the Canadian Arctic.

name: Hoff crab
fact: The Hoff crab, named for its hairy chest after actor David Hasselhoff, crowds by the thousand onto hot vent chimneys on the Antarctic East Scotia Ridge.

name: Hogchoker
fact: The hogchoker is a small American sole that swims up rivers and got its name because pigs fed on the rough-skinned fish supposedly choked on them.

name: Hogfish
fact: The hogfish of the western Atlantic roots in sand with its long pig-like snout and is prized by spearfishers for its taste.

name: Hoki
fact: Hoki is a deep-water cod relative of New Zealand's biggest fishery, and ends up in fish fingers and fast-food fish sandwiches.

name: Honeycomb cowfish
fact: The honeycomb cowfish of Caribbean reefs has two horns over its eyes and a boxy body patterned like a honeycomb.

name: Honeycomb moray
fact: The honeycomb moray, or laced moray, is a large white moray covered in black honeycomb spots, common on Indo-Pacific reefs.

name: Honeycomb stingray
fact: The honeycomb stingray has a tail up to three times its body length and a net-like pattern on its back.

name: Hooded seal
