fact: Male hooded seals inflate a bright red nasal balloon from one nostril to impress rivals, and pups are weaned in only four days.

name: Horn shark
fact: The horn shark has a sharp spine in front of each dorsal fin and crushes sea urchins and molluscs with flat, molar-like back teeth.

name: Horned sea snake
fact: The horned sea snake has small spines over its eyes and is the only sea snake with spiny scales on its head.

name: Horse mackerel
fact: Horse mackerel, or scad, are not true mackerel but jacks with a row of bony scales along the lateral line, and they school in vast numbers.

name: Horsehair crab
fact: The horsehair crab of Hokkaido is covered in short bristles and is prized in Japan for its sweet meat and rich crab liver.

name: Horseshoe crab
fact: Horseshoe crabs have blue, copper-based blood that is harvested to test medicines and vaccines for bacterial contamination.

name: Houndfish
fact: The houndfish is a 1.5-metre needlefish that leaps from the water at speed and has impaled fishermen with its beak.

name: Hourglass dolphin
fact: The hourglass dolphin is the only small dolphin found regularly in Antarctic waters, and its bold black-and-white pattern gives it its name.

name: Hubbs' beaked whale
fact: Hubbs' beaked whale is known mostly from strandings on the US west coast and Japan, and males carry a white cap on their heads.

name: Huchen
fact: The huchen, or Danube salmon, is a giant trout relative of the Danube basin that can grow to more than a metre long and never goes to sea.

name: Hudson Bay
fact: Hudson Bay is a vast inland sea in Canada named after the English explorer Henry Hudson, who was set adrift there by mutineers in 1611 and never seen again.

name: Hudson Canyon
fact: Hudson Canyon is the largest submarine canyon on the US Atlantic coast, continuing the course of the Hudson River across the seabed off New York.

name: Hudson Strait
fact: Hudson Strait links Hudson Bay to the Labrador Sea and the Atlantic and is named after the English explorer Henry Hudson.

name: Humboldt Current
fact: The Humboldt Current carries cold, nutrient-rich water north along the coast of Chile and Peru, feeding the world's largest anchovy fishery.

name: Humboldt squid
fact: Humboldt squid hunt in packs of hundreds and flash red and white across their skin, earning the nickname 'red devil' from fishermen.

name: Humbug dascyllus
fact: The humbug dascyllus is a small black-and-white banded damselfish that lives in tight groups inside branching Acropora corals.

name: Humpback anglerfish
fact: The humpback anglerfish is the classic toothy black seadevil of the deep; females reach about 15 centimetres while the males are only around 2 centimetres long.

name: Humpback dolphin
fact: Humpback dolphins live in shallow coastal waters and estuaries and have a distinctive hump beneath the dorsal fin.

name: Humpback grouper
fact: The humpback grouper, or panther grouper, is a polka-dotted, small-headed grouper that swims head-down and is farmed as a luxury fish in Asia.

name: Humpback whale
fact: Male humpbacks sing long, complex songs, and the scientific name Megaptera novaeangliae means 'big-winged New Englander'.

name: Hydroid
fact: Hydroids are plant-like colonies of stinging polyps, the attached stage of many jellyfish, and have been dredged from more than 8,200 metres in the Kermadec Trench.

name: Icarian Sea
fact: The Icarian Sea is the part of the Aegean around the island of Icaria, where in legend Icarus fell into the sea after flying too close to the sun.

name: Iceland
fact: Iceland sits astride the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, which is why it is so volcanic.

name: Ichthyosaur
fact: Ichthyosaurs were dolphin-shaped reptiles that gave birth to live young at sea, and Mary Anning found the first complete skeleton in 1811.

name: Ifremeria snail
fact: Ifremeria snails cluster in dense beds at western Pacific vents and brood their young inside a pouch in the foot.

name: Immortal jellyfish
fact: The immortal jellyfish can turn its adult body back into a juvenile polyp when injured or starving, restarting its life cycle indefinitely.

name: Inanga
fact: The inanga of New Zealand and Australia lays its eggs on grasses flooded by spring tides, and the larvae are swept out to sea before returning as whitebait.

name: Inca tern
fact: The Inca tern of the Humboldt Current coast of Peru and Chile sports a dashing white moustache and snatches anchovies from the surface.

name: Indian mackerel
fact: The Indian mackerel is the everyday fish of South and Southeast Asia, caught in huge numbers and fried, curried or dried.

name: Indian Ocean humpback dolphin
fact: The Indian Ocean humpback dolphin has a pronounced hump under its dorsal fin and lives in estuaries and shallow coasts from South Africa to India.

name: Indian oil sardine
fact: The Indian oil sardine is the most important fish of India's west coast, caught by the hundreds of thousands of tonnes in the monsoon season.

name: Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin
fact: Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins in Shark Bay, Australia, carry sponges on their beaks as tools to protect them while foraging on the seabed.

name: Indo-Pacific finless porpoise
fact: The Indo-Pacific finless porpoise lives in estuaries and shallow coasts from the Persian Gulf to the Taiwan Strait, including the Pearl River estuary.

name: Indo-Pacific humpback dolphin
fact: Chinese white dolphins of the Pearl River estuary are actually pink as adults, and Hong Kong adopted them as its 1997 handover mascot.

name: Indus river dolphin
fact: The Indus river dolphin often swims on its side in the shallow, muddy Indus and was long trapped between irrigation barrages.

name: INS Dakar
fact: The Israeli submarine Dakar vanished in 1968 and was found in 1999 about 2,900 metres down between Crete and Cyprus.

name: Ionian Sea
fact: The Ionian Sea lies between southern Italy and western Greece and holds the deepest point in the Mediterranean, the Calypso Deep at about 5,100 metres.

name: Ireland
fact: Ireland is the second-largest island of the British Isles, and the Gulf Stream keeps its climate mild enough for subtropical gardens to thrive on its west coast.

name: Irish moss
fact: Irish moss, or carrageen, is a small red seaweed whose extract carrageenan thickens ice cream, toothpaste and plant milks.

name: Irish Sea
fact: The Irish Sea separates Ireland from Great Britain and opens to the Atlantic through the North Channel and St George's Channel.

name: Irminger Current
fact: The Irminger Current is a warm branch of the North Atlantic Drift that flows west past Iceland towards Greenland.

name: Irrawaddy dolphin
fact: Irrawaddy dolphins in Myanmar herd fish towards fishermen's nets and are rewarded with part of the catch.

name: Irukandji jellyfish
fact: The Irukandji jellyfish is barely the size of a fingernail and transparent, yet its sting causes hours of agony, vomiting and a feeling of impending doom.

name: Isles of Scilly
fact: The Isles of Scilly lie about 45 kilometres off Cornwall and are warmed by the Gulf Stream so that subtropical plants grow in their gardens.

name: Isopod
fact: Isopods, the group that includes woodlice, are found in every ocean habitat, including trench floors deeper than 6,000 metres.

name: Ivory gull
fact: The ivory gull is a pure-white gull that lives year-round among Arctic pack ice and scavenges polar bear kills.

name: Iwo Jima
fact: Iwo Jima is a small volcanic island south of Japan where US Marines raised the flag on Mount Suribachi in 1945.

name: Izu-Ogasawara Trench
fact: The Izu-Ogasawara Trench runs south from Japan to join the Mariana Trench and reaches more than 9,700 metres deep.

name: Jack Dempsey
fact: The Jack Dempsey cichlid from Central America was named after the boxer for its aggressive temper and strong-jawed face.

name: Jack mackerel
fact: The Pacific jack mackerel is a schooling jack, not a true mackerel, caught off California and Chile in enormous quantities.

name: Jacques Cousteau
fact: Jacques Cousteau co-invented the Aqua-Lung in 1943, the first successful open-circuit scuba gear, and brought the undersea world to television aboard Calypso.

name: Jacques Mayol
fact: Jacques Mayol was the free diver who first dived below 100 metres on a single breath in 1976 and inspired the film The Big Blue.

name: Jacques Piccard
fact: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reached the bottom of the Challenger Deep in the bathyscaphe Trieste in 1960, the first humans ever to do so.

name: James Bay
fact: James Bay, the southern arm of Hudson Bay, is named after Thomas James, the Welsh captain who wintered on its shore in 1631.

name: James Cameron
fact: The film director James Cameron made a solo dive to the bottom of the Challenger Deep in 2012 and has visited the Titanic wreck more than 30 times.

name: James Clark Ross
fact: James Clark Ross discovered the Ross Sea and Ross Ice Shelf in 1841 and made some of the first soundings of the deep ocean, reaching below 4,000 metres.

name: James Cook
fact: Captain James Cook charted more of the Pacific than any navigator before him, crossed the Antarctic Circle, and kept his crews free of scurvy on three great voyages.

name: Japan
fact: Japan is an archipelago of thousands of islands in the western Pacific, dominated by the four large islands of Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku.

name: Japan Trench
fact: The Japan Trench runs off north-east Honshu, and the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake that caused the Fukushima disaster ruptured along it.

name: Japanese anchovy
fact: The Japanese anchovy is one of the largest catches in the northwest Pacific, eaten dried as niboshi and as tiny boiled whitebait, shirasu.

name: Japanese eel
fact: The Japanese eel, the unagi of Japanese cooking, spawns near the Mariana Islands and its young drift thousands of kilometres back to East Asian rivers.

name: Japanese flying squid
fact: The Japanese flying squid supports one of the biggest squid fisheries in the world and can glide briefly above the waves by jetting water.

name: Japanese horse mackerel
fact: Horse mackerel, aji, is one of the most common fish in Tokyo sushi bars, served raw with grated ginger and spring onion.

name: Japanese pygmy seahorse
fact: The Japanese pygmy seahorse, nicknamed 'japapigu' or 'Japan pig', was known to local divers for years before being named as a new species in 2018.

name: Japanese sardine
fact: The Japanese sardine catch rose above 4 million tonnes in the 1980s before collapsing, one of the most dramatic booms and busts in fishing.

name: Japanese sea bass
fact: Japanese sea bass, suzuki, is a summer sashimi fish that changes its name as it grows, a 'success fish' in Japanese tradition.

name: Japanese sea cucumber
fact: The Japanese sea cucumber is farmed and dried as a luxury food across East Asia and is known in Japan as namako.

name: Japanese sea lion
fact: The Japanese sea lion bred on beaches of Japan and Korea until hunting wiped it out; the last reliable sightings were in the 1950s, with a final juvenile reported in 1974.

name: Japanese Spanish mackerel
fact: The Japanese Spanish mackerel, sawara, is a spring fish in Japan, grilled with miso or served as lightly seared sashimi.

name: Japanese spider crab
fact: The Japanese spider crab has the largest leg span of any arthropod, up to about 3.7 metres, and lives on the seabed off Japan down to about 600 metres.

name: Japanese spiny lobster
fact: The Japanese spiny lobster, Ise-ebi, is a celebration food in Japan, served grilled or raw at New Year and at weddings.

name: Java Trench
fact: The Java Trench, also called the Sunda Trench, is the deepest point in the Indian Ocean at more than 7,000 metres, and the 2004 tsunami began along it.

name: Jean-Baptiste Charcot
fact: Jean-Baptiste Charcot led French Antarctic expeditions aboard the ships Français and Pourquoi-Pas? and charted long stretches of the Antarctic Peninsula.

name: Jean-Michel Cousteau
fact: Jean-Michel Cousteau, Jacques Cousteau's elder son, founded the Ocean Futures Society and has spent his life making ocean documentaries.

name: Jellyfish
fact: Jellyfish have no brain, heart or blood and are more than 95 per cent water, yet they have drifted the oceans for more than 500 million years.

name: Jericho worm
fact: The Jericho worm is a tube worm with a ringed tube like a crumbling wall, and it is usually the first tube worm to colonise a brand-new vent.

name: Jewel damselfish
fact: The jewel damselfish of Indo-Pacific reefs is spangled with tiny blue spots as a juvenile, and the adult farms a turf of red algae.

name: Jiaolong
fact: China's submersible Jiaolong dived to more than 7,000 metres in the Mariana Trench in 2012.

name: John Dory
fact: John Dory has a dark spot on each flank said to be St Peter's thumbprint, and its sweet white fillets are prized by chefs.

name: JOIDES Resolution
fact: The drilling ship JOIDES Resolution spent decades recovering sediment cores from the deep sea floor that record millions of years of Earth's climate.

name: Jonah crab
fact: The Jonah crab of the north-west Atlantic was once lobster-pot bycatch but is now fished in its own right for its large claws.

name: Joseph Bonaparte Gulf
fact: The Joseph Bonaparte Gulf in northern Australia was named by the French explorer Nicolas Baudin after Napoleon's elder brother Joseph.

name: Juan de Fuca Ridge
fact: The Juan de Fuca Ridge off the Pacific Northwest is a spreading ridge whose vents are wired to shore by a cabled seafloor observatory.

name: Juan Fernández Islands
fact: The Juan Fernández Islands off Chile include Robinson Crusoe Island, where the marooned sailor Alexander Selkirk survived alone for four years and inspired Defoe's novel.

name: Junk
fact: The Chinese junk, with its battened sails, was sailing the seas centuries before similar rigs appeared in Europe, and Zheng He's treasure fleet used giant junks.

name: K-129
fact: The Soviet missile submarine K-129 sank in 1968 about 4,900 metres down in the Pacific; the CIA's Glomar Explorer secretly lifted part of it in 1974 and the rest still lies there.

name: Kaga
fact: The Japanese carrier Kaga, sunk at the Battle of Midway in 1942, was the first Midway carrier wreck found, in October 2019, more than 5,000 metres down.

name: Kaiko
fact: Kaiko was a Japanese robotic vehicle that in 1995 became the second craft to reach the bottom of the Challenger Deep, and it was lost at sea in 2003.

name: Kawakawa
fact: The kawakawa, or mackerel tuna, is a small coastal tuna of the Indo-Pacific with wavy stripes on its back and dark spots under its pectoral fins.

name: Kayak
fact: The kayak was developed by Inuit and other Arctic peoples as a sealed one-person hunting boat for seals and other sea animals.

name: Kelp
fact: Kelps are large brown seaweeds that form underwater forests along cold, rocky coasts, anchored by a root-like holdfast rather than true roots.

name: Kelp bass
fact: The kelp bass, or calico bass, is a mottled sea bass of California's kelp forests and one of the state's most popular sport fish.

name: Kelp crab
fact: The kelp crab lives in kelp forests of the Pacific coast of North America, where it feeds mostly on the kelp itself.

name: Kelp fly
fact: Kelp flies lay their eggs in rotting seaweed on the strandline, and their larvae feed on it, becoming food for shore birds.

name: Kelp greenling
fact: The kelp greenling of the North Pacific hides among kelp, and its males and females look so different that they were once described as separate species.

name: Kelp perch
fact: The kelp perch is a small surfperch of California kelp beds that picks parasites off other fish and gives birth to fully formed young.

name: Kelp rockfish
fact: The kelp rockfish rests motionless among kelp fronds, often head-down, and gives birth to live young like all rockfishes.

name: Kemp's ridley sea turtle
fact: Kemp's ridley is the rarest sea turtle and nests in mass daytime arrivals called arribadas, mostly on one Mexican beach, Rancho Nuevo.

name: Kerguelen Plateau
fact: The Kerguelen Plateau in the southern Indian Ocean is one of the largest submerged volcanic plateaus on Earth, with only a few island peaks breaking the surface.

name: Kermadec snailfish
fact: The Kermadec snailfish lives only in the Kermadec Trench off New Zealand, where it has been filmed feeding in groups about 7,500 metres down.

name: Kermadec Trench
fact: The Kermadec Trench north-east of New Zealand plunges to about 10,000 metres and is home to huge swarms of amphipods and snailfish.

name: Kilka
fact: Kilka are tiny sprats of the Caspian and Black seas that once made up most of the Caspian catch before the comb jelly invasion.

name: Killer shrimp
fact: The killer shrimp, a large amphipod from the Black Sea region, has spread through Europe's canals to Britain, killing far more prey than it eats.

name: Killifish
fact: Some killifish live in puddles that dry up each year, surviving as eggs in the mud that hobbyists can buy and post in the mail.

name: Kina
fact: Kina is New Zealand's native sea urchin, a kelp grazer whose roe is a traditional Māori delicacy.

name: King angelfish
fact: The king angelfish, dark blue with a white bar and orange tail, runs cleaning stations for hammerheads around the Galápagos.

name: King crab
fact: Red king crabs of the Bering Sea can span 1.5 metres across the legs and are actually closer relatives of hermit crabs than of true crabs.

name: King mackerel
fact: The king mackerel, or kingfish, is a big, fast Spanish mackerel of the western Atlantic, chased by anglers off Florida and known to leap clear of the water.

name: King penguin
fact: King penguins dive to over 300 metres for lanternfish and take more than a year to raise a chick, the longest breeding cycle of any penguin.

name: Kingman Reef
fact: Kingman Reef is a nearly submerged coral atoll in the central Pacific with almost no dry land, yet its reef is one of the most pristine on Earth.

name: Kiribati
fact: Kiribati is spread across 33 islands straddling the equator and the International Date Line, and includes Kiritimati, the largest coral atoll by land area.

name: Kissing gourami
fact: Kissing gouramis press their lips together in a test of strength, and like other gouramis they breathe air with a labyrinth organ.

name: Kitefin shark
fact: The kitefin shark, found down to around 1,800 metres, is the largest known glowing vertebrate at up to about 1.8 metres long.

name: Kittiwake
fact: The kittiwake is a small, truly oceanic gull that spends the winter far out at sea and nests on sheer cliff ledges.

name: Knarr
fact: The knarr was the broad Viking cargo ship that carried settlers and livestock across the open North Atlantic to Iceland, Greenland and Vinland.

name: Knorr
fact: The research vessel Knorr was the ship from which Robert Ballard's team found the wreck of the Titanic in 1985.

name: Knotted wrack
fact: Knotted wrack, or egg wrack, is a long-lived brown seaweed with single egg-shaped air bladders along its fronds, harvested for alginate and fertiliser.

name: Knysna seahorse
fact: The Knysna seahorse lives only in a few estuaries on South Africa's southern coast and is listed as endangered.

name: Koi
fact: Koi are ornamental common carp bred in Japan, and prized fish have sold for more than a million dollars.

name: Kole tang
fact: The kole tang, or goldring bristletooth, is a Hawaiian surgeonfish with a gold ring around each eye and comb-like teeth for brushing up algae and detritus.

name: Kombu
fact: Kombu is dried kelp, the seaweed that gives Japanese dashi stock its savoury umami taste; monosodium glutamate was first isolated from it in 1908.

name: Komodo National Park
fact: Komodo National Park in Indonesia protects not only its dragons but strong-current reefs where manta rays gather to be cleaned.

name: Komsomolets
fact: The Soviet nuclear submarine Komsomolets sank in the Norwegian Sea in 1989 and lies about 1,700 metres down with its reactor and two nuclear torpedoes.

name: Koran angelfish
fact: The koran angelfish gets its name from the arabesque markings on the tail of some adults, said to resemble Arabic script; juveniles are blue with white arcs.

name: Korea Strait
fact: The Korea Strait between South Korea and Japan links the East China Sea to the Sea of Japan, and the Russian fleet was destroyed there at Tsushima in 1905.

name: Krill
fact: Antarctic krill swarms can stretch for kilometres, and their total weight of several hundred million tonnes is among the largest of any animal species.

name: Kronosaurus
fact: Kronosaurus was a Cretaceous pliosaur from Queensland, Australia, whose skull alone is estimated at over 2 metres long.

name: Kuhli loach
fact: The kuhli loach is a striped eel-like fish from South-east Asia that burrows into aquarium sand and comes out at night.

name: Kuril Islands
fact: The Kuril Islands are a volcanic chain between Kamchatka and Japan, still disputed between Russia and Japan since the end of the Second World War.

name: Kuril-Kamchatka Trench
fact: The Kuril-Kamchatka Trench runs south from Kamchatka past the Kuril Islands and reaches more than 9,000 metres deep.

name: Kuroshio Current
fact: The Kuroshio, or Black Stream, is the Pacific's counterpart to the Gulf Stream, carrying warm water north past Japan.

name: Kursk
fact: The Russian submarine Kursk sank in the Barents Sea in August 2000 after torpedo explosions, with the loss of all 118 aboard.

name: Kuruma prawn
fact: The kuruma prawn, with its banded tail, is one of the most expensive prawns in Japan and the first prawn ever reared in a hatchery, in the 1930s.

name: Kvarner Gulf
fact: The Kvarner Gulf is a bay of the northern Adriatic in Croatia, sheltered by the islands of Krk, Cres and Rab, with the port of Rijeka at its head.

name: Kwajalein Atoll
fact: Kwajalein Atoll in the Marshall Islands encloses one of the largest lagoons in the world, about 2,000 square kilometres.

name: Labrador Current
fact: The Labrador Current carries cold Arctic water and icebergs south past Newfoundland, and it was one of its icebergs that sank the Titanic.

name: Labrador duck
fact: The Labrador duck, a sea duck of the North American Atlantic coast, was the first bird endemic to North America to go extinct, last seen in 1878.

name: Labrador Sea
fact: The Labrador Sea between Canada and Greenland is one of the few places where surface water sinks to the deep ocean, helping drive global circulation.

name: Ladyfish
fact: The ladyfish is a slim silver fish of warm estuaries that leaps and skips repeatedly across the surface when hooked.

name: Lagos
fact: Lagos, Nigeria's largest city, grew around a lagoon opening onto the Atlantic, and its name is Portuguese for 'lakes'.

name: Lahontan cutthroat trout
fact: The Lahontan cutthroat is the largest subspecies of cutthroat trout, native to Nevada's Pyramid Lake, and is the state fish of Nevada.

name: Lake sturgeon
fact: The lake sturgeon of the Great Lakes and Mississippi can live for more than 100 years and does not breed until it is about 20.

name: Lake trout
fact: Lake trout are big, slow-growing char of cold northern lakes that can live for more than 25 years.

name: Lamp shell
fact: Lamp shells look like clams but belong to a separate ancient group, the brachiopods, and filter food with a coiled, tentacled organ called the lophophore.

name: Lancaster Sound
fact: Lancaster Sound, the eastern entrance to the Northwest Passage, is named after Sir James Lancaster, a sponsor of William Baffin's 1616 voyage.

name: Lancastria
fact: The troopship Lancastria was bombed and sunk off Saint-Nazaire in June 1940, Britain's worst ever maritime disaster.

name: Lancelet
fact: The lancelet, a finger-length fish-like animal that burrows in sand, has a body plan close to the ancestor of all vertebrates.

name: Lancetfish
fact: The lancetfish is a 2-metre deep-sea predator with a huge sail fin and fangs, and its watery flesh is so flabby that it is rarely eaten.

name: Lane snapper
fact: The lane snapper is a pink-and-yellow striped Caribbean snapper with a black spot on its side, common on grass flats and reefs.

name: Langoustine
fact: Langoustines live in burrows in muddy seabeds and are one of the most valuable catches landed in Britain, where they are sold as scampi.

name: Lanternfish
fact: Lanternfish may make up more than half of all deep-sea fish by weight, and their nightly rise towards the surface is the largest animal migration on Earth.

name: Lanternshark
fact: Lanternsharks are small deep-sea sharks that glow along their bellies, hiding their silhouettes from predators looking up.

name: Laptev Sea
fact: The Laptev Sea off Siberia is named after the Russian explorer cousins Dmitry and Khariton Laptev, who charted the Arctic coast in the 1730s and 1740s.

name: Largehead hairtail
fact: The largehead hairtail is a ribbon-like, silver predator with fangs that is one of the largest fish catches in the world, mostly off China.

name: Largemouth bass
fact: The male largemouth bass sweeps out a nest in the shallows and guards the eggs and fry for weeks, attacking anything that comes near.

name: Larger Pacific striped octopus
fact: The larger Pacific striped octopus is unusually social: pairs share dens and mate beak to beak, and the female lays several clutches instead of dying after one.

name: Largetooth sawfish
fact: The largetooth sawfish can live in fresh water and has been caught hundreds of kilometres up rivers in Australia and Central America.

name: Larvacean
fact: Larvaceans are tadpole-shaped, transparent animals that build a disposable mucus 'house' around themselves to filter food, discarding it several times a day.

name: Las Palmas
fact: Las Palmas de Gran Canaria is a major Atlantic port where Columbus's ships stopped for repairs in 1492 before crossing to the Americas.

name: Lawnmower blenny
fact: The lawnmower blenny is named for its habit of cropping algae, which makes it a popular cleaner for reef aquariums.

name: Laysan albatross
fact: A Laysan albatross named Wisdom, ringed on Midway Atoll in 1956, was still hatching chicks in her seventies, the oldest known wild bird.

name: Leaf-scaled sea snake
fact: The leaf-scaled sea snake vanished from Ashmore Reef and was feared extinct until it turned up again off Western Australia in 2015.

name: Leafscale gulper shark
fact: The leafscale gulper shark, named for its leaf-shaped scales, lives on continental slopes down to about 2,400 metres.

name: Leafy sea dragon
fact: The leafy sea dragon's leaf-like flaps are camouflage only; it swims with tiny transparent fins, and the male carries the eggs under his tail.

name: Least darter
fact: The least darter is one of the smallest freshwater fish in North America, a 4-centimetre perch relative of weedy streams and lakes.

name: Least killifish
fact: The least killifish is one of the smallest fish in North America, a 2-to-3-centimetre livebearer of the southeastern United States, and not a true killifish.

name: Leather coral
fact: Leather corals are soft corals shaped like a toadstool with a leathery surface, and they shed a waxy film to clean themselves.

name: Leather star
fact: The leather star has a smooth, leathery skin and is said to smell of garlic when it is lifted from the water.

name: Leatherback turtle
fact: Leatherback turtles have been tracked crossing the entire Pacific, more than 10,000 kilometres, from Indonesian nesting beaches to feeding grounds off California.

name: Leedsichthys
fact: Leedsichthys was a Jurassic filter-feeding fish perhaps 16 metres long, the largest bony fish known to have lived.

name: Leeuwin Current
fact: The Leeuwin Current flows south along the coast of Western Australia, carrying warm tropical water that lets corals grow as far south as the Abrolhos Islands.

name: Lemon shark
fact: Lemon sharks return to the same mangrove nurseries where they were born to give birth to their own pups.

name: Lemon sole
fact: Despite its name, the lemon sole is not a true sole but a right-eyed flounder found around the British Isles.

name: Lenok
fact: The lenok, sometimes called the Asiatic trout, lives in the cold rivers of Siberia, Mongolia, China and Korea.

name: Leopard seal
fact: Leopard seals are the Antarctic's top seal predator, hunting penguins and the pups of other seals.

name: Leopard shark
fact: Leopard sharks gather in warm shallows off California each summer, with pregnant females basking in the waters off La Jolla.

name: Leopard whipray
fact: The leopard whipray has a leopard-like pattern of dark rings and was only separated from the honeycomb stingray as a species in 2008.

name: Leptocephalus
fact: The leptocephalus is the leaf-shaped, see-through larva of eels, tarpon and bonefish, which drifts in the current for months before changing shape.

name: Lesser electric ray
fact: The lesser electric ray of the western Atlantic is small enough to hold in two hands yet can deliver a shock of around 14 to 37 volts.

name: Lettuce coral
fact: Lettuce coral grows in thin, ruffled plates like the leaves of a lettuce and is common on Caribbean reef slopes.

name: Lettuce sea slug
fact: The lettuce sea slug eats green algae and keeps their chloroplasts alive inside its frilly body, where they go on making sugar from sunlight.

name: Levantine Sea
fact: The Levantine Sea is the easternmost part of the Mediterranean, off Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Israel and Egypt, and the saltiest part of the whole sea.

name: Leyte Gulf
fact: Leyte Gulf in the Philippines saw the largest naval battle of the Second World War in October 1944.

name: Libyan Sea
fact: The Libyan Sea is the stretch of the Mediterranean between Crete and the coast of Libya.

name: Lighthouse Reef
fact: Lighthouse Reef is an atoll off Belize whose lagoon contains the Great Blue Hole, a sinkhole about 125 metres deep made famous by Jacques Cousteau.

name: Ligurian Sea
fact: The Ligurian Sea, between the Italian Riviera and Corsica, is part of the Pelagos Sanctuary, a protected area rich in fin whales and dolphins.

name: Limiting Factor
fact: Limiting Factor is the submersible in which Victor Vescovo became the first person to dive to the deepest point of all five oceans, in 2018 and 2019.

name: Limpet
fact: Limpets clamp their cone-shaped shells to rocks and return to the exact same 'home scar' after every grazing trip.

name: Lincoln Sea
fact: The Lincoln Sea, north of Greenland and Ellesmere Island, is named after Robert Todd Lincoln, US Secretary of War and son of Abraham Lincoln.

name: Lined butterflyfish
fact: The lined butterflyfish is the largest butterflyfish, growing to about 30 centimetres, with thin vertical lines and a black band through the eye.

name: Lined seahorse
fact: The lined seahorse is the seahorse of the western Atlantic, found from Nova Scotia to Venezuela, including the eelgrass beds of Chesapeake Bay.

name: Ling
fact: The ling is a long, slender cod relative of deep North Atlantic waters that can reach 2 metres; its salted, dried flesh is a traditional Norwegian export.

name: Lingcod
fact: The male lingcod guards the egg mass on the kelp-forest floor through winter, and its flesh is sometimes blue-green, fading to white when cooked.

name: Lingula
fact: Lingula, a burrowing brachiopod on a fleshy stalk, looks much like fossils more than 450 million years old and was one of Darwin's original examples of a living fossil.

name: Lionfish
fact: Lionfish have 18 venomous spines and, released from aquariums, have invaded the Caribbean and western Atlantic, where they have no natural predators.

name: Lion's mane jellyfish
fact: The lion's mane jellyfish of cold northern seas is the largest known jellyfish, with tentacles that can trail over 30 metres.

name: Liopleurodon
fact: Liopleurodon was a Jurassic pliosaur of European seas with a skull well over a metre long, far smaller than the 25-metre giant once shown on television.

name: Lisbon
fact: Lisbon sits where the Tagus meets the Atlantic, and Vasco da Gama sailed from here in 1497 on the first voyage from Europe to India.

name: Little auk
fact: The little auk is one of the most numerous seabirds in the Arctic, breeding in colonies of millions in Greenland and Svalbard.

name: Little skate
fact: The little skate is a small, common skate of the north-west Atlantic that walks along the seabed on modified pelvic fins.

name: Little tunny
fact: The little tunny, or false albacore, is the most common tuna in the Atlantic, a small, fast, scribble-patterned fish loved by fly anglers but rarely eaten.

name: Livyatan
fact: Livyatan was a sperm whale of about 12 million years ago with teeth more than 30 centimetres long, named after Moby-Dick's author.

name: Lizardfish
fact: Lizardfish are toothy ambush hunters that sit on the sand, often with most of the body buried, and dart up to grab passing fish.

name: Lobster
fact: Lobsters keep growing throughout their lives by moulting their shells, and some may live for decades.

name: Loggerhead turtle
fact: The loggerhead sea turtle has a huge head and powerful jaws for crushing conchs and crabs, and can live for 70 years or more.

name: Loihi Seamount
fact: Loihi, now officially Kamaʻehuakanaloa, is an active undersea volcano south-east of Hawaii that may one day grow into the next Hawaiian island.

name: Lombok Strait
fact: The Lombok Strait between Bali and Lombok marks part of the Wallace Line, the boundary between Asian and Australian wildlife.

name: Lomonosov Ridge
fact: The Lomonosov Ridge crosses the Arctic Ocean floor near the North Pole and is claimed by Russia, Canada and Denmark in competing seabed submissions.

name: Long-beaked common dolphin
fact: The long-beaked common dolphin hugs the coasts of California, Peru and West Africa and has a noticeably longer snout than its short-beaked cousin.

name: Long-finned pilot whale
fact: Long-finned pilot whales are the target of the Faroe Islands' drive hunt, and their pods follow a leader so closely that they strand together.

name: Long Island
fact: Long Island stretches about 190 kilometres east from New York City into the Atlantic and is the largest island in the contiguous United States.

name: Long-nosed chimaera
fact: Long-nosed chimaeras are deep-sea ghost sharks with a long pointed snout covered in electric-sensing pores.

name: Long-snouted seahorse
fact: The long-snouted seahorse lives in seagrass meadows from the British Isles to the Mediterranean and Black Sea, and often grows a mane of skin filaments.

name: Long-spine porcupinefish
fact: The long-spine porcupinefish has spines that lie flat until it inflates, when they stand straight out, and it is found in warm seas worldwide.

name: Long-spined sea urchin
fact: The mass die-off of long-spined sea urchins in the Caribbean in 1983 let algae overgrow many reefs, showing how important their grazing was.

name: Longfin bannerfish
fact: The longfin bannerfish is a black-and-white butterflyfish with a long white dorsal banner, often mistaken for the Moorish idol.

name: Longfin inshore squid
fact: The longfin inshore squid of the US Atlantic coast is a workhorse of neuroscience: its giant nerve fibre helped reveal how nerves fire.

name: Longfin mako
fact: The longfin mako has much longer pectoral fins than its shortfin cousin and is far more rarely seen.

name: Longhorn cowfish
fact: The longhorn cowfish is a boxfish with two horns over its eyes and can release a toxin into the water when it is stressed.

name: Longliner
fact: A longliner fishes with a main line that can stretch for tens of kilometres, hung with thousands of baited hooks.

name: Longman's beaked whale
fact: Longman's beaked whale was known only from two skulls for most of the 20th century and lives in warm Indo-Pacific waters.

name: Longnose batfish
fact: The longnose batfish walks across the seabed on arm-like fins, has a pointed snout, and dangles a tiny lure from beneath it to attract prey.

name: Longnose butterflyfish
fact: The longnose butterflyfish, or forcepsfish, uses its tweezer-like snout to pick tiny animals from coral crevices; it is Hawaii's lauwiliwilinukunukuoioi.

name: Longnose gar
fact: The longnose gar gulps air at the surface and has a long, narrow snout filled with needle-like teeth.

name: Longnose hawkfish
fact: The longnose hawkfish perches on deep gorgonian sea fans wearing a red check pattern, with a long snout for plucking tiny shrimps.

name: Longnose skate
fact: The longnose skate of the North American Pacific coast has a long pointed snout and lays eggs in leathery cases known as mermaid's purses.

name: Longship
fact: Viking longships were long, narrow and shallow-draughted, able to cross open sea and yet be rowed up shallow rivers to raid inland.

name: Longtail tuna
fact: The longtail tuna is a coastal tuna of the Indo-Pacific that stays in shallow seas rather than roaming the open ocean.

name: Loop Current
fact: The Loop Current curls up into the Gulf of Mexico and back out past Florida, and its deep warm water can strengthen hurricanes passing over it.

name: Lophelia
fact: Lophelia is a cold-water coral that builds reefs in the dark, hundreds of metres down, from Norway to the Gulf of Mexico.

name: Lord Howe Island reef
fact: The reef around Lord Howe Island, between Australia and New Zealand, is the southernmost coral reef in the world.

name: Lost City hydrothermal field
fact: The Lost City is a field of pale carbonate chimneys up to 60 metres tall on the Atlantis Massif in the mid-Atlantic, venting warm alkaline fluid rather than black smoke.

name: Louvar
fact: The louvar is a rare open-ocean fish that looks like a tuna but is related to surgeonfish and feeds on jellyfish.

name: Luanda
fact: Luanda, Angola's capital, is a major Atlantic port whose bay is sheltered by the long sand island of Ilha de Luanda.

name: Lumpsucker
fact: The male lumpsucker, or lumpfish, clings to a rock with a sucker on its belly and guards a pink mass of eggs through the spring tides.

name: Lungfish
fact: Lungfish have true lungs as well as gills and are the closest living fish relatives of land animals.

name: Lusitania
fact: The Lusitania was torpedoed by a German U-boat off Ireland in 1915 and lies on its side in about 93 metres of water, slowly collapsing.

name: Lusitanian toadfish
fact: The Lusitanian toadfish of Portuguese estuaries hums and 'boat-whistles' from its nest, and larger males even sing in choruses to attract females.

name: Macaroni penguin
fact: Macaroni penguins are the most numerous penguin and together eat more krill than any other seabird species.

name: Mackerel
fact: Mackerels are fast, striped schooling fish with tiny finlets before the tail; they spoil quickly, so for sushi (saba) they are cured in salt and vinegar.

name: Mackerel icefish
fact: The mackerel icefish has no red blood cells, so its blood runs clear, and it feeds almost entirely on Antarctic krill.

name: Mackerel scad
fact: The mackerel scad is a small schooling jack of tropical waters that is a staple bait and food fish from Hawaii to the Caribbean.

name: Madeira
fact: Madeira is a Portuguese volcanic island in the Atlantic north of the Canaries, famous for its fortified wine and the laurel forests that once covered it.

name: Madtom
fact: Madtoms are tiny North American catfish, mostly under 10 centimetres, with venom glands at the base of their pectoral spines that give a painful sting.

name: Maerl
fact: Maerl is a free-living coralline seaweed that grows into gravel-like nodules, forming seabed beds that take centuries to build up.

name: Mahi-mahi
fact: Mahi-mahi, or dorado, is a fast-growing, brilliantly coloured open-ocean fish that is among the fastest swimmers in the sea and a popular restaurant catch.

name: Mahseer
fact: The golden mahseer of Himalayan rivers was the prized game fish of British India and is now endangered.

name: Mako shark
fact: Makos are widely regarded as the fastest sharks, built for speed with a crescent-shaped tail and a torpedo-shaped body.

name: Makran Trench
fact: The Makran Trench in the Arabian Sea, off Pakistan and Iran, is a shallow trench where the Arabian Plate slides beneath Eurasia.

name: Malpelo Island
fact: Malpelo, a bare rock in the Colombian Pacific, is a sanctuary where hundreds of hammerheads and silky sharks gather around its steep walls.

name: Man-of-war fish
fact: The man-of-war fish lives among the deadly tentacles of the Portuguese man o' war, nibbling on them while sheltering from predators.

name: Manatee
fact: Manatees are gentle plant-eaters whose closest living relatives on land are elephants.

name: Mandarinfish
fact: The mandarinfish is one of only two vertebrates known to make a true blue pigment, and it has no scales but a bitter, toxic coating.

name: Mangrove
fact: Mangroves are trees that grow in salt water along tropical shores, with tangled stilt roots that trap mud and shelter young fish.

name: Mangrove jack
fact: The mangrove jack is a snapper that lurks among mangrove roots in Australia and Asia when young and moves offshore to reefs as it matures.

name: Mangrove killifish
fact: The mangrove killifish can live for weeks out of water inside rotting logs, flipping itself across land with its tail, and most are self-fertilising hermaphrodites.

name: Mangrove monitor
fact: The mangrove monitor is a lizard of Australia and the western Pacific that swims through mangrove swamps and has a salt-excreting gland in its nose.

name: Mangrove whipray
fact: The mangrove whipray spends its youth in mangroves and lagoons of the Indo-Pacific and has a white-spotted dark back.

name: Manila clam
fact: The Manila clam is the most farmed clam in the world and reached North America by accident, mixed in with oyster seed shipped from Japan.

name: Manila Trench
fact: The Manila Trench lies west of Luzon in the South China Sea and reaches about 5,400 metres deep.

name: Manta ray
fact: Manta rays filter plankton through their gills and somersault repeatedly to stay in a dense patch of food.

name: Mantis shrimp
fact: A mantis shrimp strikes with the acceleration of a bullet and sees with up to 16 types of light-sensing cell, compared with our three.

name: Map puffer
fact: The map puffer is named for the maze of dark lines over its body, which look like the contour lines on a map.

name: Mar del Plata
fact: Mar del Plata is Argentina's main seaside resort and its biggest fishing port.

name: Marble trout
fact: The marble trout of Slovenia and northern Italy has a marbled pattern instead of spots and can grow to well over a metre long.

name: Marbled electric ray
fact: The marbled electric ray of the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean stuns its prey with powerful electric shocks.

name: Marbled lungfish
fact: The marbled lungfish breathes air with paired lungs and has one of the largest genomes known, roughly 40 times the size of a human's.

name: Marbled murrelet
fact: The marbled murrelet fishes at sea but nests on mossy branches high in old-growth conifers, sometimes far inland; its nest was not found until 1974.

name: Mariana snailfish
fact: The Mariana snailfish, named in 2017, has been collected from nearly 8,000 metres and has a see-through pink body with no scales.

name: Mariana Trench
fact: The Mariana Trench holds the Challenger Deep, the deepest known point in the ocean at about 10,935 metres.

name: Marianas Trench Marine National Monument
fact: The Marianas Trench Marine National Monument protects the waters and seabed around the deepest trench on Earth and its mud volcanoes.

name: Marie Tharp
fact: Marie Tharp drew the first map of the entire ocean floor and spotted the rift valley running down the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, key evidence for continental drift.

name: Marine flatworm
fact: Marine flatworms cut into pieces can regrow into complete animals, and some are decorated as brightly as the nudibranchs they mimic.

name: Marine iguana
fact: The marine iguana of the Galápagos is the only lizard that feeds in the sea, grazing algae underwater and sneezing out salt.

name: Marine otter
fact: The marine otter, or chungungo, of Chile and Peru is the smallest marine mammal, weighing about 4 kilograms, and lives along rocky shores.

name: Marine virus
fact: Marine viruses are the most numerous biological entities in the sea, around 10 million in every millilitre of seawater, and they kill about a fifth of the ocean's microbes every day.

name: Market squid
fact: Market squid gather in vast spawning schools off California, supporting one of the state's most valuable fisheries.

name: Marlin
fact: Marlins are big, spear-nosed billfish among the fastest fish in the ocean; Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea is the story of a fight with a giant marlin.

name: Maroon clownfish
fact: The maroon clownfish is the largest clownfish, up to about 17 centimetres, with cheek spines and a female far bigger and more aggressive than her mate.

name: Marquesas Islands
fact: The Marquesas are rugged volcanic islands in French Polynesia without protecting reefs, where the painter Paul Gauguin spent his last years.

name: Marron
fact: The marron of Western Australia is one of the largest freshwater crayfish, reaching more than 2 kilograms, and is farmed for restaurants.

name: Marshall Islands
fact: The Marshall Islands are 29 low coral atolls in the central Pacific, including Bikini and Enewetak, where the United States tested nuclear weapons.

name: Mary Rose
fact: Henry VIII's warship Mary Rose sank in the Solent in 1545 and was raised in 1982; its hull is now displayed in Portsmouth.

name: Masked angelfish
fact: The masked angelfish lives only on the deep reefs of the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands and is pure white with a black mask as a female.

name: Masked butterflyfish
fact: The masked butterflyfish lives only in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where it is usually seen in pairs sheltering under table corals.

name: Masked crab
fact: The masked crab buries itself in sand and breathes through a snorkel made of its two long antennae pressed together.

name: Masu salmon
fact: The masu or cherry salmon is the Pacific salmon of Japan, Korea and the Russian Far East, and some populations never leave their rivers.

name: Matthew Flinders
fact: Matthew Flinders was the first to sail right around Australia, from 1801 to 1803, and popularised the continent's name.

name: Matthew Fontaine Maury
fact: Matthew Fontaine Maury, known as the Pathfinder of the Seas, compiled ships' logs into the first charts of ocean winds and currents in the 1840s and 1850s.

name: Māui dolphin
fact: The Māui dolphin, a subspecies of Hector's dolphin off New Zealand's North Island, is among the rarest dolphins with only around 50 adults left.

name: Mauve stinger
fact: The mauve stinger glows when disturbed at night and has caused mass stingings on Mediterranean beaches; one swarm wiped out a salmon farm in Northern Ireland.

name: Mbu puffer
fact: The mbu puffer of the Congo River is a freshwater giant that can reach about 67 centimetres long.

name: McCulloch's anemonefish
fact: McCulloch's anemonefish is a dark clownfish with a white face found only at Lord Howe and Norfolk Islands, one of the most restricted ranges of any clownfish.

name: Medaka
fact: The medaka, or Japanese rice fish, is a 3-centimetre fish that became the first vertebrate to mate and lay eggs in space, aboard the space shuttle in 1994.

name: Mediterranean damselfish
fact: The Mediterranean damselfish is the only native damselfish in the Mediterranean, a dark fish whose juveniles are brilliant blue, common in shoals above rocks.

name: Mediterranean monk seal
fact: The Mediterranean monk seal gives birth in sea caves and numbers fewer than a thousand, most of them in Greece and off Mauritania.

name: Mediterranean moray
fact: The Mediterranean moray was a Roman delicacy, kept in seaside fish ponds by wealthy Romans.

name: Mediterranean parrotfish
fact: The Mediterranean parrotfish is the only native parrotfish in the Mediterranean, prized by the Romans, and is spreading north as the sea warms.

name: Mediterranean Sea
fact: The Mediterranean is almost landlocked, connected to the Atlantic only through the Strait of Gibraltar, and evaporates far more water than its rivers bring in.

name: Megalodon
fact: Megalodon, a shark perhaps 15 to 20 metres long, died out roughly 3.6 million years ago, and its teeth are the size of a human hand.

name: Megamouth shark
fact: The megamouth shark was unknown to science until 1976, when one was hauled up tangled in a US Navy sea anchor off Hawaii.

name: Megrim
fact: The megrim is a slender, left-eyed flatfish of deep European slopes that was long overlooked by British diners and sold mostly to Spain.

name: Mekong giant catfish
fact: The Mekong giant catfish is one of the largest freshwater fish on Earth, reaching about 3 metres and 300 kilograms, and is critically endangered.

name: Melon-headed whale
fact: Melon-headed whales travel in pods of hundreds and are actually dolphins, despite their name.

name: Menhaden
fact: Menhaden are oily filter-feeding fish of the American Atlantic coast, caught in huge numbers for fish oil and fish meal.

name: Mesoamerican Reef
fact: The Mesoamerican Reef runs about 1,000 kilometres from Mexico's Yucatán to Honduras and is the largest barrier reef in the Western Hemisphere.

name: Meteor
fact: The German ship Meteor criss-crossed the South Atlantic from 1925 to 1927 using echo sounding to produce the first detailed picture of a whole ocean basin's floor.

name: Mexican golden trout
fact: The Mexican golden trout lives in mountain streams of the Sierra Madre Occidental and is one of the southernmost native trout in North America.

name: Miami
fact: The Port of Miami on Biscayne Bay calls itself the cruise capital of the world and handles more cruise passengers than any other port.

name: Mid-Atlantic Ridge
fact: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a chain of underwater volcanoes where new seafloor forms as Europe and Africa drift away from the Americas.

name: Middle America Trench
fact: The Middle America Trench runs along the Pacific coast of Central America from Mexico to Costa Rica and reaches about 6,600 metres deep.

name: Midnight parrotfish
fact: The midnight parrotfish is a dark blue Caribbean parrotfish with bright blue markings on its head that often grazes in schools with other species.

name: Midshipman
fact: The plainfin midshipman has rows of photophores like the buttons on a naval uniform, and the humming of the males keeps houseboat residents awake in Sausalito.

name: Midway Atoll
fact: Midway Atoll lies near the end of the Hawaiian chain and gave its name to the 1942 battle that turned the Pacific War.

name: Milkfish
fact: Milkfish is the national fish of the Philippines, farmed in coastal ponds for centuries and eaten despite its many fine bones.

name: Mimic filefish
fact: The mimic filefish copies the look of the poisonous saddled toby so closely that predators leave it alone, though it is not toxic itself.

name: Mimic octopus
fact: The mimic octopus of Indonesia impersonates lionfish, flatfish and sea snakes by changing its shape, colour and the way it moves.

name: Minerva Reefs
fact: The Minerva Reefs are two remote atolls south of Fiji, claimed by Tonga, that briefly hosted a self-declared micronation in 1972.

name: Minke whale
fact: Minke whales are the smallest of the rorquals and the main target of whaling by Norway, Japan and Iceland today.

name: Mir
fact: The Russian submersibles Mir-1 and Mir-2 filmed the Titanic wreck for James Cameron's 1997 film and in 2007 planted a flag on the sea floor at the North Pole.

name: Molasses Reef
fact: Molasses Reef off Key Largo, Florida, lies inside the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary and is one of the most popular dive and snorkel sites in the Keys.

name: Mole crab
fact: Mole crabs burrow backwards into the sand of surf beaches and filter food from the receding waves with their feathery antennae.

name: Molly
fact: Mollies are hardy livebearers from Central America that thrive in anything from fresh to fully salty water.

name: Molokini
fact: Molokini is a crescent-shaped volcanic crater off Maui whose sheltered inner reef is one of Hawaii's most visited snorkelling spots.

name: Molucca Sea
fact: The Molucca Sea lies between Sulawesi and the Maluku Islands, the Spice Islands that drew European traders to Indonesia.

name: Monk seal
fact: Monk seals are the only seals adapted to warm tropical and subtropical waters, and only two species survive today.

name: Monkfish
fact: Monkfish lie flattened on the seabed and twitch a fleshy lure on their heads to draw fish into their enormous mouths.

name: Monterey Bay
fact: Monterey Bay in California lies above a submarine canyon as deep as the Grand Canyon and is a sanctuary for sea otters and whales.

name: Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary
fact: Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary stretches along central California and shelters kelp forests, sea otters and a submarine canyon deeper than the Grand Canyon.

name: Monterey Canyon
fact: Monterey Canyon off California is a submarine canyon comparable in scale to the Grand Canyon, plunging to more than 3,000 metres.

name: Montevideo
fact: Montevideo, Uruguay's capital and main port, lies on the Río de la Plata near where the Graf Spee was scuttled in 1939.

name: Montipora
fact: Montipora corals grow as plates, crusts and branches and are popular in reef aquariums for their bright colours.

name: Moon jellyfish
fact: The moon jellyfish is see-through with four horseshoe-shaped gonads visible through its bell, and its sting is too weak to hurt most people.

name: Moon snail
fact: Moon snails plough through sand on a huge foot, drilling neat round holes in clam shells, and lay their eggs in a collar of sand.

name: Moon wrasse
fact: The moon wrasse, or lunar wrasse, is a green-and-blue wrasse with a yellow crescent on the tail, common on reefs across the Indo-Pacific.

name: Moorish idol
fact: The Moorish idol, with its long trailing dorsal fin, is notoriously hard to keep in aquariums because it feeds mainly on sponges.

name: Moray eel
fact: Moray eels have a second set of jaws in their throat that shoots forward to drag prey down the gullet.

name: Mosasaur
fact: Mosasaurs were giant sea lizards related to monitor lizards and snakes that ruled the late Cretaceous seas until the asteroid struck.

name: Moses sole
fact: The Moses sole of the Red Sea oozes a milky, soap-like toxin from its fins that makes sharks spit it out, and the toxin was studied as a shark repellent.

name: Mosquitofish
fact: The mosquitofish was released worldwide to eat mosquito larvae and has instead wiped out native fish and frogs from Australia to Spain.

name: Mozambique Channel
fact: The Mozambique Channel separates Madagascar from the African mainland, and the coelacanth was found alive in the Comoros at its northern end.

name: Estonia
fact: The ferry Estonia sank in a Baltic storm in September 1994 with the loss of 852 lives, and lies on the seabed at about 80 metres.

name: Mud crab
fact: The giant mud crab of mangrove estuaries has claws strong enough to crack a mussel shell or a careless finger, and is the crab in Singapore chilli crab.

name: Mud lobster
fact: The mud lobster of Indo-Pacific mangroves builds volcano-shaped mounds of mud over a metre high, which other mangrove animals use as homes.

name: Mudskipper
fact: Mudskippers are fish that walk and skip across mud flats, breathe through their skin, and retreat into burrows they dig in the mud.

name: Mullet
fact: Mullet feed on algae and detritus in estuaries and mangrove creeks and are famous for leaping clear of the water for no obvious reason.

name: Munk's devil ray
fact: Munk's devil rays gather in schools of thousands off Baja California and the Galápagos and leap metres into the air, landing with a slap.

name: Murex
fact: Murex are spiny sea snails whose glands gave the ancient Phoenicians the precious purple dye of Tyre, worn by emperors.

name: Murray cod
fact: The Murray cod is Australia's largest freshwater fish, growing well over a metre in the Murray-Darling rivers.

name: Musashi
fact: The battleship Musashi, sister of the Yamato, was sunk in the Sibuyan Sea in 1944 and found by Paul Allen's team in 2015 more than 1,000 metres down.

name: Mushroom coral
fact: Mushroom corals are single large polyps that live unattached on the sea floor and can creep slowly across the sand.

name: Muskellunge
fact: The muskellunge, 'fish of ten thousand casts', is the largest pike and can top 1.5 metres in the lakes of the Great Lakes region.

name: Musky octopus
fact: The musky octopus of the Mediterranean gives off a distinct musky smell and has a single row of suckers on each arm.

name: Mussau Trench
fact: The Mussau Trench north of Papua New Guinea is a young, short trench reaching about 7,000 metres deep.

name: Mussel
fact: Mussels anchor themselves to rocks with tough byssal threads, which have inspired new surgical glues.

name: Mutton snapper
fact: The mutton snapper is a large Caribbean snapper with a black spot on its side and blue lines on its face, prized for the table.

name: MV Derbyshire
fact: The bulk carrier Derbyshire, the largest British ship ever lost at sea, went down in a typhoon in 1980 with 44 people and was found in 1994 about 4,200 metres down.

name: Myrtoan Sea
fact: The Myrtoan Sea is the part of the Aegean between the Cyclades and the eastern coast of the Peloponnese.

name: Nankai Trough
fact: The Nankai Trough off southern Japan is a subduction trench feared for the huge earthquakes it produces roughly every 100 to 150 years.

name: Napoleon wrasse
fact: The Napoleon wrasse can grow to about 2 metres long and is one of the few fish that eats the toxic crown-of-thorns starfish.

name: Nares Strait
fact: Nares Strait between Greenland and Ellesmere Island is named after George Nares, the British admiral who led an expedition towards the North Pole in 1875.

name: Narrow-barred Spanish mackerel
fact: The narrow-barred Spanish mackerel is a big, fast Indo-Pacific fish with wavy bars on its flanks, a prize of Australian and Gulf fishing.

name: Narrow sawfish
fact: The narrow sawfish, or knifetooth sawfish, has a slimmer snout than other sawfish and is the only member of its genus, Anoxypristis.

name: Narwhal
fact: The narwhal's spiral tusk is actually a tooth that can grow to about 3 metres and is packed with nerve endings.

name: Naso tang
fact: The naso tang, or orangespine unicornfish, has bright orange tail spines like a lipstick, and the males trail a long filament from each tail lobe.

name: Nassau
fact: Nassau, capital of the Bahamas, was a notorious pirate haven in the early 1700s, home to Blackbeard and Charles Vane.

name: Nassau grouper
fact: The Nassau grouper gathers in huge spawning groups at the same Caribbean sites each winter full moon, which made it easy to overfish; it is now endangered.

name: Natalia Molchanova
fact: Natalia Molchanova was the most decorated free diver in history, holding dozens of world records, before disappearing on a dive off Ibiza in 2015.

name: Nauru
fact: Nauru is a single raised coral island in the Pacific, the smallest island nation in the world, once rich from mining phosphate formed from seabird droppings.

name: Nautile
fact: Nautile is the French crewed submersible that explored the wreck of the Titanic and recovered thousands of artefacts from it.

name: Nautilus
fact: The nautilus controls its buoyancy by adjusting gas in the chambers of its spiral shell, and its lineage has changed little in hundreds of millions of years.

name: Navaga
fact: The navaga is a small Arctic cod of the White and Barents Seas, fished through the ice in Russia in winter.

name: Needlefish
fact: Needlefish have long beak-like jaws full of teeth and skim the surface at speed, occasionally spearing boaters when they leap.

name: Nematode
fact: Nematodes are the most abundant animals in deep-sea mud, including the sediments of the Challenger Deep, nearly 11 kilometres down.

name: Neon flying squid
fact: Neon flying squid have been photographed gliding about 30 metres through the air, spreading their fins and arms like wings.

name: Neon goby
fact: The neon goby is a 4-centimetre Caribbean cleaner fish with a blue stripe that picks parasites from much larger fish at cleaning stations.

name: Neon tetra
fact: The neon tetra, with its electric blue stripe over red, grows to only about 3 centimetres and is one of the most popular aquarium fish, with millions bred each year.

name: Neopilina
fact: Neopilina, a limpet-like deep-sea mollusc dredged up in 1952, belongs to a group thought extinct for 350 million years.

name: Neptune grass
fact: Neptune grass, Posidonia oceanica, forms vast Mediterranean meadows; one clone off Ibiza is thought to be up to about 100,000 years old.

name: Neptune's necklace
fact: Neptune's necklace is a seaweed of strings of water-filled beads, common on rocky shores of Australia and New Zealand.

name: Nereus
fact: Nereus was a hybrid robot submarine that reached the Challenger Deep in 2009 and was lost in the Kermadec Trench in 2014 when it imploded at nearly 10,000 metres.

name: New Bedford
fact: New Bedford, Massachusetts, was the whaling capital of the world in the 1800s and is today the highest-value fishing port in the United States.

name: New Britain Trench
fact: The New Britain Trench off Papua New Guinea drops to about 9,000 metres and has been explored by robotic landers dropped from the surface.

name: New Caledonia
fact: New Caledonia is a French territory in the south-west Pacific whose main island is ringed by one of the longest barrier reefs in the world.

name: New Caledonia Barrier Reef
fact: The New Caledonia Barrier Reef is the second-longest double barrier reef in the world and encloses one of the largest lagoons on Earth.

name: New England Seamounts
fact: The New England Seamounts are a chain of extinct volcanoes running south-east from Georges Bank into the deep Atlantic, home to cold-water coral gardens.

name: New Guinea
fact: New Guinea is the second-largest island in the world and is home to the birds of paradise and more than 800 languages.

name: New Hebrides Trench
fact: The New Hebrides Trench near Vanuatu reaches about 7,600 metres, and a 2013 expedition found it full of cusk eels and prawns rather than the snailfish seen in other trenches.

name: New York
fact: New York Harbour is one of the great natural harbours of the world and was the main gateway for immigrants arriving in the United States.

name: New Zealand
fact: New Zealand's two main islands sit alone in the South Pacific, and their isolation produced flightless birds like the kiwi and the extinct giant moa.

name: New Zealand longfin eel
fact: The New Zealand longfin eel is one of the largest and longest-lived freshwater eels; females can live for more than 60 years before heading to sea to spawn once.

name: New Zealand mud snail
fact: The tiny New Zealand mud snail spreads on anglers' boots and can reach hundreds of thousands per square metre in rivers of the western USA and Europe.

name: New Zealand sea lion
fact: The New Zealand sea lion, or Hooker's sea lion, is one of the rarest sea lions and breeds mainly on the remote Auckland Islands.

name: Newfoundland
fact: Newfoundland is a large island off eastern Canada where Vikings landed around the year 1000 and whose Grand Banks were once the richest cod fishery on Earth.

name: Night shark
fact: The night shark has large green eyes and lives along the edge of the continental shelf in the Atlantic, rising to feed at night.

name: Nile perch
fact: The Nile perch, introduced to Lake Victoria in the 1950s, grows to about 2 metres and drove hundreds of native cichlid species to extinction.

name: Ninety East Ridge
fact: The Ninety East Ridge is a remarkably straight underwater mountain chain in the Indian Ocean, named because it follows the 90th meridian east.

name: Ningaloo Marine Park
fact: Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia is a fringing reef you can swim to from the beach, famous for whale sharks that gather every autumn.

name: Ningaloo Reef
fact: Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia is a fringing reef that hugs the shore so closely you can swim to it from the beach, and whale sharks gather there each year.

name: Ninja lanternshark
fact: The ninja lanternshark, a black glowing shark described in 2015, was named by the describer's young cousins, and its species name honours Jaws author Peter Benchley.

name: Noble pen shell
fact: The noble pen shell is a metre-long fan mussel of Mediterranean seagrass meadows whose silky threads were once woven into 'sea silk', and a parasite has nearly wiped it out since 2016.

name: Noctiluca
fact: Noctiluca, the 'sea sparkle', is a bubble-like dinoflagellate that lights up breaking waves at night with blue bioluminescence.

name: Nomura's jellyfish
fact: Nomura's jellyfish can weigh 200 kilograms and measure 2 metres across, and swarms drifting from China into Japanese waters have capsized a fishing boat.

name: Norfolk
fact: Norfolk, Virginia, at the mouth of Chesapeake Bay, is home to the largest naval base in the world.

name: Nori
fact: Nori is dried, pressed sheets of the red seaweed laver, grown on nets in shallow Japanese bays and used to wrap sushi rolls.

name: Norris's top snail
fact: Norris's top snail crawls up giant kelp to graze, then lets go and sinks when it senses a sea star hunting it.

name: North Atlantic Drift
fact: The North Atlantic Drift is the continuation of the Gulf Stream that carries warm water towards Britain, Norway and the Arctic.

name: North Atlantic Gyre
fact: The North Atlantic Gyre is the clockwise loop formed by the Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift, Canary Current and North Equatorial Current, enclosing the Sargasso Sea.

name: North Atlantic right whale
fact: The North Atlantic right whale is one of the most endangered great whales, with only around 370 left off eastern North America.

name: North Equatorial Current
fact: The North Equatorial Current flows westward just north of the equator in both the Atlantic and the Pacific, driven by the trade winds.

name: North Pacific Gyre
fact: The North Pacific Gyre is the huge clockwise circulation of the North Pacific whose calm centre collects floating plastic in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.

name: North Pacific right whale
fact: The North Pacific right whale is one of the rarest whales, with perhaps only about 30 animals left in the eastern North Pacific.

name: North Sea
fact: The North Sea is a shallow arm of the Atlantic between Britain and mainland Europe, averaging only about 90 metres deep.

name: Northern anchovy
fact: The northern anchovy schools along the North American Pacific coast and feeds everything from humpback whales to brown pelicans.

name: Northern bottlenose whale
fact: Northern bottlenose whales were heavily hunted in the North Atlantic for their oil and are famously curious about boats.

name: Northern elephant seal
fact: Northern elephant seals were hunted to the brink of extinction in the 19th century, with perhaps fewer than 100 left, and now number well over 100,000.

name: Northern fur seal
fact: Most of the world's northern fur seals breed on the Pribilof Islands in the Bering Sea, where they were once hunted by the hundreds of thousands.

name: Northern gannet
fact: Northern gannets plunge-dive from up to 30 metres, hitting the water at around 100 kilometres per hour, with air sacs under the skin to cushion the impact.

name: Northern pike
fact: Northern pike lunge at prey from cover and leap clear of the water when hooked, and they can reach well over a metre long.

name: Northern pipefish
fact: The northern pipefish lives in eelgrass beds along the western Atlantic coast, often alongside the lined seahorse.

name: Northern prawn
fact: The northern prawn starts life as a male and changes into a female after a few years, and is the cold-water prawn in most prawn cocktails.

name: Northern puffer
fact: The northern puffer of the US east coast is sold as 'sea squab', its flesh being far less toxic than that of tropical puffers.

name: Northern right whale dolphin
fact: The northern right whale dolphin of the North Pacific has no dorsal fin and skims along the surface in low, long leaps.

name: Norway pout
fact: The Norway pout is a small cod relative of the North Sea caught almost entirely for fishmeal and oil.

name: Norwegian Current
fact: The Norwegian Current carries warm Atlantic water north along the coast of Norway, keeping its harbours ice-free even beyond the Arctic Circle.

name: Nudibranch
fact: Nudibranchs are sea slugs, and some steal the stinging cells from the anemones they eat and reuse them for their own defence.

name: Nuestra Señora de Atocha
fact: The Spanish treasure galleon Nuestra Señora de Atocha sank in a hurricane off the Florida Keys in 1622; its gold and silver were found in 1985.

name: Numbfish
fact: The Australian numbfish is a flabby electric ray that lies buried in sand and can deliver a strong shock, and it is sometimes stranded alive on beaches.

name: Nurse shark
fact: Nurse sharks rest in groups on the seabed by day and suck prey out of crevices with a powerful vacuum-like gulp.

name: Nursehound
fact: The nursehound is a large spotted catshark of the eastern Atlantic that lays its eggs in tough cases attached to seaweed.

name: Nurseryfish
fact: The male nurseryfish of northern Australia and New Guinea carries the egg cluster hooked onto a bony hook on his forehead until the eggs hatch.

name: Nuuk
fact: Nuuk, Greenland's capital, lies on the Labrador Sea and is one of the smallest capital cities in the world.

name: Oarfish
fact: The giant oarfish is the longest bony fish, reaching about 8 metres, and its rare strandings probably inspired sea-serpent legends.

name: Oarweed
fact: Oarweed is a common European kelp with a thick stem and a blade split into fingers, exposed only at the lowest tides.

name: Oasisia tube worm
fact: Oasisia is a slender tube worm that grows in tangles among giant tube worms at East Pacific vents and, like them, feeds through bacteria instead of a mouth.

name: Ocean quahog
fact: An ocean quahog dredged up off Iceland in 2006 was 507 years old, the oldest known individual animal ever found.

name: Ocean sunfish
fact: The ocean sunfish, or mola, is the heaviest bony fish, weighing over 2 tonnes, and drifts the open ocean eating jellyfish.

name: Oceanic whitetip shark
fact: Oceanic whitetips were blamed for many of the deaths of USS Indianapolis sailors adrift in the Pacific in 1945.

name: Ocellaris clownfish
fact: The ocellaris clownfish is the orange, three-barred fish made famous as Nemo; the film's success made it one of the most traded reef fish in the world.

name: Ocellate river stingray
fact: The ocellate river stingray lives in the Amazon and Paraná river systems and is one of the few rays found only in fresh water.

name: Ochre sea star
fact: The ochre sea star comes in purple or orange and is a keystone predator that stops mussels from taking over the rocky shore.

name: Octopus
fact: An octopus has three hearts and blue, copper-based blood, and about two-thirds of its neurons sit in its eight arms rather than its brain.

name: Odd bobtail squid
fact: The odd bobtail squid defends itself by squirting a glowing cloud of luminous mucus instead of dark ink.

name: Ohrid trout
fact: The Ohrid trout lives only in Lake Ohrid, one of the oldest lakes in Europe, on the border of North Macedonia and Albania.

name: Oil tanker
fact: The largest oil tankers ever built, the ultra-large crude carriers, could carry more than 500,000 tonnes of oil in a single voyage.

name: Okeanos Explorer
fact: Okeanos Explorer is a US government ship dedicated entirely to exploring unknown parts of the ocean, broadcasting its dives live online.

name: Okinawa
fact: Okinawa is the largest of Japan's Ryukyu Islands, in the East China Sea, and was the site of the last great battle of the Second World War in 1945.

name: Olive flounder
fact: The olive flounder, or hirame, is the most widely farmed flatfish in Japan and South Korea and is served raw as sashimi.

name: Olive ridley sea turtle
fact: Olive ridleys nest in arribadas of tens of thousands of females on single beaches in Costa Rica, Mexico and India.

name: Olive sea snake
fact: The olive sea snake of Australian reefs has light-sensing cells in its tail, so it can keep its tail hidden in a crevice.

name: Oman anemonefish
fact: The Oman anemonefish is found only along the coast of Oman, where it lives in anemones on rocky reefs.

name: Omura's whale
fact: Omura's whale was only recognised as a species in 2003 and was first filmed alive off Madagascar in 2015.

name: Opabinia
fact: Opabinia, a Cambrian sea creature with five eyes and a clawed trunk, reportedly drew laughter when first shown to scientists in 1972.

name: Opah
fact: The opah, or moonfish, is the only fish known to keep its whole body warm, circulating heated blood through its gills.

name: Opalescent nudibranch
fact: The opalescent nudibranch of Pacific Northwest tide pools stores stinging cells from the hydroids it eats in the orange tips of its back.

name: Opaleye
fact: The opaleye is a Californian kelp-forest fish with bright blue-green eyes that feeds mainly on seaweed.

name: Opossum shrimp
fact: Opossum shrimp carry their young in a pouch like a possum and swarm in glassy clouds in caves, estuaries and the deep sea.

name: Orange clownfish
fact: The orange clownfish, or percula, looks almost identical to the ocellaris but has thicker black edges to its white bars, and lives around New Guinea and the Great Barrier Reef.

name: Orange-lined triggerfish
fact: The orange-lined triggerfish is dark green with curving orange lines and is notoriously aggressive, both on the reef and in aquariums.

name: Orange roughy
fact: The orange roughy lives at 500 to 1,500 metres, does not breed until its twenties and can live for about 150 years, which is why it was so easily overfished.

name: Orange-spotted grouper
fact: The orange-spotted grouper, or estuary cod, is a brown grouper with orange spots that is farmed widely in Southeast Asia for live-fish restaurants.

name: Orca
fact: Orcas are actually the largest dolphins, and different populations have their own dialects and hunting traditions.

name: Oresund
fact: The Oresund between Denmark and Sweden is one of the three Danish straits linking the Baltic to the North Sea, now spanned by the Oresund Bridge.

name: Organ pipe coral
fact: Organ pipe coral has a bright red skeleton of parallel tubes like organ pipes, hidden under greyish-green polyps.

name: Oriental sweetlips
fact: The oriental sweetlips of Indian Ocean reefs hangs under ledges in striped schools by day, and its juveniles wriggle like poisonous flatworms.

name: Orkney
fact: Orkney, just north of mainland Scotland, is home to Skara Brae, a stone village older than the pyramids, and the natural harbour of Scapa Flow.

name: Ormer
fact: The ormer is the European abalone, gathered by hand on Channel Island beaches at low tide on a handful of strictly controlled days each year.

name: Ornate ghost pipefish
fact: In ornate ghost pipefish it is the female, not the male, that broods the eggs, in a pouch formed by her enlarged pelvic fins.

name: Ornate sea snake
fact: The ornate sea snake lives on reefs and sandy flats around northern Australia and feeds on fish and fish eggs.

name: Ornate wobbegong
fact: The ornate wobbegong is a carpet shark of eastern Australian reefs that lies camouflaged on the bottom by day and hunts at night.

name: Oscar
fact: The oscar is a big Amazon cichlid that recognises its owner, begs at the glass and rearranges the gravel in its tank.

name: Osprey
fact: The osprey hits the water feet-first and has a reversible outer toe and spiny foot pads to grip slippery fish.

name: Osprey Reef
fact: Osprey Reef is a submerged atoll in the Coral Sea off Queensland whose walls plunge about 1,000 metres and attract shark-diving expeditions.

name: Ostracod
fact: Ostracods, or seed shrimps, are tiny crustaceans sealed in a hinged shell, and some species flash blue light to attract mates.

name: Otis Barton
fact: Otis Barton designed and paid for the bathysphere in which he and William Beebe dived in the 1930s, and in 1949 reached about 1,370 metres alone in his benthoscope.

name: Otocinclus
fact: Otocinclus, or 'otos', are tiny suckermouth catfish from South America, kept in aquariums to graze algae and barely 4 centimetres long.

name: Otodus
fact: Otodus obliquus was a giant mackerel shark of about 50 million years ago whose lineage led to megalodon.

name: Outer Banks
fact: The Outer Banks are a long chain of barrier islands off North Carolina, where the Wright brothers first flew and the pirate Blackbeard was killed.

name: Outrigger canoe
fact: An outrigger canoe has a float lashed alongside the hull for stability, and such canoes carried Austronesian peoples across the Pacific and Indian Oceans.

name: Oyashio Current
fact: The Oyashio is a cold current flowing south from the Bering Sea past Kamchatka, and where it meets the warm Kuroshio it creates rich fishing grounds off Japan.

name: Oyster
fact: A single oyster can filter up to around 190 litres of water a day, and oyster reefs once lined estuaries such as New York Harbour.

name: Oyster toadfish
fact: The male oyster toadfish guards the eggs in a den and calls females with a foghorn-like 'boat whistle' that can be heard from boats above.

name: Pacific angelshark
fact: The Pacific angelshark lies buried in sand off California and Mexico and snaps upward at passing fish faster than the eye can follow.

name: Pacific bluefin tuna
fact: The Pacific bluefin tuna is the species behind Tokyo's record new-year auctions; one sold for about 333 million yen in 2019.

name: Pacific cod
fact: The Pacific cod is a major fishery of the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska, with catches of several hundred thousand tonnes a year.

name: Pacific electric ray
fact: The Pacific electric ray hunts at night off California, enveloping fish in its disc and shocking them with up to about 45 volts.

name: Pacific halibut
fact: Pacific halibut are a mainstay of Alaskan fisheries, and anglers call the biggest ones, over 45 kilograms, barn doors.

name: Pacific herring
fact: The Pacific herring is fished mainly for its roe, sold to Japan as kazunoko, and its eggs laid on kelp are a traditional food of the Pacific Northwest.

name: Pacific lamprey
fact: The Pacific lamprey climbs waterfalls with its sucker mouth on its way up Columbia River tributaries and is a traditional food of Native peoples.

name: Pacific leaping blenny
fact: The Pacific leaping blenny of Guam lives entirely out of water on wave-splashed rocks, leaping between them by curling and flicking its tail.

name: Pacific oyster
fact: The Pacific oyster, native to Japan, is now the most farmed oyster in the world and grows on coasts from France to Australia.

name: Pacific sand lance
fact: Pacific sand lance spend the night and much of the winter buried in coarse sand, which is why mapping their sand beds matters for salmon and seabirds.

name: Pacific sandfish
fact: The Pacific sandfish buries itself in sand with just its upturned mouth exposed, and is a key prey of seabirds and salmon in Alaska.

name: Pacific sardine
fact: The Pacific sardine fuelled Monterey's Cannery Row until the stock collapsed in the 1950s, and it still booms and busts with ocean cycles.

name: Pacific saury
