fact: Pacific saury, sanma, is caught by the hundreds of thousands of tonnes in the northwest Pacific and is an autumn favourite grilled whole in Japan.

name: Pacific seahorse
fact: The Pacific seahorse is the only seahorse in the eastern Pacific, ranging from California to Peru and the Galápagos Islands.

name: Pacific sleeper shark
fact: The Pacific sleeper shark is a sluggish giant of cold northern waters that has been recorded at depths of around 2,000 metres.

name: Pacific spiny lumpsucker
fact: The Pacific spiny lumpsucker is a golf-ball-sized fish of the Pacific Northwest that sticks to eelgrass and rocks with a suction disc.

name: Pacific white-sided dolphin
fact: Pacific white-sided dolphins travel in boisterous groups of hundreds in the cool North Pacific and often ride the bow waves of ships.

name: Paddlefish
fact: The American paddlefish's long paddle-shaped snout is packed with tens of thousands of electroreceptors used to detect swarms of plankton.

name: Paedocypris
fact: Paedocypris progenetica, from the peat swamps of Sumatra, matures at under 8 millimetres and is among the smallest fish known.

name: Pagasetic Gulf
fact: The Pagasetic Gulf is an almost enclosed bay of the Aegean in Thessaly from whose shore, in legend, Jason and the Argonauts set sail for the Golden Fleece.

name: Palancar Reef
fact: Palancar Reef off Cozumel, Mexico, is part of the Mesoamerican Reef and became a famous dive site after Jacques Cousteau filmed it in the 1960s.

name: Palau
fact: Palau in the western Pacific is famous for its Rock Islands and for Jellyfish Lake, where millions of harmless jellyfish drift in a marine lake.

name: Palau National Marine Sanctuary
fact: Palau closed about 80 percent of its waters to fishing in 2020, creating one of the largest fully protected marine sanctuaries in the world.

name: Palau Trench
fact: The Palau Trench lies east of the islands of Palau in the western Pacific and reaches about 8,000 metres deep.

name: Palk Strait
fact: Palk Strait between India and Sri Lanka is so shallow that large ships cannot pass, and a chain of shoals called Adam's Bridge lies at its southern end.

name: Palm worm
fact: The palm worm builds mucus tubes on Pacific vent chimneys and spreads a crown of tentacles like a palm tree to feed in the hot water.

name: Palmyra Atoll
fact: Palmyra Atoll, an uninhabited US territory south of Hawaii, has reefs so untouched that predators like sharks make up most of the fish biomass.

name: Pancake batfish
fact: The pancake batfish is a round, flattened fish of the Gulf of Mexico seabed that hops along on arm-like fins.

name: Pangasius
fact: Pangasius, sold as basa or river cobbler, is a Vietnamese Mekong catfish farmed in vast numbers and exported as cheap white fillets.

name: Pantropical spotted dolphin
fact: Pantropical spotted dolphins swim above yellowfin tuna in the eastern Pacific, where millions died in tuna nets before dolphin-safe fishing.

name: Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument
fact: Papahānaumokuākea protects the uninhabited north-western Hawaiian Islands and is one of the largest marine protected areas in the world.

name: Paradise fish
fact: The paradise fish breathes air with a labyrinth organ and was one of the first tropical fish kept in home aquariums.

name: Parrotfish
fact: Parrotfish grind coral with beak-like teeth and excrete the remains as fine white sand, producing much of the sand on tropical beaches.

name: Patagonian red octopus
fact: The Patagonian red octopus is fished along the coasts of Chile and Argentina and is a close relative of the giant Pacific octopus.

name: Patagonian toothfish
fact: The Patagonian toothfish was renamed 'Chilean sea bass' by a fish wholesaler in 1977 to sell it, and lives down to about 3,800 metres.

name: Payara
fact: The payara of the Orinoco and Amazon has two lower fangs so long that they fit into holes in its upper jaw.

name: Pea crab
fact: The pea crab is a tiny crab that lives inside the shells of living mussels and oysters, stealing food from its host's gills.

name: Pea puffer
fact: The pea puffer from the rivers of south-west India is one of the smallest pufferfish, about 3 centimetres long.

name: Peacock bass
fact: The peacock bass is an Amazon cichlid, not a bass, and was released in Florida canals, where anglers now chase it.

name: Peacock flounder
fact: The peacock flounder is covered in bright blue rings and can change its pattern to match the reef in seconds.

name: Peacock mantis shrimp
fact: The peacock mantis shrimp's club-like arms hit so hard they can crack aquarium glass and shatter crab shells in a single blow.

name: Peacock's tail
fact: Peacock's tail is a small fan-shaped brown seaweed of warm rock pools, banded with white lime and shimmering blue-green.

name: Peale's dolphin
fact: Peale's dolphin lives among the kelp beds and channels of Patagonia and the Falkland Islands and is named after artist Titian Peale.

name: Pearlfish
fact: The pearlfish spends the day hiding inside the body of a sea cucumber, slipping in tail-first through its anus.

name: Pearly razorfish
fact: The pearly razorfish is a wrasse with a blade-thin head that dives headfirst into sand in an instant to escape, and sleeps buried there.

name: Pederson's cleaner shrimp
fact: Pederson's cleaner shrimp is see-through with violet spots and lives on Caribbean anemones, where it cleans parasites from visiting fish.

name: Pelagibacter
fact: Pelagibacter ubique, from the SAR11 group, is probably the most abundant organism on Earth, a bacterium with hundreds of thousands in every millilitre of surface seawater.

name: Pelagic stingray
fact: The pelagic stingray is the only stingray that lives in the open ocean rather than on the seabed.

name: Pelagic thresher
fact: Pelagic threshers rise to a reef cleaning station at Malapascua in the Philippines each dawn to have parasites picked off by cleaner wrasses.

name: Pelagos Sanctuary
aliases: Pelagos Sanctuary for Mediterranean Marine Mammals
fact: The Pelagos Sanctuary is a marine mammal reserve between France, Monaco and Italy where fin whales and striped dolphins feed in the Ligurian Sea.

name: Pelican
fact: A pelican scoops fish in a throat pouch that can hold around 10 litres of water, which it drains before swallowing the catch.

name: Penguin
fact: Penguins have backward-pointing spines on the tongue and roof of the mouth that stop slippery krill and fish escaping as they swallow.

name: Pentland Firth
fact: The Pentland Firth between mainland Scotland and Orkney has some of the fastest tidal currents in the world, used today to generate electricity.

name: Peppermint angelfish
fact: The peppermint angelfish, striped red and white, lives on deep reefs in the Cook Islands below 100 metres; one at Hawaii's Waikiki Aquarium drew offers of 30,000 dollars.

name: Peppermint shrimp
fact: The peppermint shrimp is stocked in reef aquariums because it eats the pest anemone Aiptasia.

name: Periwinkle
fact: Periwinkles are small shore snails that seal themselves inside their shells with a trapdoor to survive hours out of water at low tide.

name: Permit
fact: The permit is a wary, deep-bodied flats fish of the Caribbean that fly anglers consider among the hardest to catch.

name: Peru-Chile Trench
fact: The Peru-Chile Trench, or Atacama Trench, runs about 5,900 kilometres along South America's Pacific coast and reaches about 8,000 metres deep.

name: Peruvian anchoveta
fact: The Peruvian anchoveta is the most heavily fished species on Earth, with catches that have topped 10 million tonnes a year, nearly all ground into fishmeal.

name: Petrale sole
fact: The petrale sole, a right-eyed flounder of the US and Canadian Pacific coast, is one of the most prized flatfish caught there.

name: Petrel
fact: Petrels are tube-nosed seabirds with a keen sense of smell that pick fish, squid and krill from the water, and the giant petrels also scavenge.

name: Phaeocystis
fact: Phaeocystis is a colony-forming alga whose spring blooms whip up thick brown foam on North Sea beaches.

name: Pharaoh cuttlefish
fact: The pharaoh cuttlefish of the Indo-Pacific is one of the most heavily fished cuttlefish and is also bred in labs for research.

name: Philippe Cousteau
fact: Philippe Cousteau, Jacques Cousteau's younger son, filmed and co-produced many of his father's undersea documentaries before dying in a seaplane crash in 1979.

name: Philippine Sea
fact: The Philippine Sea, east of the Philippines, is the largest sea in the world by area and contains the Mariana Trench.

name: Philippine Trench
fact: The Philippine Trench off Mindanao reaches about 10,500 metres at the Emden Deep, named after the German cruiser that sounded it in 1927.

name: Philippines
fact: The Philippines is an archipelago of more than 7,000 islands between the South China Sea and the Pacific.

name: Phoenix Islands Protected Area
fact: The Phoenix Islands Protected Area in Kiribati covers more than 400,000 square kilometres of the central Pacific around eight coral atolls.

name: Phronima
fact: Phronima is a transparent amphipod that hollows out a salp and lives inside the barrel, rearing its young there as it drifts.

name: Phytoplankton
fact: Phytoplankton are the drifting microscopic algae and bacteria that produce roughly half of the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere.

name: Picasso triggerfish
fact: The Picasso triggerfish wears a pattern of blue, black and yellow stripes that looks painted on, and it drums by beating its pectoral fins against its swim bladder.

name: Pictus catfish
fact: The pictus catfish is a spotted, long-whiskered aquarium catfish from the Amazon and Orinoco whose barbels can be as long as its body.

name: Piglet squid
fact: The piglet squid is a see-through, balloon-shaped deep-sea squid whose tuft of arms above a snout-like funnel gives it a comical piggy face.

name: Pike conger
fact: The daggertooth pike conger is a fanged eel of Indo-Pacific coasts eaten in Japan as hamo, famously in Kyoto in summer.

name: Pillar coral
fact: Pillar coral grows in tall columns up to about 3 metres high and, unlike most corals, extends its feeding polyps by day.

name: Pilot fish
fact: Pilot fish swim alongside sharks, rays and turtles, feeding on scraps and parasites, and are rarely attacked by their hosts.

name: Pilot whale
fact: Pilot whales are large dolphins that travel in tight-knit pods and are prone to mass strandings on beaches.

name: Pincushion starfish
fact: The pincushion starfish of Indo-Pacific reefs is so plump and rounded that its five arms are barely visible, making it look like a puffed-up pillow.

name: Pinecone fish
fact: The pinecone fish is armoured in big plated scales and carries glowing bacteria in two light organs on its lower jaw to lure prey at night.

name: Pinfish
fact: The pinfish of the western Atlantic eats more and more seagrass as it grows, and is a common bait fish in Florida.

name: Pink salmon
fact: Pink salmon are the smallest and most abundant Pacific salmon and live on a strict two-year cycle, so odd-year and even-year runs never mix.

name: Pink skunk clownfish
fact: The pink skunk clownfish is a pale pink anemonefish with a white stripe along its back, like a skunk, living in magnificent anemones.

name: Pink vent fish
fact: The pink vent fish is an eelpout found only at East Pacific vents, where it lies among the tube worms and eats limpets and amphipods.

name: Pink whipray
fact: The pink whipray is a large Indo-Pacific stingray that often rests in piles of several individuals on sandy lagoon floors.

name: Pipefish
fact: Pipefish are straightened-out relatives of seahorses, and the males carry the eggs on their belly or in a brood pouch until they hatch.

name: Pipi
fact: Pipi are wedge-shaped surf clams dug from sandy beaches in Australia and New Zealand, traditionally found by twisting your feet into the wet sand.

name: Piraíba
fact: The piraíba is the giant catfish of the Amazon, reaching about 3 metres and more than 150 kilograms, the largest catfish in the Americas.

name: Piranha
fact: Piranhas bark, drum and croak by vibrating their swim bladder, with different sounds for warning, confronting and snapping at rivals.

name: Pistol shrimp
fact: A pistol shrimp snaps its claw shut so fast it creates a collapsing bubble that briefly approaches the temperature of the Sun's surface and stuns prey.

name: Pitcairn Islands
fact: Pitcairn Island was settled in 1790 by the mutineers of HMS Bounty and remains one of the least populated territories on Earth.

name: Placoderm
fact: Placoderms, the first jawed fish, wore bony armour on their heads and vanished entirely about 360 million years ago.

name: Plaice
fact: Plaice are easy to recognise by the bright orange spots scattered across their brown upper side.

name: Plain bonito
fact: The plain bonito is an unstriped, deep-bodied bonito of the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean.

name: Plankton
fact: Plankton means 'wanderer' in Greek: it is every organism, from bacteria to jellyfish, that cannot swim against the current.

name: Platy
fact: The platy is a small Mexican livebearer bred into dozens of colour forms and recommended for every beginner's tank.

name: Platypus
fact: The platypus hunts with its eyes, ears and nostrils closed, finding prey entirely with about 40,000 electric sensors in its rubbery bill.

name: Pleco
fact: Plecos gulp air at the surface and absorb the oxygen through their stomach lining when the water runs low in oxygen.

name: Plesiosaur
fact: Plesiosaurs were long-necked marine reptiles that flew through the water on four flippers and vanished with the dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

name: Pliosaur
fact: Pliosaurs were short-necked, huge-headed marine reptiles whose bite was among the most powerful of any animal that ever lived.

name: Plumose anemone
fact: The plumose anemone is a tall white or orange anemone with a feathery crown of hundreds of fine tentacles, common on wrecks and pier legs.

name: Pocket shark
fact: Only two pocket sharks have ever been found, and the tiny shark's pocket glands near its front fins are thought to squirt glowing fluid.

name: Polar bear
fact: Polar bears are classed as marine mammals because they spend most of their lives on sea ice hunting seals, and they can swim for days.

name: Polarstern
fact: The German icebreaker Polarstern spent a year frozen into Arctic sea ice for the MOSAiC expedition of 2019 to 2020, the largest polar research expedition ever mounted.

name: Pollack
fact: The pollack is a golden-brown European cousin of cod with a jutting lower jaw, popular with sea anglers around rocky coasts and wrecks.

name: Pollock
fact: Pollock, a cod relative, produce thumping sounds with their swim bladder when handled or cornered, a trait shared with cod and haddock, which grunt during spawning.

name: Pom-pom crab
fact: The pom-pom crab holds a live sea anemone in each claw and waves them like boxing gloves; if it loses one it tears the other in half to grow a new pair.

name: Pompeii worm
fact: The Pompeii worm lives in tubes on vent chimneys with its tail in water of around 80 degrees Celsius, making it one of the most heat-tolerant animals known.

name: Ponta Delgada
fact: Ponta Delgada, the largest city of the Azores, sits on the island of São Miguel in the middle of the North Atlantic.

name: Pontoh's pygmy seahorse
fact: Pontoh's pygmy seahorse is a free-living pygmy seahorse of about 1.7 centimetres that clings to algae and hydroids rather than sea fans.

name: Ponyfish
fact: Ponyfish keep glowing bacteria in a ring-shaped organ around the throat and shine the light out through transparent windows in their bellies.

name: Poor cod
fact: The poor cod is a small, coppery cod relative of European coasts, too small to be worth eating but important food for larger fish.

name: Poor Knights Islands
fact: The Poor Knights Islands off New Zealand's North Island are a marine reserve that Jacques Cousteau rated among the best dive sites in the world.

name: Porbeagle
fact: The porbeagle, a cold-water cousin of the great white, keeps its muscles warm and ranges as far north as Iceland and Norway.

name: Porcelain crab
fact: Porcelain crabs are flat, fragile crab-like animals that filter plankton with feathery mouthparts and readily drop a leg to escape.

name: Porcupine Bank
fact: Porcupine Bank, west of Ireland, is a raised area of seabed named after HMS Porcupine, the survey ship that charted it in the 1860s.

name: Porcupine ray
fact: The porcupine ray has no stinging spine at all; instead its back is covered in sharp thorns.

name: Porcupinefish
fact: The porcupinefish inflates into a spiky ball when threatened, and its skin and organs carry tetrodotoxin, so it is poisonous to eat.

name: Porites
fact: Porites corals grow in massive domes so slowly and steadily that scientists drill cores from them to read centuries of ocean climate.

name: Porkfish
fact: The porkfish, a yellow-striped grunt with two black bars on its head, schools under Caribbean ledges by day and feeds at night.

name: Porpoise
fact: Porpoises are small toothed whales with spade-shaped teeth and blunt snouts, unlike the cone-shaped teeth and beaks of dolphins.

name: Port Jackson shark
fact: Port Jackson sharks lay spiral-shaped eggs that the mother wedges into rock crevices.

name: Porto
fact: Porto, at the mouth of the Douro river, gave its name both to Portugal and to port wine.

name: Portuguese dogfish
fact: The Portuguese dogfish has been caught at nearly 3,700 metres, deeper than any other shark known.

name: Portuguese man o' war
fact: The Portuguese man o' war is not a jellyfish but a colony of specialised animals under a gas-filled sail, trailing tentacles that can reach 30 metres.

name: Potato cod
fact: The potato cod is a grouper of the Indo-Pacific covered in large dark blotches like potatoes; the tame giants of the Cod Hole on the Great Barrier Reef are famous among divers.

name: Potter's angelfish
fact: Potter's angelfish is a dwarf angelfish found only in Hawaii, orange with blue-black scribbles.

name: Pouting
fact: The pouting, or bib, is a small, deep-bodied cod relative with coppery bands, common around piers and wrecks in European waters.

name: Powder blue tang
fact: The powder blue tang is a pale blue surgeonfish with a black face and yellow dorsal fin, found on Indian Ocean reefs, often in large grazing schools.

name: Prawn
fact: Prawn and shrimp are not scientific terms: Britain and Australia mostly say prawn and North America mostly says shrimp for the same animals.

name: Predatory tunicate
fact: The predatory tunicate is a sea squirt anchored in deep-sea canyons that holds its hood open like a Venus flytrap and snaps it shut on passing animals.

name: Priapulid worm
fact: Priapulid worms burrow in cold seafloor mud and look much as their relatives did in the Cambrian, more than 500 million years ago.

name: Prickly shark
fact: The prickly shark is a bulky Pacific relative of the bramble shark, covered in thorn-like scales, and lives on deep slopes.

name: Prince Albert I of Monaco
fact: Prince Albert I of Monaco spent his fortune on oceanographic cruises in the 1880s and 1890s and founded the Oceanographic Museum of Monaco.

name: Princess parrotfish
fact: The princess parrotfish is a Caribbean parrotfish whose males are blue-green with pink stripes, and it grazes in mixed schools over the reef.

name: Proboscis monkey
fact: The proboscis monkey lives only in Borneo's mangrove and riverside forests, swims well with partly webbed feet, and the male's huge nose amplifies its calls.

name: Prochlorococcus
fact: Prochlorococcus is the most abundant photosynthetic organism on Earth, yet this tiny ocean bacterium was not discovered until 1986.

name: Puerto Rico
fact: Puerto Rico lies at the eastern end of the Greater Antilles, and just north of it the Puerto Rico Trench drops to the deepest point in the Atlantic.

name: Puerto Rico Trench
fact: The Puerto Rico Trench is the deepest point in the Atlantic Ocean, reaching about 8,400 metres at the Milwaukee Deep.

name: Puffadder shyshark
fact: The puffadder shyshark of South African kelp forests curls into a ring and covers its eyes with its tail when threatened, hence the name shyshark.

name: Pufferfish
fact: Pufferfish carry tetrodotoxin, a poison with no antidote that is about 1,200 times deadlier than cyanide, yet fugu is a Japanese delicacy.

name: Puget Sound
fact: Puget Sound is a deep, glacier-carved inlet of the Pacific in Washington state, named by George Vancouver after his lieutenant Peter Puget, with Seattle on its shore.

name: Pumpkinseed
fact: The pumpkinseed sunfish is a brightly coloured pond fish of North America that has become invasive across Europe.

name: Purple sea urchin
fact: Purple sea urchins can bore shallow pits into solid rock and, left unchecked, can mow down whole kelp forests.

name: Purse seiner
fact: A purse seiner surrounds a school of fish with a long wall of net, then draws the bottom closed like a purse; most tuna and sardines are caught this way.

name: Puysegur Trench
fact: The Puysegur Trench off the south-west tip of New Zealand is where the Australian Plate begins to slide beneath the Pacific Plate.

name: Pygmy corydoras
fact: The pygmy corydoras is a 2.5-centimetre armoured catfish from Brazil that, unlike its relatives, swims in mid-water in shoals.

name: Pygmy killer whale
fact: The pygmy killer whale is a small, little-known dark dolphin of tropical seas that was known only from two skulls until the 1950s.

name: Pygmy right whale
fact: The pygmy right whale is the smallest and least-known baleen whale, rarely seen alive in the cool waters of the Southern Hemisphere.

name: Pygmy seahorse
fact: Pygmy seahorses are mostly under 2.5 centimetres long and so well camouflaged on sea fans and corals that the first was found only when its host fan was collected.

name: Pygmy sperm whale
fact: The pygmy sperm whale squirts a cloud of reddish-brown fluid to confuse predators, much as a squid uses ink.

name: Pygmy squid
fact: Pygmy squid are among the smallest cephalopods, about the size of a fingernail, and glue themselves to seagrass blades with a sticky patch on their back.

name: Pygmy sunfish
fact: Pygmy sunfishes of the southeastern United States are 2-to-3-centimetre swamp fish, not true sunfish, that flash iridescent blue when breeding.

name: Pyjama shark
fact: The pyjama shark, a striped catshark of South African kelp forests, starred in the film My Octopus Teacher and hunts at night.

name: Pyrosome
fact: A pyrosome is a hollow tube of thousands of cloned tunicates that glows blue-green, and some grow longer than a bus.

name: Quagga mussel
fact: The quagga mussel followed the zebra mussel into the Great Lakes and has largely replaced it, carpeting the lake beds in their trillions.

name: Quahog
fact: The quahog is the hard clam of New England chowder, and its cousin the ocean quahog, dredged off Iceland, lived to 507 years, the oldest animal ever aged.

name: Queen angelfish
fact: The queen angelfish of the Caribbean wears a blue 'crown' ringed with spots on its forehead and feeds mostly on sponges.

name: Queen Anne's Revenge
fact: Blackbeard's flagship Queen Anne's Revenge ran aground and was lost off Beaufort, North Carolina, in 1718; its wreck was found in 1996.

name: Queen parrotfish
fact: The queen parrotfish of the Caribbean sleeps at night inside a cocoon of mucus that it secretes, which may hide its scent from predators.

name: Queen triggerfish
fact: The queen triggerfish of the Caribbean and tropical Atlantic blows jets of water to flip sea urchins over and eat their soft undersides.

name: Rabbitfish
fact: Rabbitfish are harmless-looking reef grazers with venomous spines in their fins that cause an agonising sting if handled.

name: Raccoon butterflyfish
fact: The raccoon butterflyfish has a black mask across its eyes like a raccoon and feeds at night on coral polyps and small animals.

name: Rachel Carson
fact: Rachel Carson was a marine biologist whose book The Sea Around Us, published in 1951, introduced millions of readers to the science of the oceans.

name: Radiolarian
fact: Radiolarians are single-celled plankton with intricate glassy skeletons of silica, so beautiful that Ernst Haeckel drew hundreds of them in the 1800s.

name: Rainbow parrotfish
fact: The rainbow parrotfish is the largest parrotfish in the Atlantic, up to about 1.2 metres, with a coppery body and green fins, and its young grow up in mangroves.

name: Rainbow smelt
fact: Rainbow smelt live in coastal seas and run up rivers to spawn in early spring, and freshly caught smelt smell faintly of cucumber.

name: Rainbow trout
fact: Rainbow trout that migrate to sea are called steelhead; they return silver and powerful to spawn in their home rivers and can spawn more than once.

name: Rainbow Warrior
fact: The Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior was sunk by bombs planted by French agents in Auckland harbour in 1985.

name: Rainbowfish
fact: Rainbowfish from New Guinea and Australia shimmer with shifting colours and are among the most peaceful community aquarium fish.

name: Raja Ampat
fact: The reefs of Raja Ampat in Indonesia hold more coral and reef-fish species than almost anywhere else on Earth, at the heart of the Coral Triangle.

name: Ram cichlid
fact: The ram cichlid is a small, brilliantly coloured dwarf cichlid from Venezuelan and Colombian streams that pairs up to guard its eggs.

name: Ramari's beaked whale
fact: Ramari's beaked whale, described in 2021, is named after Māori whale expert Ramari Stewart, the first cetacean named after an indigenous woman.

name: Ram's horn squid
fact: The ram's horn squid carries a coiled, chambered shell inside its body, and the little white shells wash up on beaches worldwide.

name: Rangiroa
fact: Rangiroa in French Polynesia is one of the largest atolls in the world, with a lagoon so big that the whole island of Tahiti would fit inside it.

name: Ras Mohammed National Park
fact: Ras Mohammed, Egypt's first national park, sits at the tip of the Sinai where the Red Sea's Shark Reef and Yolanda Reef draw divers from around the world.

name: Razor clam
fact: Razor clams can dig down through wet sand faster than a person can dig, which is why collectors sprinkle salt to make them pop up.

name: Razor surgeonfish
fact: The razor surgeonfish grazes the rocky shores of the Galápagos in huge grey schools with bright yellow tails.

name: Razorbill
fact: The razorbill is the closest living relative of the extinct great auk and chases fish underwater using its wings.

name: Red bass
fact: The red bass is a big reef snapper that so often carries ciguatera poison that it is a no-take species in Queensland, banned from being kept or sold.

name: Red cod
fact: The red cod of New Zealand is a morid cod, a distant relative of the Atlantic cod, with a single chin barbel and pinkish skin.

name: Red coral
fact: Red coral from the Mediterranean has been harvested for jewellery for thousands of years and grows only a few millimetres a year.

name: Red drum
fact: The red drum, or redfish, is farmed in ponds and cages in Texas and China after blackened redfish made the wild fish a craze in the 1980s.

name: Red-eared slider
fact: The red-eared slider, the pet-shop turtle, has been dumped into ponds worldwide and is now one of the most widespread invasive reptiles.

name: Red grouper
fact: The red grouper of the Gulf of Mexico digs and maintains pits in the seabed that become homes for many other reef animals.

name: Red gurnard
fact: The red gurnard walks over the North Sea floor on finger-like fin rays and grunts audibly when caught.

name: Red hind
fact: The red hind is a small Caribbean grouper with red spots that gathers to spawn at traditional sites and is a staple catch in the Virgin Islands.

name: Red-lipped batfish
fact: The red-lipped batfish of the Galápagos is a poor swimmer and instead walks across the seabed on its stiff, limb-like fins.

name: Red mangrove
fact: The red mangrove stands on arching prop roots and drops long, pencil-shaped seedlings that float away to take root on other shores.

name: Red mullet
fact: Red mullet feel for prey with two chin barbels, and the ancient Romans paid fortunes for large ones and watched them change colour as they died.

name: Red rock crab
fact: The red rock crab of the Pacific Northwest has big black-tipped claws strong enough to crush barnacles and snails.

name: Red scorpionfish
fact: The red scorpionfish, the rascasse, has venomous spines and is the essential fish of a true Marseille bouillabaisse.

name: Red Sea bannerfish
fact: The Red Sea bannerfish trails a long white dorsal filament like a pennant and lives only in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

name: Red sea bream
fact: Red sea bream, tai, is Japan's celebration fish, served as sashimi at weddings and New Year because its name sounds like 'medetai', meaning happy.

name: Red sea urchin
fact: The red sea urchin of the Pacific coast can live for more than 100 years, and its roe is sold as uni in sushi restaurants.

name: Red snapper
fact: The northern red snapper of the Gulf of Mexico can live for over 50 years and is so popular that many cheaper fish are passed off as it in restaurants.

name: Red swamp crayfish
fact: The red swamp crayfish is the star of Louisiana crawfish boils and has spread as an invader to rivers and rice paddies across Europe, Africa and Asia.

name: Redtail catfish
fact: The redtail catfish of the Amazon has a bright orange-red tail and grows well over a metre, a giant that aquarists often regret buying.

name: Redtoothed triggerfish
fact: The redtoothed triggerfish is blue-black with red teeth and feeds on plankton in the water column above Indo-Pacific reefs.

name: Reef manta ray
fact: Reef mantas visit cleaning stations on coral reefs and can be told apart by the unique spot patterns on their bellies.

name: Reef shark
fact: Reef sharks are the sleek, mostly harmless sharks that patrol coral reefs, and their numbers are a good sign of a healthy reef.

name: Reef triggerfish
fact: The reef triggerfish is Hawaii's state fish, with the famous Hawaiian name humuhumunukunukuāpuaʻa, meaning roughly 'triggerfish with a snout like a pig'.

name: Regal angelfish
fact: The regal angelfish, striped in orange, white and blue, is a shy sponge-eater of Indo-Pacific reefs that is notoriously difficult to keep in aquariums.

name: Remora
fact: Remoras hitch rides on sharks, whales, turtles and even ships using a suction disc on top of the head, eating scraps and parasites.

name: Revillagigedo Archipelago
fact: The Revillagigedo Islands, often just called Socorro, are a Mexican national park where giant oceanic manta rays approach divers to be cleaned.

name: Rex sole
fact: The rex sole is a slender, thin-bodied flatfish of the North Pacific with a very small mouth, usually fried whole on the bone.

name: Reykjanes Ridge
fact: The Reykjanes Ridge is the stretch of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that runs south-west from Iceland, where the ridge actually rises above sea level.

name: Reykjavik
fact: Reykjavik, the world's northernmost national capital, grew up around its harbour and Iceland's fishing fleet.

name: Ribbon eel
fact: The ribbon eel lives in a burrow in sand or rubble and changes from black to blue to yellow as it turns from juvenile to male to female.

name: Ribbon Reefs
fact: The Ribbon Reefs are a chain of ten long, narrow reefs on the outer Great Barrier Reef, home to the famous Cod Hole dive site.

name: Ribbon seal
fact: Ribbon seals have striking white bands around the neck and flippers and spend most of the year in the open Bering Sea and Sea of Okhotsk.

name: Ribbon worm
fact: Ribbon worms fire a sticky proboscis to catch prey, and some species regrow a complete worm from a small fragment.

name: Rice's whale
fact: Rice's whale, named in 2021 after biologist Dale Rice, lives only in the Gulf of Mexico and numbers only around 50 animals.

name: Richelieu Rock
fact: Richelieu Rock, a horseshoe-shaped pinnacle in the Andaman Sea off Thailand, is prized for whale shark sightings and purple soft corals.

name: Ridgeia tube worm
fact: Ridgeia tube worms blanket the vents of the Juan de Fuca Ridge off Canada, growing tall and thin or short and fat depending on how hot their spot is.

name: Right whale
fact: Right whales got their name from whalers because they were the 'right' whale to hunt: slow, rich in oil, and floating when dead.

name: Ringed seal
fact: Ringed seals are the smallest and most common Arctic seal, keeping breathing holes open in the ice with their claws, and are the polar bear's main prey.

name: Rio de Janeiro
fact: Rio de Janeiro means 'River of January', the name given by Portuguese sailors who reached Guanabara Bay in January 1502.

name: Risso's dolphin
fact: Risso's dolphins are born dark grey and turn almost white with age as they accumulate scars from fights and squid.

name: River dolphin
fact: River dolphins have long slender beaks, tiny eyes and flexible necks suited to hunting in murky, cluttered water.

name: Roach
fact: The roach, with its red fins and silver body, is the fish most often caught by beginners in European rivers and canals.

name: Robben Island
fact: Robben Island in Table Bay off Cape Town is where Nelson Mandela was imprisoned for 18 of his 27 years in jail.

name: Robert Ballard
fact: Robert Ballard led the team that found the wreck of the Titanic in 1985 and also located the Bismarck and took part in the discovery of hydrothermal vents.

name: Rock beauty
fact: The rock beauty is a Caribbean angelfish, yellow at the front and black behind, that feeds mainly on sponges.

name: Rock cook
fact: The rock cook is a small wrasse of European waters that cleans parasites from other fish, and is used to de-louse farmed salmon.

name: Rockall
fact: Rockall is a lone granite rock about 20 metres high in the North Atlantic, west of Scotland, claimed by Britain and argued over for its fishing waters.

name: Rockall Bank
fact: Rockall Bank is a submerged plateau west of Scotland from which only the tiny granite islet of Rockall breaks the surface.

name: Rockfish
fact: Rockfishes of the North Pacific are among the longest-lived fish; several species live well past 100 years, and the rougheye may reach 200.

name: Rockhopper penguin
fact: Rockhopper penguins hop up cliffs with both feet together and feed on krill, squid and small fish.

name: Rohu
fact: Rohu is a carp of South Asian rivers, the most popular eating fish in Bangladesh and eastern India.

name: Roosterfish
fact: The roosterfish of the eastern Pacific raises a comb of seven long dorsal spines and is caught from the beaches of Baja and Costa Rica.

name: Ropefish
fact: The ropefish has lungs as well as gills and can survive for a while out of water, slithering along like a snake.

name: Roseate spoonbill
fact: The roseate spoonbill sweeps its flat bill from side to side through estuary shallows, snapping it shut on shrimps and small fish.

name: Ross Sea
fact: The Ross Sea is a deep bay of Antarctica named after James Clark Ross, who discovered it in 1841, and it is fringed by the Ross Ice Shelf, the largest in the world.

name: Ross Sea Marine Protected Area
fact: The Ross Sea Marine Protected Area in Antarctica, agreed in 2016, is among the largest protected areas on the planet and shelters Adélie penguins and toothfish.

name: Ross seal
fact: The Ross seal is the least-known Antarctic seal, living deep in the pack ice and making eerie siren-like calls.

name: Rough-toothed dolphin
fact: The rough-toothed dolphin has a sloping, reptile-like head with no crease between beak and forehead, and finely ridged teeth.

name: Rougheye rockfish
fact: The rougheye rockfish is one of the longest-lived fish known, with individuals aged at more than 200 years from the growth rings in their ear bones.

name: Roughtail stingray
fact: The roughtail stingray is one of the largest whiptail stingrays in the Atlantic, over 2 metres across, with rows of thorns on its tail.

name: Round goby
fact: The round goby from the Black and Caspian seas arrived in the Great Lakes in ballast water in 1990 and now numbers in the billions there and in the Baltic.

name: Round herring
fact: Round herrings are slim schooling fish of warm seas including the Gulf of Mexico, caught as bait and for fishmeal.

name: Round sardinella
fact: The round sardinella is a small schooling fish caught in huge numbers off West Africa, where it is a staple protein.

name: Round stingray
fact: Round stingrays cause most of the stingray injuries on southern California beaches, which is why bathers do the 'stingray shuffle'.

name: Roundnose grenadier
fact: The roundnose grenadier is a deep-sea cod relative trawled at over 1,000 metres in the North Atlantic that can live for more than 50 years.

name: Rowley Shoals
fact: The Rowley Shoals are three atolls off north-west Australia that rise steeply from deep water and are famous for strong tidal currents and clear water.

name: Royal gramma
fact: The royal gramma, or fairy basslet, is a purple-and-yellow Caribbean reef fish that often swims upside down beneath ledges.

name: RRS Discovery
fact: The Discovery was built for Scott's first Antarctic expedition in 1901, and three later British research ships of the same name have continued its work.

name: RRS Sir David Attenborough
fact: The polar research ship RRS Sir David Attenborough got its name after a 2016 public vote overwhelmingly chose Boaty McBoatface, a name given to one of its robot submarines instead.

name: Ruby sea dragon
fact: The ruby sea dragon, deep red and living below the reach of most divers off Western Australia, was named as a new species only in 2015 and first filmed alive in 2016.

name: Rudist
fact: Rudists were strange cone-shaped clams that built reefs in Cretaceous seas and died out along with the dinosaurs.

name: Ryukyu Trench
fact: The Ryukyu Trench runs along the Ryukyu Islands between Japan and Taiwan and reaches about 7,500 metres deep.

name: Sabertooth fish
fact: Sabertooth fish are small deep-sea hunters with upward-looking eyes and fangs that stick out past the jaw.

name: Sable Island
fact: Sable Island is a crescent of sand off Nova Scotia known as the Graveyard of the Atlantic for its hundreds of shipwrecks, and home to wild horses.

name: Sablefish
fact: Sablefish, sold as black cod, is a buttery deep-water fish of the North Pacific, famous miso-marinated, and it can live for more than 90 years.

name: Saddleback clownfish
fact: The saddleback clownfish has a white saddle on its back rather than a full bar, and lives in anemones on open sand rather than on the reef.

name: Saddled toby
fact: The saddled toby is so poisonous that the harmless mimic filefish has evolved to copy its black saddles and colours almost exactly.

name: Sailboat
fact: Sailboats are driven by the wind alone, and the oldest known picture of a sail, on an Egyptian pot, is more than 5,000 years old.

name: Sailfin tang
fact: The sailfin tang raises enormous dorsal and anal fins to look twice its size, and is banded brown and yellow.

name: Sailfish
fact: The sailfish is widely held to be the fastest fish in the sea, raising its huge dorsal sail when it herds sardines into tight balls.

name: Saithe
fact: Saithe, or coley, is a dark-fleshed cousin of cod caught in huge numbers in the North Atlantic; cheaper than cod, it is often used in fish pies.

name: Sakhalin taimen
fact: The Sakhalin taimen of Japan and the Russian Far East is a critically endangered giant that migrates between rivers and the sea.

name: Salema
fact: The salema, a striped Mediterranean bream, can cause vivid hallucinations lasting days when eaten, earning it the nickname 'the dreamfish'.

name: Salish Sea
fact: The Salish Sea, which includes Puget Sound and the Strait of Georgia, was only officially named in 2009, after the Coast Salish peoples.

name: Sally Lightfoot crab
fact: Sally Lightfoot crabs skitter over Galápagos lava rocks in bright red and blue, and pick ticks off basking marine iguanas.

name: Salmon
fact: Pacific salmon at sea feed heavily on krill, and the pigment from those crustaceans is what turns their flesh pink.

name: Salmon shark
fact: The salmon shark can hold its body temperature well above that of the cold North Pacific, letting it chase salmon in near-freezing seas.

name: Salp
fact: Salps are barrel-shaped, transparent relatives of vertebrates that pump water through their bodies, and can link into chains many metres long.

name: Saltwater crocodile
fact: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile, over 6 metres long, and swims between islands across hundreds of kilometres of open sea.

name: Salvador
fact: Salvador, Brazil's first capital, sits on the Bay of All Saints, one of the largest bays on the Atlantic coast of South America.

name: Samoa
fact: The Samoan Islands in the central Pacific are divided between the independent nation of Samoa and the US territory of American Samoa.

name: Sampan
fact: The sampan is a flat-bottomed wooden boat of China and Southeast Asia, used for fishing and as a floating home in harbours and rivers.

name: San Cristobal Trench
fact: The San Cristobal Trench runs south of the Solomon Islands and is part of the chain of trenches along the Pacific's Ring of Fire.

name: San Francisco Bay
fact: San Francisco Bay is the largest estuary on the Pacific coast of the Americas, entered through the Golden Gate strait.

name: San José
fact: The Spanish galleon San José, sunk by the British off Cartagena in 1708 with a cargo of gold, silver and emeralds, was located in 2015 about 600 metres down.

name: San Juan
fact: San Juan, Puerto Rico, is guarded by El Morro, a Spanish fortress begun in 1539 to protect the harbour entrance.

name: Sand bubbler crab
fact: Sand bubbler crabs sift sand for food and leave thousands of tiny sand balls radiating from their burrows on tropical beaches at low tide.

name: Sand dollar
fact: Sand dollars are flattened sea urchins, and the bleached white 'shell' found on beaches is the animal's skeleton, or test.

name: Sand eel
fact: Sand eels are slim silvery fish that dive headfirst into sand to hide, and puffins and kittiwakes depend on them to feed their chicks.

name: Sand hopper
fact: Sand hoppers are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that live in and feed on rotting seaweed washed up along the strandline.

name: Sand tiger shark
fact: Sand tiger embryos eat their siblings in the womb, so only one pup from each uterus survives to birth.

name: Sandbar shark
fact: Sandbar sharks have an unusually tall dorsal fin and were once the mainstay of the shark fishery on the US east coast.

name: Sanddab
fact: Pacific sanddabs are small left-eyed flounders of the US west coast, pan-fried whole and a speciality of Monterey and San Francisco restaurants.

name: Sanganeb Atoll
fact: Sanganeb is the only atoll in the Red Sea, rising off the coast of Sudan and protected as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Santos
fact: Santos, near São Paulo, is the busiest port in Latin America and the main gateway for Brazil's coffee exports.

name: São Tomé and Príncipe
fact: São Tomé and Príncipe are two volcanic islands in the Gulf of Guinea that make up Africa's second-smallest country.

name: Sarcastic fringehead
fact: The sarcastic fringehead of the Californian coast defends its burrow by gaping an enormous fluorescent mouth at rivals.

name: Sardine
fact: Sardines filter copepods and krill from the water, and their immense schools off South Africa form the annual sardine run.

name: Sardinella
fact: Sardinellas are small sardine-like fish that support huge fisheries off West Africa, where they are smoked and dried for food.

name: Sargasso Sea
fact: The Sargasso Sea is the only sea with no coastline, bounded instead by Atlantic currents, and both European and American eels spawn there.

name: Sargassum
fact: Sargassum is a floating brown seaweed held up by gas-filled bladders; huge rafts of it give the Sargasso Sea its name and shelter young sea turtles.

name: Saronic Gulf
fact: The Saronic Gulf is the bay of the Aegean on which Athens and its port Piraeus stand, where the Greeks crushed the Persian fleet at Salamis in 480 BC.

name: Satomi's pygmy seahorse
fact: Satomi's pygmy seahorse, from Indonesia, is about 1.4 centimetres long and is the smallest known seahorse.

name: Sawfish
fact: A sawfish's toothed snout is lined with sensors that detect prey, and it slashes sideways to stun fish.

name: Sawshark
fact: Sawsharks carry a long flat saw-like snout with a pair of trailing barbels, and unlike sawfish they have gills on the sides of the head.

name: Sawtooth eel
fact: Sawtooth eels are small deep-sea eels with saw-like rows of teeth, drifting in the midwater of all the oceans.

name: Scaldfish
fact: The scaldfish is a small, translucent flatfish of European seas whose loose scales come off so easily that it looks scalded when caught.

name: Scallop
fact: Scallops have dozens of tiny blue eyes along the edge of their shells and can swim by clapping their shells together.

name: Scalloped hammerhead
fact: Scalloped hammerheads gather in schools of hundreds around seamounts such as Cocos Island and the Galápagos.

name: Scaly-foot snail
fact: The scaly-foot snail armours its foot with plates of iron sulphide and is the first species declared endangered because of deep-sea mining.

name: Scapa Flow
fact: Scapa Flow in Orkney is where the interned German High Seas Fleet was scuttled in 1919, leaving battleships and cruisers that divers still explore.

name: Scarlet badis
fact: The scarlet badis is a 2-centimetre fish from India with scarlet and blue bars, one of the smallest perch-like fish.

name: Scarlet ibis
fact: The scarlet ibis gets its brilliant red colour from pigments in the crabs and shrimps it probes out of mangrove mud.

name: Schoolmaster snapper
fact: The schoolmaster is a yellow-finned Caribbean snapper that gathers in daytime schools beneath elkhorn coral and mangroves.

name: Schooner
fact: A schooner is a sailing ship with two or more masts whose main sails run fore-and-aft, a rig that made it a favourite of fishermen and smugglers.

name: Scorpionfish
fact: Scorpionfish are camouflaged ambush hunters with venomous fin spines, and the family includes the lionfish and the stonefish.

name: Scott Reef
fact: Scott Reef is a remote atoll system off north-west Australia that recovered remarkably after being devastated by coral bleaching in 1998.

name: Scrawled filefish
fact: The scrawled filefish has blue scribbles over an olive body that it can lighten, darken or mottle to match its surroundings.

name: Sculpin
fact: Sculpins are spiny bottom fish of cold waters, and several species grunt and hum during territorial disputes and courtship.

name: Sea anemone
fact: Sea anemones look like flowers but are predators armed with stinging tentacles, found from rock pools to the floors of ocean trenches.

name: Sea angel
fact: The sea angel is a tiny swimming sea slug of Arctic waters that flaps two wing-like lobes and preys only on sea butterflies.

name: Sea apple
fact: The sea apple is a brightly coloured sea cucumber that feeds with a crown of tentacles and can release a toxin that kills everything in an aquarium.

name: Sea bass
fact: The European sea bass, sold as branzino, is a prized angling fish of the North Sea and Atlantic coasts and is widely farmed in the Mediterranean.

name: Sea biscuit
fact: A sea biscuit is a thick, domed relative of the sand dollar that burrows through sand on tropical sea floors.

name: Sea bream
fact: The gilthead sea bream, named for the gold bar between its eyes, is one of the most farmed fish in the Mediterranean.

name: Sea butterfly
fact: Sea butterflies are tiny swimming snails that flap wing-like flaps, and their thin shells are threatened by ocean acidification.

name: Sea chub
fact: Sea chubs, or rudderfish, are unusual among reef fish in eating mostly brown seaweeds such as sargassum, and they often follow boats.

name: Sea cow
fact: Sea cows, the manatees and dugong, are the only plant-eating marine mammals and are related to elephants rather than seals.

name: Sea cucumber
fact: Sea cucumbers breathe through their bottoms and can eject their sticky internal organs at attackers, growing them back within weeks.

name: Sea daisy
fact: Sea daisies are tiny disc-shaped echinoderms found on sunken wood in the deep sea and were only discovered in 1986.

name: Sea dragon
fact: Sea dragons are seahorse relatives found only in the coastal waters of southern Australia, where they drift among kelp and seagrass.

name: Sea fan
fact: A sea fan is a soft coral whose colony grows into a flat, lacy fan held side-on to the current to catch drifting plankton.

name: Sea firefly
fact: The sea firefly is a 3-millimetre ostracod that squirts glowing blue mucus; dried ones were used by Japanese soldiers as a dim reading light.

name: Sea gooseberry
fact: The sea gooseberry is a glassy, marble-sized comb jelly that trails two long sticky tentacles to snare copepods.

name: Sea grapes
fact: Sea grapes are a green seaweed with tiny bubble-like beads that pop in the mouth, eaten fresh in Okinawa and the Philippines.

name: Sea hare
fact: The sea hare is a large sea slug that squirts a cloud of purple ink when it is disturbed.

name: Sea krait
fact: Sea kraits are the only sea snakes that come ashore to lay eggs, and they have highly potent venom but rarely bite people.

name: Sea lamprey
fact: The sea lamprey grows up at sea clamped onto fish, rasping through their skin to feed on blood, then swims up rivers to spawn and die.

name: Sea lemon
fact: The sea lemon is a yellow, warty nudibranch of Atlantic and Pacific shores that eats sponges, and the Pacific species gives off a fruity, citrus-like smell.

name: Sea lettuce
fact: Sea lettuce is a bright green seaweed with fronds only two cells thick, which can bloom into 'green tides' where sewage or farm runoff enriches the water.

name: Sea lily
fact: Sea lilies are animals, not plants: feathery filter feeders on a stalk that were common 300 million years ago and today live densely on rocks more than 9,000 metres down in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench.

name: Sea lion
fact: Sea lions differ from true seals in having small external ear flaps and in walking on all four flippers on land.

name: Sea louse
fact: Sea lice are tiny copepods that attach to salmon and feed on their skin and blood, and they are a major problem on salmon farms.

name: Sea mink
fact: The sea mink, a large coastal mink of New England and Atlantic Canada, was trapped to extinction for its fur by about 1900.

name: Sea moth
fact: Sea moths are small armoured fish of Indo-Pacific sand flats that walk on their pelvic fins and spread wing-like pectoral fins.

name: Sea mouse
fact: The sea mouse is a furry-looking marine worm whose iridescent bristles were among the first natural structures found to work like optical fibres.

name: Sea nettle
fact: Sea nettles are golden-brown jellyfish with long frilly oral arms whose sting feels like brushing a stinging nettle, hence the name.

name: Sea of Azov
fact: The Sea of Azov, linked to the Black Sea by the Kerch Strait, is the shallowest sea in the world, averaging only about 7 metres deep.

name: Sea of Crete
fact: The Sea of Crete is the southern part of the Aegean between Crete and the Cyclades, and is deeper than most of the Aegean.

name: Sea of Japan
fact: The Sea of Japan, called the East Sea in Korea, is a marginal sea of the Pacific nearly enclosed by Japan, Korea and Russia.

name: Sea of Marmara
fact: The Sea of Marmara is a small inland sea entirely within Turkey, linking the Black Sea to the Aegean through the Bosporus and Dardanelles.

name: Sea of Okhotsk
fact: The Sea of Okhotsk, off Russia's far east, is the coldest sea in East Asia and is covered by drifting ice for much of the winter.

name: Sea of Sardinia
fact: The Sea of Sardinia is the stretch of the western Mediterranean between Sardinia and the Balearic Islands.

name: Sea otter
fact: Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal and use rocks as tools to crack open shellfish.

name: Sea palm
fact: The sea palm looks like a tiny palm tree and lives only on the most wave-battered rocks of the Pacific coast of North America.

name: Sea pansy
fact: The sea pansy is a flat, purple soft coral colony on sand that glows green when touched, thanks to a protein now used in laboratories.

name: Sea pen
fact: A sea pen is a colony of polyps shaped like an old quill pen, rooted in soft mud, and many species glow green when touched.

name: Sea pig
fact: Sea pigs are pink, pudgy sea cucumbers that walk on tube feet across abyssal plains, often in herds all facing the current, 1,000 to 6,000 metres down.

name: Sea raven
fact: The sea raven is a lumpy, ragged-finned sculpin of the North American Atlantic coast that puffs itself up with water when caught.

name: Sea robin
fact: Sea robins 'walk' on finger-like fin rays and grunt or croak by vibrating their swim bladder, a sound anglers hear when they lift them from the water.

name: Sea sapphire
fact: The sea sapphire is a copepod whose males flash brilliant blue, then turn transparent and vanish as they tilt, thanks to crystal plates in their skin.

name: Sea scorpion
fact: Sea scorpions, or eurypterids, were armoured arthropods that died out about 250 million years ago, and the largest reached about 2.5 metres.

name: Sea slater
fact: The sea slater is a large woodlouse of the splash zone that hides in crevices by day and scavenges over the rocks at night.

name: Sea snail
fact: Sea snails build their spiral shells from calcium carbonate drawn from seawater, adding to the opening as they grow.

name: Sea snake
fact: Sea snakes are venomous relatives of cobras with paddle-shaped tails, and most give birth to live young at sea.

name: Sea spider
fact: Sea spiders are not true spiders but leggy marine arthropods, and in Antarctic waters they grow as wide as a dinner plate.

name: Sea squirt
fact: A sea squirt starts life as a swimming tadpole-like larva, then glues itself to a rock and spends the rest of its life pumping water through its body to filter food.

name: Sea star
fact: Sea stars have no brain or blood, pumping seawater through their bodies to move hundreds of tiny tube feet.

name: Sea toad
fact: Sea toads, or coffinfish, are deep-sea anglerfish that can inflate their bodies with water and hold their breath for minutes to save energy.

name: Sea trout
fact: The sea trout is a brown trout that goes to sea to feed, and anglers fish for it at night in rivers draining into the North and Baltic seas.

name: Sea turtle
fact: Sea turtles cannot pull their heads into their shells, and females return to the beach where they hatched to lay their own eggs.

name: Sea urchin
fact: A sea urchin's spines sit on a rigid shell called a test, which is made of plates of calcium carbonate.

name: Sea walnut
fact: The sea walnut, a comb jelly from the American Atlantic, invaded the Black Sea in ballast water and helped collapse its anchovy fishery in the 1980s.

name: Sea wasp
fact: The sea wasp, a box jellyfish of northern Australia, carries enough venom in its tentacles to kill a person within minutes.

name: Sea whip
fact: A sea whip is a soft coral that grows as a single long, flexible rod, often brightly coloured, swaying in the current.

name: Seagrass
fact: Seagrasses are true flowering plants, not seaweeds, with roots and underwater flowers, and their meadows store carbon far faster than forests on land.

name: Seahorse
fact: Seahorses are reef fish that swim upright, grip coral with their tails, and leave the males to carry the eggs in a pouch.

name: Seal
fact: Seals are marine mammals with streamlined bodies and flippers, and true seals have no external ear flaps.

name: Seamoth
fact: Seamoths are small armoured fish with wing-like fins and a long flat snout, and they walk across the sand on their pelvic fins.

name: Sebae clownfish
fact: The sebae clownfish is a dark anemonefish with a yellow tail and two white bars from the northern Indian Ocean; many fish sold under its name are actually Clark's.

name: Sei whale
fact: The sei whale is one of the fastest great whales and was hunted hard in the 1960s once fin whale numbers had collapsed.

name: Senegal bichir
fact: The Senegal bichir has paired lungs and is sometimes sold in aquariums as the dinosaur eel for its ancient look.

name: Señorita
fact: The señorita is a slim, cigar-shaped wrasse of California's kelp forests that cleans parasites off other fish and sleeps buried in sand.

name: Sergeant major
fact: The sergeant major is a striped damselfish found on reefs around the world, named for the stripes on a sergeant's sleeve; it swarms around divers for crumbs.

name: Serrated wrack
fact: Serrated wrack is the toothed-edged brown seaweed of the lower shore, with no air bladders, sheltering many small animals beneath it.

name: Seto Inland Sea
fact: The Seto Inland Sea separates three of Japan's main islands, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, and is dotted with about 3,000 islands.

name: Sevan trout
fact: The Sevan trout is found naturally only in Lake Sevan in Armenia and is endangered after the lake was lowered for irrigation and power.

name: Seven-arm octopus
fact: The seven-arm octopus is one of the largest octopuses, with a 4-metre specimen known, and has been photographed holding and eating jellyfish.

name: Seven-figure pygmy goby
fact: The seven-figure pygmy goby, a 2-centimetre reef fish, has the shortest lifespan of any vertebrate, living for about two months.

name: Sewol
fact: The South Korean ferry Sewol capsized and sank in April 2014 with the loss of more than 300 people, most of them schoolchildren.

name: Sexy shrimp
fact: The sexy shrimp got its name from the way it constantly sways its tail up and down while sitting on a sea anemone.

name: Shark
fact: Every shark has ampullae of Lorenzini, jelly-filled pores on its snout that detect the faint electric fields of a hidden animal's muscles and heartbeat.

name: Sharpnose puffer
fact: The sharpnose puffer is a thumb-sized Caribbean puffer with a pointed snout and bright blue lines around its eyes.

name: Sharpnose sevengill shark
fact: The sharpnose sevengill is a slender deep-water shark with seven gill slits and large green eyes.

name: Shearwater
fact: Shearwaters skim the waves on stiff wings and dive after fish and squid, some chasing them tens of metres down.

name: Sheepshead
fact: The sheepshead of the Gulf of Mexico has eerily human-looking teeth for crunching barnacles and crabs off pilings.

name: Shepherd's beaked whale
fact: Shepherd's beaked whale is the only beaked whale with a full set of functional teeth in both jaws.

name: Shetland
fact: Shetland is the northernmost part of the British Isles, closer to Norway than to Edinburgh, with a long Norse history.

name: Shinkai 6500
fact: Japan's Shinkai 6500 can dive to 6,500 metres and was for many years the deepest-diving crewed research submersible in service.

name: Shonisaurus
fact: Shonisaurus was a Triassic ichthyosaur the size of a bus, and dozens of its skeletons lie together at Berlin-Ichthyosaur State Park in Nevada.

name: Shore crab
fact: The shore crab, the common rock-pool crab of Europe, has spread around the world in ships' ballast water and is one of the most invasive marine species.

name: Shore rockling
fact: The shore rockling is a small, eel-like cod relative with three barbels, found under stones in rock pools around Britain.

name: Short-finned eel
fact: The short-finned eel of Australia and New Zealand migrates thousands of kilometres to spawn in the Coral Sea.

name: Short-finned pilot whale
fact: Short-finned pilot whales sprint after squid in the deep, earning the nickname 'cheetahs of the deep', and females live decades past menopause.

name: Short-nosed sea snake
fact: The short-nosed sea snake was feared extinct for 15 years until a pair was photographed courting on Ningaloo Reef in 2015.

name: Short-snouted seahorse
fact: The short-snouted seahorse is one of two seahorse species native to British waters and has even been found in the Thames estuary.

name: Short-tail stingray
fact: The short-tail stingray is among the largest stingrays, reaching over 2 metres across and about 350 kilograms.

name: Short-tailed shearwater
fact: Short-tailed shearwaters, Australia's muttonbirds, loop around the Pacific to Alaska and back each year, a journey of roughly 30,000 kilometres.

name: Shortbill spearfish
fact: The shortbill spearfish is a slim, fast billfish of the Pacific with a bill barely longer than its lower jaw.

name: Shovelnose guitarfish
fact: The shovelnose guitarfish is a ray with a pointed shovel-shaped snout and a shark-like tail, lying on sandy bottoms off California and Mexico.

name: Shrimp
fact: Shrimps and prawns wear a thin, flexible shell that they shed many times as they grow.

name: Shrimp goby
fact: Shrimp gobies stand guard at the mouth of a burrow dug by a pistol shrimp, warning the shrimp with a flick of the tail when danger approaches.

name: Shrimpfish
fact: Shrimpfish, or razorfish, are thin armoured relatives of seahorses that swim head-down in synchronised groups, often hiding among sea urchin spines.

name: Siamese algae eater
fact: The Siamese algae eater is valued by aquarists because it is one of the few fish that eats stringy black beard algae.

name: Sicklefin lemon shark
fact: The sicklefin lemon shark is the Indo-Pacific cousin of the lemon shark and is a favourite of shark-feeding dives in French Polynesia.

name: Signal crayfish
fact: The signal crayfish, named for the white patch at its claw joints, was introduced from North America and now dominates rivers across Europe.

name: Silfra
fact: Silfra in Iceland is a flooded crack between the North American and Eurasian plates, with glacial water so clear that visibility exceeds 100 metres.

name: Silky shark
fact: Silky sharks get their name from the smooth feel of their skin and are among the most heavily fished sharks in the world.

name: Silver carp
fact: The silver carp is among the most farmed fish in the world in China, yet in American rivers it is an invader notorious for leaping out of the water at boats.

name: Silver-cheeked toadfish
fact: The silver-cheeked toadfish, a highly toxic puffer, spread from the Red Sea through the Suez Canal and now plagues fisheries across the Mediterranean.

name: Silver dollar
fact: The silver dollar is a flat, coin-shaped Amazon fish kept in aquariums, a plant-eating cousin of the piranha.

name: Silver hake
fact: The silver hake is the main hake of the US east coast, a fast-swimming predator of small fish that is sold there under the name whiting.

name: Silver perch
fact: The silver perch is a small drum of US Atlantic estuaries that joins loud evening drumming choruses in summer, picked up by hydrophones in Chesapeake Bay.

name: Silvertip shark
fact: Silvertip sharks, with white edges on every fin, patrol the drop-offs of Indo-Pacific reefs and are bold around divers.

name: Sipadan
fact: Sipadan, off Malaysian Borneo, is an oceanic island rising 600 metres from the seabed, famed for green turtles and swirling barracuda tornadoes.

name: Siphonophore
fact: A siphonophore is a chain of specialised clones acting as one animal; one filmed off Western Australia in 2020 was estimated at about 45 metres long.

name: Six-line wrasse
fact: The six-line wrasse is a tiny purple-and-orange striped wrasse from Indo-Pacific reefs that hunts pests such as flatworms in aquariums.

name: Sixgill shark
fact: The bluntnose sixgill shark has six gill slits instead of five, grows to about 5 metres and spends the day down to about 2,500 metres.

name: Sixgill stingray
fact: The sixgill stingray lives in deep water and is the only stingray with six pairs of gill slits instead of five.

name: Skagerrak
fact: The Skagerrak is the strait between Norway, Denmark and Sweden that links the North Sea to the Baltic, and it was the scene of the Battle of Jutland in 1916.

name: Skate
fact: Skates lay their eggs in leathery cases called mermaid's purses that often wash up on beaches.

name: Skellig Michael
fact: Skellig Michael is a jagged rock off Ireland with a sixth-century monastery on its summit, later used as Luke Skywalker's hideout in Star Wars.

name: Skipjack tuna
fact: Skipjack is the most-caught tuna in the world and the one in most tins; in Japan it is katsuo, dried into bonito flakes and seared as tataki.

name: Slate pencil urchin
fact: The slate pencil urchin's thick, blunt reddish spines look like old-fashioned slate pencils and have been used to make wind chimes and jewellery.

name: Sleeper shark
fact: Sleeper sharks are sluggish cold-water sharks of the deep, and the flesh of some species is toxic until it is fermented or dried.

name: Slender giant moray
fact: The slender giant moray is the longest eel in the world, reaching about 4 metres, and lives in muddy estuaries of the Indo-Pacific.

name: Slender seahorse
fact: The slender seahorse of the Caribbean and Brazil is a popular aquarium species that comes in yellow, orange, red and black.

name: Slender tuna
fact: The slender tuna is a Southern Ocean member of the tuna family that feeds on krill and is rarely seen by anyone but longline crews.

name: Slingjaw wrasse
fact: The slingjaw wrasse can shoot its jaws forward to half its body length to snatch prey, the most extreme jaw protrusion of any fish.

name: Slipper limpet
fact: Slipper limpets live in stacks, with the males on top turning female as they age, and they have become invasive on European coasts.

name: Slipper lobster
fact: Slipper lobsters have flat, plate-like antennae instead of long feelers and are sold in Australia as Moreton Bay bugs and Balmain bugs.

name: Slippery dick
fact: The slippery dick is a common Caribbean wrasse named for its slimy, hard-to-hold body; it changes from a striped female to a greener male.

name: Slit shell snail
fact: Slit shell snails of deep tropical slopes belong to a family with a fossil record back to the Cambrian, around 500 million years ago, and their shells are prized by collectors.

name: Sloop
fact: A sloop is a sailing boat with a single mast and one headsail, the most common rig on modern yachts.

name: Small-spotted catshark
fact: The small-spotted catshark lays its eggs in curly-tendrilled cases known as mermaid's purses and is one of the commonest sharks around Britain.

name: Smallmouth bass
fact: The smallmouth bass prefers cooler, rockier rivers and lakes than its largemouth cousin and fights hard for its size.

name: Smalltooth sand tiger
fact: The smalltooth sand tiger is a bulky deep-water shark that lives down to around 900 metres and is rarely seen alive.

name: Smalltooth sawfish
fact: The smalltooth sawfish was once found from New York to Brazil but now survives mainly in south-west Florida, where it is protected.

name: Smooth hammerhead
fact: The smooth hammerhead has no notch in the middle of its head and ranges further into cool water than other hammerheads.

name: Smooth handfish
fact: The smooth handfish of Tasmania, known from one specimen collected in 1802, was declared extinct in 2020, the first modern marine fish so listed, though the IUCN later reset it to data deficient.

name: Smooth-hound
fact: Smooth-hounds are small, harmless sharks with flat crushing teeth for eating crabs, and anglers catch them along European shores.

name: Smooth trunkfish
fact: The smooth trunkfish of the Caribbean blows jets of water into the sand to uncover the worms and crustaceans it eats.

name: Snailfish
fact: Snailfish are the deepest-living fish known: one was filmed at 8,336 metres in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench in 2022.

name: Snake eel
fact: Snake eels have a hard, pointed tail that they use to burrow backwards into sand, leaving only the head poking out.

name: Snake pipefish
fact: The snake pipefish of the north-east Atlantic has almost no tail fin, and its numbers exploded across the North Sea in the mid-2000s.

name: Snakehead
fact: Snakeheads breathe air with a chamber above their gills and can wriggle short distances over land between ponds.

name: Snakelocks anemone
fact: The snakelocks anemone cannot fully pull in its long green tentacles, which get their colour from algae living inside them and their purple tips from a pigment.

name: Snapper
fact: Snappers are schooling reef predators prized as food fish, and the red snapper can live for more than 50 years.

name: Snipe eel
fact: The snipe eel has a body like a ribbon and thin, outward-curving jaws like a bird's beak that cannot close, which it uses to snag shrimp by their antennae.

name: Snipefish
fact: The snipefish is a small deep-water relative of seahorses with a long tube snout, named after the wading bird with a long bill.

name: Snook
fact: The common snook lives in the mangrove estuaries of Florida and the Gulf of Mexico and changes from male to female as it grows.

name: Snow crab
fact: Snow crabs live on cold northern seabeds, and billions vanished from the Bering Sea after a marine heatwave, closing the fishery in 2022.

name: Snow petrel
fact: The snow petrel is pure white, breeds farther south than almost any other bird, and has been seen at the South Pole itself.

name: Snowflake moray
fact: The snowflake moray has blunt, pebble-like teeth for crushing crabs and shrimp, and is a popular aquarium moray.

name: Snowy grouper
fact: The snowy grouper lives on deep rocky bottoms of the western Atlantic; its juveniles are dotted with white spots like snow.

name: Sockeye salmon
fact: Sockeye salmon turn brilliant red with green heads when they return from the sea to spawn, and landlocked populations are known as kokanee.

name: Soft coral
fact: Soft corals have no hard skeleton and sway in the current, supported by tiny limestone needles in their flesh.

name: Soft-shell clam
fact: Soft-shell clams, the 'steamers' of New England clam shacks, have a long neck that squirts water when you walk over the mud flat.

name: Sohal surgeonfish
fact: The sohal tang of the Red Sea is a striped surgeonfish with bright orange tail blades that it uses fiercely to defend its territory against divers and other fish.

name: Soldierfish
fact: Soldierfish are red night-active reef fish that grunt, growl and click with swim-bladder muscles to defend their caves.

name: Sole
fact: Soles are oval, right-eyed flatfish named after the Latin word for a sandal, which the Romans thought they resembled.

name: Solenette
fact: The solenette is a tiny sole, rarely more than 12 centimetres long, that lies on sandy seabeds around Britain and is thrown back by trawlers.

name: Solomon Islands
fact: The Solomon Islands in the south-west Pacific include Guadalcanal, where a brutal six-month battle was fought in 1942 and 1943.

name: Solomon Sea
fact: The Solomon Sea lies between the Solomon Islands and Papua New Guinea and was the scene of fierce naval battles in the Second World War.

name: Somali Current
fact: The Somali Current off the Horn of Africa is one of the few currents that reverses direction, flowing north in the summer monsoon and south in winter.

name: Sooty shearwater
fact: Sooty shearwaters fly a figure-of-eight loop around the entire Pacific each year, a round trip of about 64,000 kilometres.

name: South American lungfish
fact: The South American lungfish breathes mostly with its two lungs and digs a burrow in the mud when its swamp dries out.

name: South American sea lion
fact: South American sea lion males have a huge mane-like neck that earned the species its 'lion' name, and some hunt penguins and fur seal pups.

name: South China Sea
fact: The South China Sea is a marginal sea of the western Pacific crossed by roughly a third of the world's shipping.

name: South Equatorial Current
fact: The South Equatorial Current flows westward along the equator, and in the Atlantic it splits on the coast of Brazil to feed both the Brazil Current and the Guiana Current.

name: South Georgia
fact: South Georgia is a mountainous, glacier-covered island in the South Atlantic where Ernest Shackleton is buried and millions of king penguins and fur seals breed.

name: South polar skua
fact: The south polar skua breeds on the Antarctic coast, steals penguin eggs and chicks, and has been recorded at the South Pole.

name: South Sandwich Trench
fact: The South Sandwich Trench east of the South Sandwich Islands is the deepest trench in the South Atlantic, reaching about 8,300 metres at the Meteor Deep.

name: South Shetland Trench
fact: The South Shetland Trench north of the Antarctic Peninsula is one of the few ocean trenches in Antarctic waters.

name: Southern blue-ringed octopus
fact: The southern blue-ringed octopus lives in tide pools and shallow reefs of southern Australia and delivers its venom through a bite that is often painless.

name: Southern blue whiting
fact: The southern blue whiting is a cod relative of sub-Antarctic waters fished off New Zealand, Argentina and the Falklands.

name: Southern bluefin tuna
fact: The southern bluefin tuna was fished down to a small fraction of its original numbers and is now ranched in sea pens off South Australia.

name: Southern bottlenose whale
fact: The southern bottlenose whale feeds near the Antarctic ice edge and is one of the most often sighted beaked whales in the Southern Ocean.

name: Southern bull kelp
fact: Southern bull kelp has a honeycomb-like inner flesh that keeps it afloat, and Māori once used its blades as bags to store food.

name: Southern elephant seal
fact: The southern elephant seal is the largest seal and the largest carnivoran, with bulls weighing up to about 4 tonnes.

name: Southern flounder
fact: The southern flounder of the Gulf of Mexico is speared at night by 'floundering' anglers wading the shallows with lights.

name: Southern right whale
fact: Southern right whales 'sail' by holding their tail flukes up in the wind, and they gather to calve off Argentina, South Africa and Australia.

name: Southern right whale dolphin
fact: The southern right whale dolphin has no dorsal fin at all and is strikingly black and white.

name: Southern stingray
fact: Southern stingrays gather in the shallows of Stingray City in the Cayman Islands, where they have been hand-fed by visitors for decades.

name: Sowerby's beaked whale
fact: Sowerby's beaked whale was the first beaked whale described, from an animal stranded in the Moray Firth in Scotland in 1800.

name: Spade-toothed whale
fact: The spade-toothed whale is the rarest whale known; only a handful of specimens have ever been found, and none has been seen alive at sea.

name: Spaghetti eel
fact: Spaghetti eels are extremely thin, worm-like eels of the Indo-Pacific that burrow in sand and are found in rivers as well as the sea.

name: Spanish dancer
fact: The Spanish dancer is a large red nudibranch that swims by flapping its body like a flamenco skirt and lays a red rose-shaped ribbon of eggs.

name: Spanish hogfish
fact: The Spanish hogfish is a purple-and-yellow Caribbean wrasse whose juveniles work as cleaners on larger fish.

name: Spanish mackerel
fact: The Atlantic Spanish mackerel is a spotted, fast-swimming schooling fish of the US east coast and Gulf of Mexico, popular with anglers and on the plate.

name: Spanish shawl
fact: The Spanish shawl is a purple nudibranch of the California coast with orange frills, which it waves while swimming to escape predators.

name: Spanner crab
fact: The spanner crab walks forwards instead of sideways and has flattened claws shaped like spanners, used to dig into sand.

name: Sparkling gourami
fact: The sparkling gourami is a 4-centimetre fish from Southeast Asia that makes audible croaking sounds when courting or fighting.

name: Speckled hind
fact: The speckled hind is a deep-water grouper of the southeastern US, dusted with tiny white spots, so overfished that it is now protected.

name: Spectacled porpoise
fact: The spectacled porpoise has dark rings around its eyes like glasses and lives in cold sub-Antarctic waters, where it is rarely seen alive.

name: Sperm whale
fact: Sperm whales dive over 2 kilometres deep hunting squid and have the largest brain of any animal.

name: Spider crab
fact: European spider crabs pile up in mounds of hundreds during their summer moult and decorate their spiny shells with seaweed.

name: Spine-bellied sea snake
fact: The spine-bellied sea snake is a stout, aggressive sea snake often caught in trawl nets off Australia and Southeast Asia.

name: Spined pygmy shark
fact: The spined pygmy shark is one of the smallest sharks, about 25 centimetres long, and glows from its belly far below the surface.

name: Spinner dolphin
fact: Spinner dolphins leap and spin several times in the air, and rest in shallow bays by day after hunting offshore at night.

name: Spinner shark
fact: Spinner sharks charge up through schools of fish and burst from the water spinning, sometimes turning three times in the air.

name: Spiny chromis
fact: The spiny chromis of the Great Barrier Reef is unusual among reef fish in that both parents guard their young for weeks after hatching.

name: Spiny dogfish
fact: Spiny dogfish carry their pups for up to two years, one of the longest pregnancies of any vertebrate.

name: Spiny lobster
fact: Spiny lobsters have no big claws and march across the seabed in single-file lines of dozens during autumn migrations.

name: Spiny starfish
fact: The spiny starfish of European coasts can reach about 70 centimetres across and is armed with rows of blunt spines ringed by tiny pincers.

name: Splendid toadfish
fact: The splendid toadfish is found only around Cozumel, Mexico, where it hides under coral ledges and whistles to attract mates.

name: Sponge
fact: Sponges are the simplest animals, with no organs or nerves, yet a carnivorous sponge was dredged from 9,990 metres in the Philippine Trench.

name: Sponge crab
fact: Sponge crabs cut a living sponge to size and hold it over their backs with their hind legs as a hat that grows with them.

name: Spot prawn
fact: The spot prawn is the largest shrimp on the North American Pacific coast and is eaten raw as amaebi in sushi bars.

name: Spotted boxfish
fact: Male spotted boxfish are blue with gold spots while females are black with white spots, so different that they were once thought to be separate species.

name: Spotted drum
fact: The spotted drum of the Caribbean has a tall ribbon-like dorsal fin as a juvenile and hides under ledges by day to feed at night.

name: Spotted eagle ray
fact: Spotted eagle rays can leap clear of the water and have a white-spotted back and a whip-like tail armed with venomous spines.

name: Spotted garden eel
fact: The spotted garden eel lives in colonies of hundreds on Indo-Pacific sand slopes, each eel anchored tail-first in its own burrow.

name: Spotted handfish
fact: The spotted handfish of Tasmania walks along the seabed on hand-like fins and is critically endangered, with only a few thousand left.

name: Spotted jelly
fact: Millions of golden jellyfish follow the sun across Palau's Jellyfish Lake each day to feed the algae in their tissues, and their sting is too mild to notice.

name: Spotted ratfish
fact: The spotted ratfish, a chimaera with rabbit-like teeth and a rat-like tail, carries a venomous spine on its back.

name: Spotted seahorse
fact: The spotted seahorse of the Indo-Pacific is one of the species most heavily traded dried for use in traditional medicine.

name: Spotted seal
fact: Spotted seals breed on the sea ice of the Bering and Okhotsk Seas and are closely related to harbour seals.

name: Spotted seatrout
