fact: The spotted seatrout, a drum rather than a trout, makes staccato drumming calls at dusk in spawning season across Gulf of Mexico estuaries.

name: Spotted wobbegong
fact: The spotted wobbegong lies camouflaged on Australian reefs, usually under 2 metres long though reported up to about 3, and has bitten people who stepped on or disturbed it.

name: Sprat
fact: Sprats are tiny herring relatives caught by the hundreds of thousands of tonnes, smoked whole in Baltic countries and tinned as 'brisling sardines'.

name: Squat lobster
fact: Squat lobsters are flattened crab-like relatives of hermit crabs that tuck their tails under their bodies and swarm on deep-sea coral and vent fields.

name: Squid
fact: Squid swim by jet propulsion, squirting water from a flexible funnel, and some species can launch themselves clear of the surface.

name: Squirrelfish
fact: Squirrelfish are red, big-eyed reef fish that hide in caves by day and come out to hunt at night.

name: SS Central America
fact: The SS Central America, the 'Ship of Gold', sank in an 1857 hurricane with tonnes of California gold, and was found in 1988 about 2,200 metres down off the Carolinas.

name: SS Gairsoppa
fact: The SS Gairsoppa, torpedoed in 1941, was found in 2011 about 4,700 metres down, and more than 100 tonnes of silver were recovered from it, the deepest such salvage.

name: SS Rio Grande
fact: The German blockade runner Rio Grande, sunk in 1944, was found in 1996 at 5,762 metres in the South Atlantic and held the record for the deepest shipwreck for decades.

name: SS Thistlegorm
fact: The SS Thistlegorm, a British freighter sunk in the Red Sea in 1941, still holds motorbikes, trucks and locomotives and is among the most dived wrecks anywhere.

name: SS Yongala
fact: The SS Yongala sank in a cyclone off Queensland in 1911 with everyone aboard, and the wreck is now smothered in corals and giant groupers.

name: St Helena
fact: St Helena is a remote volcanic island in the South Atlantic where Napoleon was exiled from 1815 until his death in 1821.

name: St. John's
fact: St. John's, Newfoundland, is the easternmost city in North America and one of the oldest English settlements on the continent.

name: Staghorn coral
fact: Staghorn coral grows fast in antler-like branches, but Caribbean staghorn has declined by more than 90 per cent since the 1980s.

name: Stalked jellyfish
fact: Stalked jellyfish are tiny trumpet-shaped jellyfish that live upside down, glued by a stalk to seaweed and seagrass instead of swimming.

name: Star coral
fact: Star corals build the massive boulders of Caribbean reefs, and their polyps leave star-shaped cups in the skeleton.

name: Star-sucker pygmy octopus
fact: The star-sucker pygmy octopus is the smallest known octopus, about 2.5 centimetres long and weighing less than a gram.

name: Stargazer
fact: Stargazers bury themselves in sand with only their upward-facing eyes showing, and some species can give an electric shock.

name: Starry flounder
fact: The starry flounder can be left- or right-eyed and is named for the star-shaped spiny scales scattered across its skin.

name: Stejneger's beaked whale
fact: Stejneger's beaked whale, also called the Bering Sea beaked whale, lives in cold North Pacific waters and often strands in the Aleutian Islands.

name: Steller sea lion
fact: Steller sea lions are the largest sea lions, with bulls reaching about a tonne, and are named after naturalist Georg Steller.

name: Steller's sea cow
fact: Steller's sea cow, an 8-metre relative of the dugong, was hunted to extinction within about 27 years of its discovery in 1741.

name: Steller's sea eagle
fact: Steller's sea eagle, one of the heaviest eagles in the world, catches salmon and cod along the coasts of Kamchatka and winters in Hokkaido.

name: Stellwagen Bank
fact: Stellwagen Bank, a sandy plateau at the mouth of Massachusetts Bay, is a national marine sanctuary famous for its humpback whale watching.

name: Stethacanthus
fact: Stethacanthus was a small shark of about 360 million years ago whose males carried a flat, anvil-shaped dorsal fin topped with tooth-like scales.

name: Stingray
fact: A stingray's venomous barb is a modified scale on its tail, used only in self-defence when the ray is stepped on or threatened.

name: Stokes's sea snake
fact: Stokes's sea snake is one of the heaviest sea snakes, with a thick body and the longest fangs of any sea snake.

name: Stone crab
fact: Florida stone crabs are fished for their claws alone: a claw is removed and the live crab is returned to the sea to grow a new one.

name: Stonefish
fact: The stonefish is the most venomous fish known, with 13 dorsal spines, and lies half-buried in sand looking exactly like an encrusted rock.

name: Stony coral
fact: Stony corals are the reef builders, each polyp laying down a cup of limestone so that colonies slowly pile up into reefs.

name: Stoplight loosejaw
fact: The stoplight loosejaw shines a red searchlight that most deep-sea animals cannot see, and has a jaw with no floor so it can snap shut faster.

name: Stoplight parrotfish
fact: The stoplight parrotfish of the Caribbean changes from a mottled red-and-brown female phase to a green male with a yellow spot, like a traffic light.

name: Stout infantfish
fact: The stout infantfish of the Great Barrier Reef matures at about 7 to 8 millimetres and weighs about a milligram, one of the smallest and lightest vertebrates.

name: Strait of Bonifacio
fact: The Strait of Bonifacio separates Corsica from Sardinia and is notorious for strong winds and shipwrecks.

name: Strait of Dover
fact: The Strait of Dover is the narrowest part of the English Channel, about 33 kilometres wide, and one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world.

name: Strait of Gibraltar
fact: The Strait of Gibraltar joins the Atlantic to the Mediterranean and is only about 14 kilometres wide at its narrowest, between Spain and Morocco.

name: Strait of Hormuz
fact: The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, and about a fifth of the world's oil passes through it.

name: Strait of Juan de Fuca
fact: The Strait of Juan de Fuca between Washington state and Vancouver Island is named after a Greek sailor, known by his Spanish name Juan de Fuca, who claimed to have found it in 1592.

name: Strait of Magellan
fact: The Strait of Magellan, named after Ferdinand Magellan who sailed through it in 1520, lets ships pass between the Atlantic and Pacific south of mainland South America.

name: Strait of Malacca
fact: The Strait of Malacca between Malaysia and Sumatra is one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world, linking the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea.

name: Strait of Messina
fact: The Strait of Messina between Sicily and mainland Italy is home to the whirlpools behind the legend of Scylla and Charybdis.

name: Strait of Otranto
fact: The Strait of Otranto between Italy and Albania is the gateway from the Ionian Sea into the Adriatic.

name: Strap-toothed whale
fact: Male strap-toothed whales, also called Layard's beaked whales, grow two tusks that curl over the upper jaw and stop the mouth opening more than a few centimetres.

name: Strawberry squid
fact: The strawberry squid has one big eye that looks up for shadows and one small eye that looks down for flashes of light, and skin dotted with photophores.

name: Striped bass
fact: Striped bass spawn in rivers such as the Hudson and the tributaries of Chesapeake Bay and spend their adult lives roaming the Atlantic coast.

name: Striped bonito
fact: The striped bonito of the Indo-Pacific is eaten as sashimi in Japan, where it is called hagatsuo.

name: Striped dolphin
fact: Striped dolphins are fast, acrobatic dolphins with blue-black stripes and are the most common dolphin in the Mediterranean.

name: Striped eel catfish
fact: Juvenile striped eel catfish swarm in tight balls on reefs, and each one carries venomous spines that have caused rare human deaths.

name: Striped marlin
fact: The striped marlin hunts in packs off Baja California, where it herds sardine bait balls at high speed and lights up its stripes as it attacks.

name: Striped mullet
fact: Striped mullet wander freely between the sea, estuaries and completely fresh water, but spawn offshore in the open sea.

name: Striped Raphael catfish
fact: The striped Raphael catfish, a 'talking catfish', squeaks by grinding its pectoral spines and is armoured with a row of sharp plates along each side.

name: Sturgeon
fact: Most sturgeons spend their adult lives in the sea or in large lakes and swim up rivers to spawn, and some live for more than 100 years.

name: Submarine
fact: Nuclear submarines can stay underwater for months at a time, limited only by the food they carry for the crew.

name: Sugar kelp
fact: Sugar kelp has a long, crinkled single blade and gets its name from the sweet white powder, mannitol, that forms on it when dried.

name: Sulphide worm
fact: The sulphide worm chooses to sit in water of about 50 degrees Celsius on vent chimneys, hotter than any other animal has been shown to prefer.

name: Sulu Sea
fact: The Sulu Sea in the south-west Philippines holds the Tubbataha Reefs and is enclosed by Palawan, Borneo and the Sulu Archipelago.

name: Summer flounder
fact: The summer flounder, or fluke, is a left-eyed flatfish prized by anglers on the US east coast and can change colour to match the bottom.

name: Sun coral
fact: Sun coral has no symbiotic algae, so it can grow in dark caves and under piers, opening its bright orange polyps at night to catch plankton.

name: Sunda Shelf
fact: The Sunda Shelf is the drowned extension of mainland South-east Asia, shallow seafloor that linked Borneo, Sumatra and Java to the continent during ice ages.

name: Sunda Strait
fact: The Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra links the Java Sea to the Indian Ocean and holds the volcano Krakatoa.

name: Sunflower sea star
fact: The sunflower sea star has up to 24 arms, speeds along on thousands of tube feet and eats sea urchins, but a wasting disease wiped out most of them after 2013.

name: Supergiant amphipod
fact: The supergiant amphipod grows to about 34 centimetres, around ten times the size of most amphipods, and was caught 7,000 metres down in the Kermadec Trench.

name: Surf clam
fact: The surf clam, hokkigai, is served in sushi with its tip blanched, which turns the foot a bright red.

name: Surfperch
fact: Surfperches of the North American Pacific coast give birth to fully formed live young, which is unusual for a marine fish.

name: Surgeonfish
fact: Surgeonfish are named for the scalpel-like spines at the base of the tail, and they graze algae that would otherwise smother coral.

name: Surtsey
fact: Surtsey is a volcanic island off Iceland that rose from the sea in 1963 and has been off limits to all but scientists ever since.

name: Swamp eel
fact: The Asian swamp eel breathes air, burrows into mud when ponds dry out, and has become an invader of Florida and Georgia wetlands.

name: Sweetlips
fact: Sweetlips are reef fish named for their thick, fleshy lips, and their juveniles often look nothing like the adults.

name: Swell shark
fact: The swell shark glows green under blue light and can gulp water to double its size and wedge itself into a crevice when threatened.

name: Swordfish
fact: Swordfish slash at squid with a flat bill and are among the fastest fish in the sea; their meaty steaks are eaten worldwide and served raw as mekajiki in Japan.

name: Swordtail
fact: The male swordtail grows a long blade from the bottom of its tail that females prefer longer, a classic example of sexual selection.

name: Sydney rock oyster
fact: The Sydney rock oyster has been farmed in New South Wales estuaries since the 1870s, making it Australia's oldest aquaculture industry.

name: Sylvia Earle
fact: Sylvia Earle, nicknamed Her Deepness, set a record in 1979 by walking the sea floor at 381 metres in a pressurised suit and has spent thousands of hours underwater.

name: Synodontis catfish
fact: Synodontis catfish of Africa are called squeakers because they chirp by rubbing their pectoral spines; the featherfin squeaker is an aquarium favourite.

name: Table coral
fact: Table coral grows outward in broad, flat plates that shade the reef below and give small fish a roof to hide under.

name: Tahiti
fact: Tahiti is the largest island of French Polynesia, a volcanic peak ringed by reef, where Captain Cook observed the transit of Venus in 1769.

name: Taimen
fact: The taimen of Siberia and Mongolia is the largest salmonid in the world, reaching about 2 metres and living for more than 50 years.

name: Taiwan Strait
fact: The Taiwan Strait separates Taiwan from mainland China and is about 130 kilometres wide at its narrowest.

name: Tanaid
fact: Tanaids are tiny, shrimp-like crustaceans that build tubes in the mud and are among the commonest animals in deep trench sediments.

name: Tarpon
fact: Tarpon gulp air into a swim bladder that works like a lung, and young tarpon grow up in brackish and freshwater backwaters before moving out to sea.

name: Tasman Sea
fact: The Tasman Sea between Australia and New Zealand is named after the Dutch explorer Abel Tasman, who sailed it in 1642, and is nicknamed the Ditch.

name: Tasmanian giant crab
fact: The Tasmanian giant crab can weigh more than 13 kilograms and has one huge claw; it lives on the edge of the continental shelf off southern Australia.

name: Tasmanian giant freshwater crayfish
fact: The Tasmanian giant freshwater crayfish is the largest freshwater invertebrate on Earth, once reaching about 6 kilograms, and can live for about 40 years.

name: Tasselled wobbegong
fact: The tasselled wobbegong has a fringe of branching skin lobes around its head, and one was photographed on the Great Barrier Reef with a whole bamboo shark head-first in its jaws.

name: Tautog
fact: The tautog, or blackfish, is a chunky wrasse of the US east coast that sleeps so soundly on the bottom at night that divers can pick it up.

name: Tawny nurse shark
fact: The tawny nurse shark is a docile Indo-Pacific reef shark that sucks prey from crevices and rests in groups in reef caves.

name: Telescope octopus
fact: The telescope octopus is a see-through deep-sea octopus with tubular eyes on stalks that point upward to spot prey against the faint light.

name: Telescopefish
fact: The telescopefish has forward-pointing tubular eyes like a pair of binoculars and can swallow prey longer than itself.

name: Tench
fact: The tench, a slimy olive fish of still European waters, was once believed to heal other fish that rubbed against it.

name: Tern
fact: Terns hover over the water and then plunge head-first to seize small fish just below the surface.

name: Thermaic Gulf
fact: The Thermaic Gulf is the arm of the Aegean at whose head stands Thessaloniki, Greece's second city.

name: Thick-billed murre
fact: Thick-billed murres of Arctic and sub-Arctic seas are among the deepest-diving flying birds, with dives recorded to 150 metres and beyond.

name: Thimble jellyfish
fact: The thumb-sized thimble jellyfish's larvae cause 'sea bather's eruption', an itchy rash under swimsuits along Florida and Caribbean beaches.

name: Thongweed
fact: Thongweed, or sea spaghetti, grows from a small button into straps up to about 2 metres long and is sold fresh as a sea vegetable.

name: Thor Heyerdahl
fact: Thor Heyerdahl sailed the balsa raft Kon-Tiki about 8,000 kilometres across the Pacific in 1947 to show that ancient people could have made such voyages.

name: Thornback ray
fact: The thornback ray, the most common skate around Britain, is covered in thorny spines and lays egg cases known as mermaid's purses.

name: Thorntail stingray
fact: The thorntail stingray of Australia, New Zealand and South Africa carries rows of thorns along its tail and can reach 1.8 metres across.

name: Thorny seahorse
fact: The thorny seahorse is covered in sharp spines and is found across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to Hawaii.

name: Thracian Sea
fact: The Thracian Sea is the northernmost part of the Aegean, off the coasts of Greek Thrace and Macedonia and the island of Thasos.

name: Threadfin butterflyfish
fact: The threadfin butterflyfish has a trailing thread on its dorsal fin and a chevron pattern on its sides; it is one of the most widespread Indo-Pacific butterflyfish.

name: Three-band anemonefish
fact: The three-band anemonefish lives only in the Marshall Islands, where some individuals turn almost completely black.

name: Three-spined stickleback
fact: Many three-spined sticklebacks live at sea and move into fresh water to breed, where the red-bellied male builds a nest and guards the eggs.

name: Thresher shark
fact: Thresher sharks whip their enormous tails, which can be as long as their bodies, to stun fish before eating them.

name: Tidepool sculpin
fact: The tidepool sculpin is a small camouflaged fish that can find its way back to its home pool after being carried to another one.

name: Tiger barb
fact: The tiger barb from Sumatra and Borneo is a striped aquarium favourite that nips fins unless kept in a school of six or more.

name: Tiger grouper
fact: The tiger grouper is a Caribbean grouper with diagonal tiger stripes that visits cleaning stations to have its gills picked clean by gobies.

name: Tiger prawn
fact: The giant tiger prawn grows to about 33 centimetres, one of the largest prawns, and has escaped from farms to invade the Gulf of Mexico.

name: Tiger puffer
fact: The tiger puffer, torafugu, is the most prized fugu; its liver and ovaries hold a deadly poison, so only licensed chefs in Japan may prepare it as sashimi.

name: Tiger shark
fact: Young tiger sharks carry the dark stripes that give them their name, and the stripes fade as the shark matures.

name: Tiger shovelnose catfish
fact: The tiger shovelnose catfish of South America has a long flat snout and bold black stripes, and can grow to over a metre long.

name: Tiger tail seahorse
fact: The tiger tail seahorse of South-East Asia is named for the dark bands on its tail and, with the common seahorse, makes up most of the Philippine seahorse catch.

name: Tilapia
fact: Tilapia is a freshwater fish farmed in warm ponds worldwide and is now one of the most eaten fish on earth; it was raised in ancient Egypt.

name: Tinker's butterflyfish
fact: Tinker's butterflyfish is a deep-reef butterflyfish from Hawaii, white with a bold black triangle, so rare that it fetches high prices from aquarists.

name: Titan triggerfish
fact: The titan triggerfish guards its nest fiercely and will charge and bite divers who swim into the cone-shaped territory above its eggs.

name: Titanic
fact: The Titanic lies in two main pieces about 3,800 metres down in the North Atlantic, where Robert Ballard's team found it in 1985.

name: Tokyo Bay
fact: Tokyo Bay, the harbour of Tokyo and Yokohama, is where Commodore Perry's black ships arrived in 1853 to open Japan to trade.

name: Tomato clownfish
fact: The tomato clownfish is a red-orange anemonefish with a single white head bar that lives in bubble-tip anemones in the western Pacific.

name: Tomopteris
fact: Tomopteris is a transparent swimming worm of the open ocean and one of the very few animals able to make yellow light.

name: Tonga
fact: Tonga is a kingdom of about 170 islands in the South Pacific, and the Tonga Trench off its coast is the second-deepest in the world.

name: Tonga Trench
fact: The Tonga Trench is the second-deepest trench on Earth, reaching about 10,800 metres at the Horizon Deep.

name: Tongue-eating louse
fact: The tongue-eating louse is an isopod that enters a fish through its gills, drains the blood from its tongue, and then takes the tongue's place.

name: Tonguefish
fact: Tonguefish are tongue-shaped flatfish with both eyes on the left side, and one species lives beside hydrothermal vents in the Pacific.

name: Top shell
fact: Top shells are cone-shaped grazing snails of rocky shores that scrape seaweed and algal film from the rocks.

name: Tope
fact: The tope, or school shark, was heavily fished for its vitamin-rich liver oil in the 1940s and can live for over 50 years.

name: Topknot
fact: The topknot is a small, rough-scaled flatfish of rocky shores that clings upside-down beneath ledges rather than lying on sand.

name: Torch coral
fact: Torch coral has long, flowing tentacles tipped with glowing knobs and is a favourite of reef aquarists.

name: Torres Strait
fact: Torres Strait between Australia and New Guinea is named after the Spanish navigator Luis Váez de Torres, who sailed through it in 1606.

name: Totoaba
fact: The totoaba, a drum of the Gulf of California, makes booming calls with its swim bladder, the organ now smuggled as a delicacy, which has driven it close to extinction.

name: Transparent goby
fact: The transparent goby is a see-through, finger-length fish of European coasts that lives only a year and is eaten by the plateful as whitebait in Italy and Spain.

name: Transpolar Drift
fact: The Transpolar Drift carries sea ice from Siberia across the North Pole towards Greenland, and it carried Nansen's ship Fram across the Arctic.

name: Trawler
fact: A trawler catches fish by dragging a large net, the trawl, through the water or along the seabed behind it.

name: Trichodesmium
fact: Trichodesmium, or sea sawdust, is a cyanobacterium that forms floating brown rafts and pulls nitrogen from the air to fertilise the tropical ocean.

name: Trieste
fact: The bathyscaphe Trieste carried Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh to the bottom of the Challenger Deep in 1960, the first crewed dive to the ocean's deepest point.

name: Triggerfish
fact: A triggerfish locks itself into a crevice at night by raising a dorsal spine that can only be released by a second, smaller trigger spine.

name: Trilobite
fact: Trilobites crawled the seafloor for about 270 million years and were among the first animals with complex eyes before dying out 252 million years ago.

name: Trimmatom nanus
fact: Trimmatom nanus, a goby of the Chagos Islands and Maldives, matures at under 1 centimetre and held the record as the smallest vertebrate from 1981 to 2004.

name: Triops
fact: Triops tadpole shrimp hatch in temporary pools from eggs that can wait years in dry dust, and tadpole shrimp that look much like them were already around more than 200 million years ago.

name: Tripletail
fact: The tripletail floats on its side under buoys and weed in the Gulf of Mexico, pretending to be a drifting leaf.

name: Tripod fish
fact: The tripod fish stands motionless on the abyssal floor on three stiff fin rays up to a metre long, facing the current with its mouth open.

name: Trireme
fact: The trireme was the ancient Greek warship rowed by three banks of oarsmen, which won the Battle of Salamis in 480 BC.

name: Tristan da Cunha
fact: Tristan da Cunha is the most remote inhabited island in the world, with about 250 people living more than 2,000 kilometres from the nearest inhabited land.

name: Triton's trumpet
fact: The Triton's trumpet is a huge sea snail that preys on crown-of-thorns starfish, and its shell has been blown as a horn for centuries.

name: Trout
fact: Several trout, including brown and rainbow trout, have sea-run forms that feed in the ocean and return to rivers to spawn.

name: True's beaked whale
fact: True's beaked whale is named after Frederick True, an American museum curator, and was first filmed underwater in the Azores in 2017.

name: Trumpetfish
fact: The trumpetfish hangs vertically among sea fans and shadows larger fish to sneak up on its prey.

name: Tsugaru Strait
fact: The Tsugaru Strait separates Honshu from Hokkaido and is crossed by the Seikan Tunnel, one of the longest rail tunnels in the world.

name: Tuamotu Islands
fact: The Tuamotus are the largest chain of coral atolls in the world, about 80 low islands strung across French Polynesia.

name: Tubbataha Reef
fact: The Tubbataha Reefs in the Philippines' Sulu Sea are two coral atolls so rich in life that they were made a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Tube anemone
fact: Tube anemones live inside a slimy tube buried in sand and can withdraw their two rings of long tentacles in a flash when disturbed.

name: Tucuxi
fact: The tucuxi is a small grey dolphin that lives in the Amazon river system yet looks like a miniature bottlenose rather than a river dolphin.

name: Tugboat
fact: Tugboats are small but extremely powerful, built to push and pull ships many times their own size in and out of harbours.

name: Tuna
fact: Tunas are warm-blooded, torpedo-shaped sprinters among the fastest fish in the sea; in Japan tuna is maguro, the most popular sushi fish of all.

name: Turbot
fact: Turbot are prized food fish with a nearly circular body and can change their colour to match the gravel they lie on.

name: Turneffe Atoll
fact: Turneffe Atoll off Belize is a large coral atoll whose mangrove islands and seagrass lagoons shelter manatees, crocodiles and bonefish.

name: Turtle barnacle
fact: Turtle barnacles settle on the shells of sea turtles and ride with them, filtering food from the water as the turtle swims.

name: Turtle grass
fact: Turtle grass is the dominant seagrass of the Caribbean, grazed by green turtles and manatees.

name: Turtle-headed sea snake
fact: The turtle-headed sea snake has almost no teeth and feeds only on fish eggs, which it scrapes from the reef.

name: Tusk shell
fact: Tusk shells are molluscs with a tapering tubular shell open at both ends, living head-down in sand.

name: Tuvalu
fact: Tuvalu is a nation of nine low coral atolls in the Pacific whose highest point is only a few metres above sea level.

name: Two-banded anemonefish
fact: The Red Sea clownfish, with two white bars on an orange body, is found only in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

name: Tylosaurus
fact: Tylosaurus, a mosasaur up to about 13 metres long, rammed prey with its bony snout in the shallow sea that once covered Kansas.

name: Tyrrhenian Sea
fact: The Tyrrhenian Sea, between Italy's west coast, Sardinia, Corsica and Sicily, is named after the Tyrrhenians, the Greek name for the Etruscans.

name: Umiak
fact: The umiak is a large open skin boat of the Inuit, rowed or paddled by several people and used for hunting whales and moving families along the coast.

name: Unicornfish
fact: Unicornfish are large surgeonfish with a horn on the forehead that graze on brown seaweeds on Indo-Pacific reefs.

name: Upside-down catfish
fact: The upside-down catfish of the Congo basin habitually swims belly-up to feed at the surface, and its belly is darker than its back as a result.

name: Upside-down jellyfish
fact: The upside-down jellyfish lies on its back in mangrove shallows so the algae in its arms get sunlight, and releases stinging blobs of mucus into the water.

name: Albatross (research ship)
fact: The Albatross, launched in 1882, is often called the first ship built specifically for marine research, and it dredged up thousands of new species.

name: USS Arizona
fact: The battleship USS Arizona exploded and sank during the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, and its wreck still leaks oil today.

name: USS Hornet
fact: The carrier USS Hornet, which launched the Doolittle Raid, was sunk in 1942 and found in 2019 about 5,300 metres down near the Solomon Islands.

name: USS Indianapolis
fact: The USS Indianapolis, sunk by a Japanese submarine in 1945 after delivering atomic bomb parts, was found in 2017 about 5,500 metres down in the Philippine Sea.

name: USS Johnston
fact: The destroyer USS Johnston, sunk off Samar in 1944, was surveyed in 2021 at 6,469 metres, briefly the deepest shipwreck ever identified.

name: USS Lexington
fact: The carrier USS Lexington, scuttled after the Battle of the Coral Sea in 1942, was found in 2018 about 3,000 metres down with aircraft still intact on the seabed.

name: USS Liberty wreck
fact: The USS Liberty, torpedoed in 1942 and pushed into the sea by a volcanic eruption in 1963, lies just off the beach at Tulamben in Bali.

name: USS Maine
fact: USS Maine exploded and sank in Havana harbour in 1898, helping to spark the Spanish-American War.

name: USS Monitor
fact: The Civil War ironclad USS Monitor sank in a storm off Cape Hatteras on the last day of 1862; its turret was raised in 2002.

name: USS Samuel B. Roberts
fact: The destroyer escort USS Samuel B. Roberts, sunk off Samar in 1944, was surveyed in 2022 at 6,895 metres, the deepest shipwreck ever identified.

name: USS Scorpion
fact: The nuclear submarine USS Scorpion was lost with 99 crew in May 1968 and lies about 3,000 metres down south-west of the Azores.

name: USS Thresher
fact: The nuclear submarine USS Thresher was lost with 129 people during deep-diving tests in 1963, and its remains lie about 2,600 metres down off New England.

name: USS Yorktown
fact: The aircraft carrier USS Yorktown, sunk at the Battle of Midway in 1942, was found by Robert Ballard in 1998 about 5,000 metres down.

name: Vampire squid
fact: The vampire squid lives in oxygen-poor water around 600 to 900 metres down and, instead of ink, squirts a cloud of glowing mucus at threats.

name: Vancouver Island
fact: Vancouver Island off Canada's west coast is the largest island on the Pacific coast of the Americas.

name: Vanuatu
fact: Vanuatu is a chain of about 80 volcanic islands in the South Pacific, including Tanna with its easily visited active volcano, Mount Yasur.

name: Vaquita
fact: The vaquita, a tiny porpoise of the upper Gulf of California near the Colorado River delta, is the most endangered marine mammal, with perhaps only about 10 left.

name: Vasa
fact: The Swedish warship Vasa sank on its maiden voyage in 1628, minutes after leaving Stockholm, and was raised almost intact in 1961.

name: Vasco da Gama
fact: Vasco da Gama sailed around the Cape of Good Hope to reach India in 1498, opening the sea route from Europe to Asia.

name: Veined rapa whelk
fact: The veined rapa whelk, a big predatory snail from Japan, invaded the Black Sea and later Chesapeake Bay, where it eats oysters and clams.

name: Veined squid
fact: The veined squid is one of the main squid caught around Britain and Ireland, and can hover in place and change colour in an instant.

name: Velvet belly lanternshark
fact: The velvet belly lanternshark glows along its underside and even on its dorsal spines, which may warn predators off.

name: Velvet crab
fact: The velvet crab of European shores has red eyes, a furry shell and a famously aggressive temper, and is caught for Spanish markets.

name: Vent amphipod
fact: Ventiella amphipods swarm in dense clouds around East Pacific vents, feeding on bacterial mats and dead tube worms.

name: Vent anemone
fact: Pale sea anemones fringe the cooler edges of hydrothermal vent fields, catching scraps carried past by the warm, murky water.

name: Vent barnacle
fact: Vent barnacles grow in dense clusters on vent chimneys, with long bristly feeding legs coated in filamentous bacteria that are thought to be part of their diet.

name: Vent clam
fact: The giant white vent clam grows to more than 25 centimetres, has bright red flesh full of haemoglobin, and gets its food from bacteria in its gills.

name: Vent copepod
fact: Dirivultid copepods are found only at hydrothermal vents, where they are often the most numerous animals crawling over tube worms and mussels.

name: Vent crab
fact: Bythograea vent crabs are the top scavengers and predators of East Pacific vent fields, picking over tube worms, mussels and dead fish.

name: Vent limpet
fact: Tiny Lepetodrilus limpets carpet tube worms and mussels at vents by the thousand, grazing the bacterial film that coats everything.

name: Vent mussel
fact: Vent mussels pack their gills with bacteria that feed them from the vent chemicals, forming beds thousands strong around warm vents and seeps.

name: Vent octopus
fact: The vent octopus is a small, pale, nearly blind octopus found only around hydrothermal vents on the East Pacific Rise.

name: Vent scale worm
fact: Branchipolynoe scale worms live inside the shells of living vent mussels, with special blood that stores oxygen for when the vent water turns foul.

name: Vent sea spider
fact: Sericosura sea spiders cluster by the hundred on vent chimneys, sucking up bacterial mats with a tube-like proboscis.

name: Vent shrimp
fact: Rimicaris vent shrimp swarm in thousands on Mid-Atlantic vent chimneys and have no normal eyes, only a light-sensing patch on the back that detects the vents' faint glow.

name: Vent spaghetti worm
fact: Vent spaghetti worms are acorn worms that drape themselves over rocks in tangled strands at the Galápagos Rift vents, mopping bacteria off the surface.

name: Vent squat lobster
fact: Munidopsis squat lobsters, pale and nearly blind, crawl in crowds around the cooler fringes of vent fields, scavenging whatever drifts their way.

name: Vent tonguefish
fact: Symphurus thermophilus is a flatfish that lives in crowds at volcanic vents of the western Pacific, resting on crusts of solid sulphur beside pools of the molten stuff.

name: Venus' flower basket
fact: The Venus' flower basket is a lattice-like glass sponge in which a pair of shrimp live trapped for life, which is why dried ones are given as wedding gifts in Japan.

name: Venus flytrap anemone
fact: The deep-sea Venus flytrap anemone folds its tentacled disc shut around prey, like the plant it is named after.

name: Venus girdle
fact: The Venus girdle is a ribbon-shaped, transparent comb jelly up to about 1.5 metres long that ripples through the water like a strip of glass.

name: Vermilion snapper
fact: The vermilion snapper, or beeliner, is a slim red snapper relative of the southeastern US that often ends up sold as red snapper.

name: Victor Vescovo
fact: Victor Vescovo became the first person to reach the deepest point of all five oceans, completing the Five Deeps Expedition in 2019.

name: Vigo
fact: Vigo, in Galicia, is one of the biggest fishing ports in the world, landing fish from fleets that work the Atlantic as far away as the Falklands.

name: Violet sea snail
fact: The violet sea snail cannot swim: it hangs upside down from a raft of mucus bubbles and drifts until it bumps into a by-the-wind sailor to eat.

name: Viper dogfish
fact: The viper dogfish has needle-like fangs on jaws it can thrust forward, and it glows along its belly in the deep waters off Japan.

name: Viperfish
fact: The viperfish's fangs are so long they do not fit inside its mouth, and it has been recorded deeper than 4,000 metres.

name: Vityaz Trench
fact: The Vityaz Trench north of Fiji is named after the Soviet research ship Vityaz, which surveyed the Pacific's deepest trenches in the 1950s.

name: Viviparous eelpout
fact: The viviparous eelpout of the North and Baltic seas gives birth to fully formed live young, rare among bony fish.

name: Wadden Sea
fact: The Wadden Sea is a shallow, tidal stretch of the North Sea with the world's largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats.

name: Wahoo
fact: The wahoo is a long, razor-toothed member of the mackerel family and one of the fastest fish in the sea; Hawaiians call it ono, meaning delicious.

name: Wakame
fact: Wakame is the brown seaweed in miso soup and seaweed salad; outside Asia it is an invasive species that spread on the hulls of ships.

name: Walking catfish
fact: The walking catfish can breathe air and wriggle across land between ponds, which helped it spread as an invasive species in Florida.

name: Wallago
fact: The wallago, or freshwater shark of South Asia, is a long, big-mouthed predatory catfish that can exceed 1.5 metres.

name: Walleye
fact: Walleye is the most popular eating fish of the Great Lakes region and the state fish of Minnesota.

name: Walrus
fact: Walruses use their tusks to haul themselves onto ice, and a big male can weigh over 1,500 kilograms.

name: Walter Munk
fact: Walter Munk, called the Einstein of the oceans, predicted surf conditions for the D-Day landings and explained how ocean waves travel across whole oceans.

name: Walvis Bay
fact: Walvis Bay on the coast of Namibia is a natural deep-water harbour whose name means whale bay in Afrikaans.

name: Walvis Ridge
fact: The Walvis Ridge is a long volcanic ridge running from the Namibian coast towards Tristan da Cunha, formed by a hotspot as the South Atlantic opened.

name: Wandering albatross
fact: The wandering albatross has the longest wingspan of any living bird, up to about 3.5 metres, and can circle the Southern Ocean on a single foraging trip.

name: Warsaw grouper
fact: The Warsaw grouper is a huge grouper of deep rocky ledges in the western Atlantic, reaching over 2 metres, with an unusually tall second dorsal spine.

name: Weakfish
fact: The weakfish is a drum of the US Atlantic coast that drums loudly during spawning; its name refers to its tender mouth, which tears on hooks.

name: Weather loach
fact: The weather loach burrows into mud to survive drought and gets its name from becoming restless when the air pressure drops before a storm.

name: Weddell Sea
fact: The Weddell Sea off Antarctica is named after the British sealer James Weddell, who sailed into it in 1823, and its pack ice crushed Shackleton's ship Endurance in 1915.

name: Weddell seal
fact: Weddell seals live further south than any other mammal, under the fast ice of Antarctica, and can dive for over an hour.

name: Weedy sea dragon
fact: The male weedy sea dragon carries the pink eggs stuck to the underside of his tail, and the species is the marine emblem of the Australian state of Victoria.

name: Weever fish
fact: The weever fish buries itself in sand with only its venomous black dorsal fin showing, and is the most common cause of fish stings on British beaches.

name: Wels catfish
fact: The wels catfish of European rivers can grow to over 2.5 metres and has been filmed lunging onto the bank to snatch pigeons.

name: West African manatee
fact: The West African manatee lives in coastal lagoons and rivers from Senegal to Angola and is the least-studied of the sirenians.

name: West Australian Current
fact: The West Australian Current is the cold northward flow on the eastern side of the Indian Ocean gyre, offshore of the warm Leeuwin Current.

name: Whale
fact: Baleen whales have no teeth; they gulp or skim water and strain out krill and small fish through fringed plates of keratin in their jaws.

name: Whale barnacle
fact: Whale barnacles grow embedded in the skin of humpback and grey whales, riding along for a free supply of plankton-rich water.

name: Whale louse
fact: Whale lice are not lice but crustaceans that cling to the skin folds and rough patches of whales, especially right whales.

name: Whale shark
fact: The whale shark is the largest fish alive, growing to over 12 metres while feeding on plankton and small fish.

name: Essex
fact: The whaleship Essex was rammed and sunk by a sperm whale in the Pacific in 1820, inspiring Herman Melville's Moby-Dick.

name: Whelk
fact: Common whelks are scavenging and predatory sea snails of the North Atlantic, and their spongy egg masses wash up as 'sea wash balls'.

name: Whip coral goby
fact: The whip coral goby is a tiny fish that spends its whole life clinging to a single strand of whip coral.

name: Whip-lash squid
fact: Whip-lash squid hover over the deep seabed and trail two long, sticky tentacles covered in tiny suckers to catch small prey.

name: White abalone
fact: The white abalone of California was the first marine invertebrate listed as endangered in the USA after divers stripped it from the reefs.

name: White bass
fact: White bass are silver schooling fish of North American lakes and rivers that boil at the surface when chasing shad.

name: White-beaked dolphin
fact: The white-beaked dolphin is a robust cold-water dolphin that ranges north into Arctic waters off Greenland, Svalbard and Norway.

name: White-bonnet anemonefish
fact: The white-bonnet anemonefish, with a white cap on its head, is a natural hybrid between the orange skunk clownfish and the orange-fin anemonefish.

name: White-clawed crayfish
fact: The white-clawed crayfish, Britain's only native crayfish, is being wiped out by a fungal plague carried by invasive American signal crayfish.

name: White Cloud Mountain minnow
fact: The White Cloud Mountain minnow is a 4-centimetre fish discovered in 1932 on a mountain near Guangzhou, now almost extinct in the wild while thriving in aquariums.

name: White marlin
fact: The white marlin is the smallest Atlantic marlin, a fast, acrobatic billfish prized by anglers off the US east coast.

name: White seabass
fact: The white seabass of the Californian coast is a large drum, not a bass, and is a prize for kayak anglers in the kelp beds.

name: White-spotted octopus
fact: The white-spotted octopus hunts at night, flushing bright red with white spots and reaching its long arms deep into coral crevices.

name: White-spotted puffer
fact: The white-spotted puffer is a common Indo-Pacific puffer with white spots on a grey body and white stripes on the belly.

name: White sturgeon
fact: The white sturgeon of the Fraser and Columbia rivers is North America's largest freshwater fish, reaching about 6 metres.

name: White-tailed eagle
fact: The white-tailed eagle, one of Europe's largest birds of prey, snatches fish from the sea surface and was reintroduced to Scotland in the 1970s.

name: Whiteleg shrimp
fact: The whiteleg shrimp is the most farmed shrimp in the world, raised in ponds from Ecuador to Vietnam and sold by the million as supermarket prawns.

name: White's seahorse
fact: White's seahorse, or Sydney seahorse, lives in New South Wales estuaries and clings to the shark nets of Sydney's swimming enclosures.

name: Whitetip reef shark
fact: Whitetip reef sharks can pump water over their gills while resting, so they spend the day lying motionless in reef caves.

name: Whiting
fact: Whiting is a small, soft-fleshed relative of cod that has long been a cheap staple of British chip shops.

name: Whydah Gally
fact: The pirate ship Whydah Gally sank in a storm off Cape Cod in 1717; its wreck, found in 1984, was the first authenticated pirate shipwreck.

name: Wide-band anemonefish
fact: The wide-band anemonefish lives only around Lord Howe Island and eastern Australia, with wide white bars that merge on some fish.

name: Wigeon
fact: The wigeon is a dabbling duck that grazes on eelgrass in estuaries in winter, often alongside brant geese.

name: Wilhelm Gustloff
fact: The German liner Wilhelm Gustloff was torpedoed in the Baltic in January 1945; with roughly 9,000 dead, it is the deadliest sinking in history.

name: William Beebe
fact: William Beebe descended more than 900 metres off Bermuda in the bathysphere in 1934 and was the first scientist to watch deep-sea animals alive in their own world.

name: Wilson's storm petrel
fact: Wilson's storm petrel patters across the water on dangling feet, picking krill and oil from the surface, and may be the most numerous wild bird on Earth.

name: Windowpane flounder
fact: The windowpane flounder is so thin that light passes through its body when it is held up to the sun.

name: Windward Passage
fact: The Windward Passage between Cuba and Haiti connects the Atlantic to the Caribbean and is the main shipping route from the US east coast to the Panama Canal.

name: Winged kelp
fact: Winged kelp, or alaria, has a long blade with a midrib and is farmed in the North Atlantic and eaten as 'Atlantic wakame'.

name: Winghead shark
fact: The winghead shark has the widest head of any hammerhead, nearly half as wide as the shark is long.

name: Winter flounder
fact: Winter flounder move inshore in winter and carry antifreeze proteins in their blood to survive icy New England waters.

name: Witch
fact: The witch is a long, thin, right-eyed flounder of deep muddy seabeds, sold as Torbay sole in Britain and grey sole in North America.

name: Wobbegong
fact: Wobbegongs are flattened, carpet-patterned sharks that lie in wait on reefs, with a fringe of skin flaps hiding their mouths.

name: Wolf eel
fact: Wolf eel pairs share a den for life, and both parents coil around their egg mass, guarding it for months.

name: Wolffish
fact: The Atlantic wolffish has a mouthful of fangs for crushing crabs and sea urchins, and makes its own antifreeze to live in near-freezing water.

name: Wrasse
fact: Many wrasses dive into the sand to sleep at night, and most species start life as females and later change into males.

name: Wreckfish
fact: The Atlantic wreckfish, or stone bass, is a big deep-water sea bass whose young shelter under floating wreckage and driftwood.

name: Wunderpus
fact: The wunderpus of Indonesian sand flats has a pattern of white bands so individual that scientists can identify each animal by its markings.

name: Xenophyophore
fact: Xenophyophores are single cells up to about 10 centimetres across that build mud shells on the seabed, and were found at 10,641 metres in the Mariana Trench.

name: Xiphactinus
fact: Xiphactinus was a 5-metre fanged fish of the Cretaceous, and one famous fossil contains a whole 2-metre fish swallowed just before it died.

name: Yabby
fact: The yabby of Australian creeks and farm dams digs so deep into mud to survive drought that its scientific name means 'destroyer'.

name: Yacht
fact: The word yacht comes from the Dutch 'jacht', meaning hunt, from the fast, light ships once used to chase pirates.

name: Yamato
fact: The Yamato, the largest battleship ever built, was sunk by US aircraft in April 1945 and lies in two main pieces about 340 metres down off Kyushu.

name: Yangtze finless porpoise
fact: The Yangtze finless porpoise is the only porpoise that lives entirely in fresh water and numbers only around a thousand.

name: Yap Trench
fact: The Yap Trench lies south-west of the Mariana Trench near the island of Yap and reaches about 8,500 metres deep.

name: Yellow-bellied sea snake
fact: The yellow-bellied sea snake is the most widespread snake on Earth, drifting across the Pacific and Indian Oceans and never coming ashore.

name: Yellow boxfish
fact: Young yellow boxfish are bright yellow cubes with black spots, and Mercedes-Benz modelled a concept car on their boxy shape in 2005.

name: Yellow clown goby
fact: The yellow clown goby is a 3.5-centimetre reef fish that lives among the branches of Acropora corals and produces a bitter skin mucus to deter predators.

name: Yellow perch
fact: The yellow perch, with its dark vertical bars, is the fish most children in North America catch first from a lake.

name: Yellow Sea
fact: The Yellow Sea between China and Korea takes its name from the yellow silt carried into it by the Yellow River.

name: Yellow stingray
fact: The yellow stingray is a small, speckled ray of the Caribbean that can change its colour to blend in with the sand.

name: Yellow tang
fact: The yellow tang is a bright lemon-yellow surgeonfish from Hawaii, one of the most popular marine aquarium fish; Hawaii now breeds them in captivity.

name: Yelloweye rockfish
fact: The yelloweye rockfish of the North Pacific grows slowly and can live for more than 100 years, which makes it very easy to overfish.

name: Yellowfin sole
fact: The yellowfin sole of the Bering Sea supports the largest flatfish fishery in the world by weight.

name: Yellowfin tuna
fact: Yellowfin tuna, sold as ahi, is a fast, warm-water tuna with long yellow fins that is the common tuna in poke and sushi outside Japan.

name: Yellowhead jawfish
fact: The male yellowhead jawfish holds the eggs in his mouth for over a week, spitting them out briefly to turn them, and cannot eat until they hatch.

name: Yellowmargin triggerfish
fact: The yellowmargin triggerfish digs large nest pits in sand and guards them as fiercely as its cousin the titan triggerfish.

name: Yellowtail
fact: Yellowtail, or hamachi, is a fast-swimming Japanese amberjack farmed in large numbers in Japan and served raw for its buttery flesh.

name: Yellowtail amberjack
fact: The yellowtail amberjack is a prized game fish off California, Baja and Australia and is served as hiramasa in sushi bars, distinct from the Japanese yellowtail sold as hamachi.

name: Yellowtail blue damsel
fact: The yellowtail blue damsel is a deep blue damselfish with a bright yellow tail, one of the most popular and peaceful damselfish for aquariums.

name: Yellowtail damselfish
fact: The juvenile yellowtail damselfish of the Caribbean is dark blue sprinkled with electric-blue spots, earning it the name jewelfish.

name: Yellowtail snapper
fact: The yellowtail snapper of the Caribbean has a yellow stripe running into a deeply forked yellow tail and often hovers in midwater above the reef.

name: Yeti crab
fact: The yeti crab, discovered in 2005 at vents south of Easter Island, has hairy arms coated in bacteria that it is thought to feed on.

name: Yucatán Channel
fact: The Yucatán Channel between Mexico and Cuba links the Caribbean Sea to the Gulf of Mexico and carries the current that becomes the Gulf Stream.

name: Zander
fact: The zander is Europe's largest perch relative and lives in rivers, lakes and the brackish Baltic Sea.

name: Zealandia
fact: Zealandia is a continent-sized block of crust around New Zealand of which about 94 percent lies underwater, drowned after it split from Gondwana.

name: Zebra moray
fact: The zebra moray, banded in dark brown and white, has flat crushing teeth and feeds almost entirely on crabs and sea urchins.

name: Zebra mussel
fact: Zebra mussels arrived in the Great Lakes in ships' ballast water from the Black and Caspian seas in the 1980s and now clog pipes across North America.

name: Zebra pleco
fact: The zebra pleco, a striking black-and-white striped catfish, lives only in a stretch of Brazil's Xingu River and is threatened by the Belo Monte dam.

name: Zebra seahorse
fact: The zebra seahorse, striped black and white, is known only from the waters of northern Australia.

name: Zebra shark
fact: Zebra sharks are born with dark stripes that break up into leopard-like spots as they grow, so adults are often called leopard sharks in Australia.

name: Zebra urchin crab
fact: The zebra crab lives among the spines of sea urchins, where its bold black and white stripes hide it from predators.

name: Zebrafish
fact: The zebrafish, a striped minnow about 3 to 4 centimetres long, is one of science's favourite lab animals because its transparent embryos develop in full view.

name: Zheng He
fact: Zheng He commanded huge Chinese treasure fleets on seven voyages across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433.

name: Zombie worm
fact: Zombie worms have no mouth or stomach; they bore roots into whale bones on the seabed and let bacteria digest the fat, and the dwarf males live inside the females.

name: Zooplankton
fact: Zooplankton are the animal drifters of the sea, from copepods to jellyfish, and each night they rise towards the surface in the largest migration on Earth.
